In that case mā remains a relative pronoun, and illā is in the position of a qualifier for a definite noun. His making "fataranī" (فَطَرَنِي) a relative clause after alladhī is a reminder that no one is worshipped and no one deserves worship except the Creator of the servants.

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 43, verse 19–32 (part 2 of 2):

﴿فَإنَّهُ سَيَهْدِينِ﴾: i.e., He will continue My guidance. Elsewhere: ﴿الَّذِي خَلَقَنِي فَهو يَهْدِينِ﴾ [al-Shu'ara’: 78], so He is his guide in the future and in the present. The pronoun in "jaʿalaha" (He made it) with the nominative (marfu') refers to Abraham, and it was said that it refers to God. The pronoun in the accusative refers to the word of tawhid (monotheism) that he uttered, which is his saying: ﴿إنَّنِي بَراءٌ مِمّا تَعْبُدُونَ﴾ ﴿إلّا الَّذِي فَطَرَنِي﴾. Qatada, Mujahid and al-Suddi said: it is "There is no god but Allah" (la ilaha illa Allah), even though it has not been mentioned explicitly, because the expression includes it. Ibn Zayd said: it is the word of Islam, based on His saying: ﴿ومِن ذُرِّيَّتِنا أُمَّةً مُسْلِمَةً لَكَ﴾ [al-Baqara: 128], ﴿إذْ قالَ لَهُ رَبُّهُ أسْلِمْ قالَ أسْلَمْتُ﴾ [al-Baqara: 131], ﴿هُوَ سَمّاكُمُ المُسْلِمِينَ﴾ [al-Hajj: 78]. Humayd ibn Qays read "kilmatan" with a kasra on the kaf and a sukun on the lam. It was also read "fi ʿaqibihi" with a sukun on the qaf, meaning in his offspring (dhurriyyatihi). It was also read "fi ʿaqibihi" meaning among his descendants, i.e., his successors. So there will always remain among them those who affirm the oneness of Allah and call to His monotheism. ﴿لَعَلَّهم﴾: i.e., perhaps those among them who associated partners will return through the supplication of those among them who affirmed the oneness. The majority read ﴿بَلْ مَتَّعْتُ﴾ with the first-person ta' (of the speaker), and the indication of "these" (هَؤُلاءِ) is to the Quraysh and those of the Arabs who were from the descendants of Abraham (peace be upon him). When He said "in his offspring," He said: but I gave enjoyment to these and blessed them in their disbelief, so they are not among those in whom the word of tawhid is continued. Qatada and al-A'mash read "bal matta'ta" with the ta' of address, and Ya'qub related it from Nafi'. The author of al-Lawami (Sahib al-Lawami) said: it is from Abraham's (peace be upon him) intimate conversation with his Lord, Exalted. The apparent reading is that it is from the intimate conversation of Muhammad (ﷺ), i.e., he said: "O my Lord, rather You have given enjoyment." Al-A'mash read "matta'na" with the plural of majesty (nun al-ʿazama), and this supports the majority reading.

﴿حَتّى جاءَهُمُ الحَقُّ﴾, which is the Qur'an, ﴿ورَسُولٌ مُبِينٌ﴾, which is Muhammad (ﷺ). Al-Zamakhshari said: If you ask: what is the reasoning of one who read "bal matta'ta" with a fatha on the ta'? I say: It is as if Allah, Exalted, objected concerning His own essence in His saying: ﴿وجَعَلَها كَلِمَةً باقِيَةً في عَقِبِهِ لَعَلَّهم يَرْجِعُونَ﴾, and so He said: rather I gave them enjoyment with what I gave them enjoyment of, namely long life and abundance in provision, until that occupied them away from the word of tawhid. He intended by this an extended rebuke of them, because when He gives them enjoyment with increased blessings, it is incumbent upon them to make that a cause for increased gratitude and steadfastness upon tawhid and faith, not that they should associate partners with Him and set up rivals to Him. Its example is: a man complains of the harm done by one who has done him good, then he turns to himself and says: "You are the cause of that by your kindness and benevolence." His purpose with this speech is to reproach the wrongdoer, not to disparage his action. If you say: He made the coming of the truth and the Messenger the endpoint of the enjoyment, then followed it with His saying: ﴿ولَمّا جاءَهُمُ الحَقُّ قالُوا هَذا سِحْرٌ﴾, what is the method and purport of this arrangement? I say: What is meant by enjoyment is that which is its cause, namely their preoccupation with enjoyment away from tawhid and its requirements. So He, Mighty and Exalted, said: rather they were occupied away from tawhid ﴿حَتّى جاءَهُمُ الحَقُّ ورَسُولٌ مُبِينٌ﴾, and by this endpoint it is imagined that they awoke from their heedlessness at that point, because it calls for awakening.

Then He began their story at the coming of the truth, saying: ﴿ولَمّا جاءَهُمُ الحَقُّ﴾, they came with something worse than their heedlessness in which they were (p-13), namely that they added to their polytheism the opposition to the truth, the obstinacy against and enmity toward the Messenger, the disdain for the Book of Allah and His laws, the persistence in the deeds of disbelievers, and the challenge to the wisdom of Allah in choosing Muhammad (ﷺ) from among the people of his time, by their saying: ﴿لَوْلا نُزِّلَ هَذا القُرْآنُ عَلى رَجُلٍ مِنَ القَرْيَتَيْنِ عَظِيمٍ﴾, which is the extreme in disfiguring the image of their affair. End of quote; it is good, but in it there is prolixity. The pronoun in "wa qalu" (and they said) is for the Quraysh; they had considered it far-fetched that Allah would send a messenger from among humans, so the matter of Abraham, Moses, Jesus and other messengers (may Allah bless them) was widely known among them. When they had no way to deny that, they contradicted themselves regarding Muhammad (ﷺ) and said: Why was Muhammad chosen, and why was the Qur'an not sent down to a great man of the two towns? They pointed to one whose rank was great by age, lineage, standing and abundance of wealth. It was read "ʿala rajulin" with a sukun on the jim. "Min al-qaryatayn" means: from one of the two towns. It was said: from a man of the two towns, and they are Mecca and al-Ta'if. Ibn ʿAbbas said: the one from Mecca is al-Walid ibn al-Mughira al-Makhzumi, and from al-Ta'if: Habib ibn ʿAmr ibn ʿUmayr al-Thaqafi. Mujahid said: ʿUtba ibn Rabi'a and Kinana ibn ʿAbd Yalil. Qatada said: al-Walid ibn al-Mughira and ʿUrwa ibn Mas'ud al-Thaqafi. Qatada said: We have been told that no clan of the Quraysh remained without claiming him, and al-Walid ibn al-Mughira was called "the basil of Quraysh," and he used to say: If what Muhammad says were true, it would have been sent down to me or to Ibn Mas'ud, meaning ʿUrwa ibn Mas'ud, who was called Abu Mas'ud.

﴿أهم يَقْسِمُونَ رَحْمَةَ رَبِّكَ﴾? This contains rebuke and wonder at their ignorance, as if it were said: Do the virtues, including prophethood and others, get divided according to their choice and will? Then in the attribution in His saying "the mercy of your Lord" there is an honoring of him (ﷺ), and that this mercy which came to you is none other than from your Lord, who reforms your state and nurtures you. Then Exalted He informed that it is He who apportioned the livelihood among them, so nothing came to anyone except what Exalted He apportioned. If He is the One who undertook that and differentiated among them, and that in worldly affairs which pass away, how then would He not undertake the grave matter, which is sending whom He wills? You have no right to choose who is suitable for that; rather you are incapable of arranging your own affairs. The majority read "maʿishatahum" in the singular, while ʿAbd Allah, al-A'mash, Ibn ʿAbbas and Sufyan read "maʿaishahum" in the plural. The majority read "sukhriyyan" with a damma on the sin, while ʿAmr ibn Maymun, Ibn Muhaysin, Ibn Abi Layla, Abu Raja', al-Walid ibn Muslim and Ibn ʿAmir read it with a kasra, and it is from taskhir, in the sense of enslaving and employing, so that some of them benefit from others and reach their benefits. Had each one undertaken all his tasks by himself, he would not have been able and would have been lost and destroyed. It is unlikely that "sukhriyyan" here is from mockery (al-huzu’), though some have said: i.e., the rich mocks the poor. In His saying "Nahnu qasamna" (We have apportioned), there is discouragement from devoting oneself to the pursuit of the world, and an ease for reliance upon Allah. Muqatil said: We made some to excel over others, so some are leaders and some are led. Qatada said: You find one weak in strength, little in resource, rich in tongue, and he is given expansion; and you find one strong in resource, eloquent in tongue, and he is restricted. Al-Shafi'i, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

Among the proof of decree and its existence
is the misery of the poor and the pleasant life of the fool.

﴿ورَحْمَةُ رَبِّكَ﴾: it was said: prophethood; it was said: guidance and faith. Qatada and al-Suddi said: Paradise is better than what these people gather of the worldly debris, and in this expression is a belittling of the world and what is gathered in it of its goods.

(p-9) And they have made the angels, who are the servants of the Most Merciful, females. Did they witness their creation? Their testimony will be recorded, and they will be questioned. And they say: "Had the Most Merciful willed, we would not have worshipped them." They have no knowledge of that; they only guess. Or have We given them a Book before this, so that they hold fast to it? Rather, they say: "We found our fathers upon a community, and we are guided upon their footsteps." And thus We did not send a warner before you to any town, but its affluent ones said: "We found our fathers upon a community, and we follow in their footsteps." He said: "Even if I brought you something better guided than what you found your fathers upon?" They said: "We disbelieve in what you have been sent with." So We took vengeance on them; so see how was the end of the deniers. And when Abraham said to his father and his people: "Indeed, I am free from what you worship, except He who created me, for He will guide me." And he made it a word remaining among his descendants, that they might return. Rather, I gave enjoyment to these and their fathers until there came to them the truth and a clear messenger. And when the truth came to them, they said: "This is magic, and we disbelieve in it." And they said: "Why was this Qur'an not sent down upon a great man from the two towns?" Is it they who distribute the mercy of your Lord? We have distributed among them their livelihood in the worldly life, and raised some of them above others in degrees, that some of them may take others in service. And the mercy of your Lord is better than what they accumulate.

(p-10) It was not enough for them that they ascribed to Allah a son, and made Him females, and made them (the angels) among the angels. This is from their ignorance of Allah and His attributes, and their belittling of the angels, in that they attributed femininity to them. 

Umar ibn al-Khattab, al-Hasan, Abu Raja', Qatada, Abu Ja'far, Shayba, al-A'raj, al-Ibnan, and Nafi' read: ʿinda al-Raḥmān (عِنْدَ الرَّحْمَنِ), as a zarf (adverbial complement of place/state, "with"), and this is more indicative of elevated rank and nearness of station, in accordance with His saying: ﴿Indeed, those who are with your Lord...﴾ [al-A'raf: 206].

ʿAbd Allah, Ibn ʿAbbas, Ibn Jubayr, ʿAlqama, and the rest of the Seven read: ʿibād al-Raḥmān (عِبادُ الرَّحْمَنِ), as the plural of ʿabd, in accordance with His saying: ﴿Rather, they are honored servants﴾ [al-Anbiya: 26]. Al-A'mash read ʿibāda al-Raḥmān (عِبادَ الرَّحْمَنِ), as a plural, in the accusative case. Ibn Khalawayh related it, and said: "It is likewise in the mushaf (codex) of Ibn Mas'ud." The accusative is governed by an implied verb, meaning: "Those who were created as servants of the Most Merciful, and brought into being as servants of the Most Merciful, females."

Ubayy read ʿabd al-Raḥmān (عَبْدُ الرَّحْمَنِ) in the singular, but its meaning is plural, because it is an ism jins (a noun of genus).

The majority read: ashahidū (أشَهِدُوا), with the interrogative hamza placed before shahidū, as a past tense verb in the active voice, meaning: "Did they attend their creation?" That is not of the kind of testimony which carries the meanings that are sought to be rendered. 

It has been said that the Messenger (ﷺ) asked them: "What makes you know that they are females?" They said: "We heard that from our fathers, and we testify that they did not lie." Then Allah, Exalted, said: ﴿Their testimony will be recorded, and they will be questioned﴾ about it, that is, in the Hereafter.

Nafi' read with a hamza placed before ushhidū (أُشْهِدُوا), a quadriliteral verb in the passive voice, without a madd (lengthening) between the two hamzas. Al-Musayyabi, from him, read with a madd between them. ʿAli ibn Abi Talib, Ibn ʿAbbas, Mujahid, and in the transmission of Abu ʿAmr and Nafi', read with the second hamza softened (tashil), without madd. A group read likewise but with a madd between them. From ʿAli and al-Mufaddal, from ʿAsim, both hamzas are pronounced clearly without madd. Al-Zuhri and others read ushhidū without interrogation, in the passive voice, quadriliteral. It was said: the meaning is by way of interrogation, and the hamza was omitted because the meaning indicates it. It was also said: the clause is a description of the females, that is, "females whose creation was witnessed by them," and they did not claim that they witnessed their creation, but when they claimed, out of their audacity, that they were females, they became as though they claimed that and that they had witnessed their creation.

The majority read: ināthan (إناثًا), and Zayd ibn ʿAli read: unuthan (أُنُثًا), the plural of a plural. It has been said: the meaning of wa-jaʿalū is "named," and they said. The better view is that the meaning is: "and they made their belief about the angels to be females." This interrogation contains mockery of them, and the intended meaning is to show the corruption of their minds, and that their claims are devoid of proof. This is similar to the verse that censures the people of astrology and natures: ﴿I did not call them to witness the creation of the heavens and the earth, nor their own creation﴾ [al-Kahf: 51].

The majority read: sa-tuktabu (سَتُكْتَبُ), with a ta' above, in the passive voice. Shahadatuhum (شَهادَتُهم) with a nominative ending, singular. Al-Zubayri likewise, except with a ya'. Al-Hasan likewise, except with a ta' and as a plural: shahadatihim. Ibn ʿAbbas, Zayd ibn ʿAli, Abu Ja'far, Abu Haywa, Ibn Abi Abla, al-Jahdari, and al-A'raj read with a nun, in the active voice, shahadatuhum in the singular. A group read: sa-yaktubu with a ya' in the active voice, meaning Allah, shahadatahum with a fatha on the ta'. The meaning is: their testimony will be recorded against the angels for their femininity. And they will be questioned. This is a threat.

﴿And they say: "Had the Most Merciful willed, we would not have worshipped them."﴾ The pronoun refers to the angels. Qatada and Muqatil said: "and others." Mujahid said: it refers to the idols. They made the absence of worship conditional upon His will, but worship existed when His will was absent. So the meaning is: He willed worship, and what He willed occurred. They took His granting them respite and His kindness toward them, while they worship other than Him, as proof that He is pleased with that as a religion. The discussion of a similar sentence has already occurred at the end of al-An'am. In the speech there is an ellipsis, meaning: we are not held accountable for that, since it is in accordance with the will of Allah. For this reason He says: ﴿They have no knowledge of that﴾, that is, of what follows from their worship of punishment, ﴿they only guess﴾: that is, they lie. It has been said: the reference of "that" is to their claim that the angels are females. Al-Zamakhshari said: "They are two disbeliefs added to the three disbeliefs: their worship of the angels (p-11) apart from Allah, and their claim that their worship is by His will, as their brethren the Jabriyya say." End of quote. He made the Ahl al-Sunna sisters of the disbelievers who worship the angels, then raised an objection and an answer running according to what he chose from the doctrine of the Mu'tazila, which is explained in his book. When he denied them knowledge that their punishment would be abandoned for worshipping other than Allah, that is, no intellect indicates that, he also denied that revelation indicates it, and said: ﴿Or have We given them a Book﴾ before the revelation of the Qur'an, or before the warning of the messengers, indicating permissibility of their worshipping other than Allah, and that no consequence follows from it. Then Allah, Exalted, informed that they, in that, are imitators of their fathers, and they have no proof from intellect or transmission. The meaning of ʿalā ummatin (عَلى أُمَّةٍ) is: upon a way, a religion, and a custom. So we followed their path, and we are guided in following their footsteps. From this is the saying of Qays ibn al-Khatim:

"We were upon the way of our fathers, and the latter follows the first."

The majority read: ummatin (أُمَّةٍ), with a damma on the hamza. Mujahid and Qutrub said: "upon a religion." Al-Jawhari said: "The ummah is the way, and what is said: 'So-and-so has no ummah,' means he has no religion nor creed." The poet said:

"Can one who has a faith (ummah) be equal to an ingrate?"

The discussion of ummah has already occurred in His saying: ﴿and he remembered after a time﴾ [Yusuf: 45]. Umar ibn ʿAbd al-Aziz, Mujahid, Qatada, and al-Jahdari read with a kasra on the hamza, which is the good way in lexical usage, as opposed to ummah with a damma, as stated by al-Jawhari. Ibn ʿAbbas read: immatin (أمَّةٍ), with a fatha on the hamza, meaning "upon an intention and a state," and the disagreement regarding the second word is like that of the first.

Muqatil related that the verse was revealed concerning al-Walid ibn al-Mughira, Abu Sufyan, Abu Jahl, ʿUtba, and Shayba ibn Abi Rabi'a from Quraysh, meaning that those before them also said it, consoling the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) with that. The mutraf (affluent one) is the pampered one, whom blessings have made insolent, so they preferred the desires and disliked the hardships of obligations.

The majority read: "Qul" (قُلْ), in the imperative. Ibn ʿAmir and Hafs read: "Qala" (قالَ) in the indicative. The majority read: ji'tukum (جِئْتُكم), with the first-person singular ta'. Ubayy, Shayba, Ibn Miqsam, al-Za'farani, Abu Shaykh al-Hunai, and Khalid read: ji'nakum (جِئْناكم), with the first-person plural nun. The apparent reading is that the pronoun in qala or in qul refers to the Messenger, that is: "Say, O Muhammad, to your people: 'Will you follow your fathers? Even if I brought you a religion more guided than the religion upon which you found your fathers?'" This is a rebuke to them, since they follow blindly and do not reflect upon the proofs.

﴿They said: "Indeed, we disbelieve in what you, and the messengers before you, have been sent with."﴾ The address overrides the third person.

﴿So We took vengeance on them﴾ through drought, killing, captivity, and exile.

﴿So see how was the end of﴾ the one who denied you. Ibn ʿAtiyya said: in qala there is a pronoun referring to the warner, and the rest of the verse indicates that "qul" in the reading of whoever reads it is not an imperative to Muhammad (ﷺ), but is rather a narration of what the warner was commanded to say. The word law (لَوْ) in this place seems to be conditional, with the meaning of in (إنْ), as if the meaning of the verse were: "Or if I brought you something clearer and more manifest than what your fathers were upon, your obstinacy and imitation would accompany you." So the disbelievers of the nations who denied their prophets answered then, as they denied Muhammad (ﷺ). What he said is not necessarily fixed; rather, the apparent meaning is what we have mentioned before.

﴿And when Abraham said to his father and his people﴾: and remind the Arabs of the condition of their highest ancestor and his prohibition of worshipping other than Allah, and his singling out of Allah in monotheism and worship, mocking them, so that they might return to the religion of their ancestor, since he was the most honorable of their forefathers and the one upon whose love there is consensus. Also, he (ﷺ) did not imitate his father in worshipping idols, so you should emulate him in abandoning the imitation of your nearest fathers, and return to reflection and following the truth.

The majority read: barāʾun (بَراءٌ), a verbal noun which is used the same for the singular, masculine, and their opposites. It is said: "We are free (al-barāʾ) from you," and this is the dialect of al-ʿĀliya. Al-Za'farani and al-Qawrasi, from Abu Ja'far, and Ibn al-Manadhiri, from Nafi', read: barūʾun with a damma on the bā'. Al-A'mash read: barīʾun, which is the dialect of Najd and its two shaykhs, and it may be pluralized and feminized, like ṭawīlun and ṭiwālun, and karīmun and kirāmun.

Al-A'mash read: innī (إنِّي), with a shadda on the nun, without the nun of protection. The majority read: innanī (إنَّنِي), with two nuns, the first with a shadda.

The apparent view is that His saying ﴿except He who created me﴾ is a disjunctive exception (munqati', a exception not of the same kind), since they did not worship Allah alongside their idols. It has been said: they associated their idols with Him, Exalted, in worship, so it is a connected exception (muttasil). In either case, alladhī is in the accusative position. And if it is a connected exception, mā is inclusive of those who know and those who do not know. Al-Zamakhshari permitted that alladhī be in the genitive, as a substitute for the genitive after min, as if he said: "Indeed I am free from what you worship, except from He who..." and that illā be an adjective meaning "other than," on the basis that mā in mā taʿbudūn is an indefinite qualified noun. The estimate is: "Indeed I am free from gods that you worship, other than He who created me," and this is like His saying: ﴿Had there been in them gods other than Allah, they would both have been ruined﴾ [al-Anbiya: 22]. End of quote.

The substitution is not permissible, because substitution occurs only in non-affirmative contexts: negation, prohibition, and interrogation. Do you not see that what follows illā can serve to empty the governing verb for it? But "innanī barīʾun" is an affirmative sentence, so the governing verb cannot be emptied for alladhī, which is the one "free," in order to be followed by illā. From al-Zamakhshari, the word barīʾ contains the meaning of negation, and yet it is affirmative, and it is not permissible for it to be emptied for what follows illā. As for his estimate of mā as an indefinite qualified noun, he did not keep it as a relative pronoun, because he believed that illā can only be a qualifier for an indefinite noun. This question is disputed among the grammarians: some say that both indefinite and definite nouns may be qualified by it. In that case mā remains a relative pronoun, and illā is in the position of a qualifier for a definite noun. His making "fataranī" (فَطَرَنِي) a relative clause after alladhī is a reminder that no one is worshipped and no one deserves worship except the Creator of the servants.

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 43, verse 19–32 (part 2 of 2):

﴿فَإنَّهُ سَيَهْدِينِ﴾: i.e., He will continue My guidance. Elsewhere: ﴿الَّذِي خَلَقَنِي فَهو يَهْدِينِ﴾ [al-Shu'ara’: 78], so He is his guide in the future and in the present. The pronoun in "jaʿalaha" (He made it) with the nominative (marfu') refers to Abraham, and it was said that it refers to God. The pronoun in the accusative refers to the word of tawhid (monotheism) that he uttered, which is his saying: ﴿إنَّنِي بَراءٌ مِمّا تَعْبُدُونَ﴾ ﴿إلّا الَّذِي فَطَرَنِي﴾. Qatada, Mujahid and al-Suddi said: it is "There is no god but Allah" (la ilaha illa Allah), even though it has not been mentioned explicitly, because the expression includes it. Ibn Zayd said: it is the word of Islam, based on His saying: ﴿ومِن ذُرِّيَّتِنا أُمَّةً مُسْلِمَةً لَكَ﴾ [al-Baqara: 128], ﴿إذْ قالَ لَهُ رَبُّهُ أسْلِمْ قالَ أسْلَمْتُ﴾ [al-Baqara: 131], ﴿هُوَ سَمّاكُمُ المُسْلِمِينَ﴾ [al-Hajj: 78]. Humayd ibn Qays read "kilmatan" with a kasra on the kaf and a sukun on the lam. It was also read "fi ʿaqibihi" with a sukun on the qaf, meaning in his offspring (dhurriyyatihi). It was also read "fi ʿaqibihi" meaning among his descendants, i.e., his successors. So there will always remain among them those who affirm the oneness of Allah and call to His monotheism. ﴿لَعَلَّهم﴾: i.e., perhaps those among them who associated partners will return through the supplication of those among them who affirmed the oneness. The majority read ﴿بَلْ مَتَّعْتُ﴾ with the first-person ta' (of the speaker), and the indication of "these" (هَؤُلاءِ) is to the Quraysh and those of the Arabs who were from the descendants of Abraham (peace be upon him). When He said "in his offspring," He said: but I gave enjoyment to these and blessed them in their disbelief, so they are not among those in whom the word of tawhid is continued. Qatada and al-A'mash read "bal matta'ta" with the ta' of address, and Ya'qub related it from Nafi'. The author of al-Lawami (Sahib al-Lawami) said: it is from Abraham's (peace be upon him) intimate conversation with his Lord, Exalted. The apparent reading is that it is from the intimate conversation of Muhammad (ﷺ), i.e., he said: "O my Lord, rather You have given enjoyment." Al-A'mash read "matta'na" with the plural of majesty (nun al-ʿazama), and this supports the majority reading.

﴿حَتّى جاءَهُمُ الحَقُّ﴾, which is the Qur'an, ﴿ورَسُولٌ مُبِينٌ﴾, which is Muhammad (ﷺ). Al-Zamakhshari said: If you ask: what is the reasoning of one who read "bal matta'ta" with a fatha on the ta'? I say: It is as if Allah, Exalted, objected concerning His own essence in His saying: ﴿وجَعَلَها كَلِمَةً باقِيَةً في عَقِبِهِ لَعَلَّهم يَرْجِعُونَ﴾, and so He said: rather I gave them enjoyment with what I gave them enjoyment of, namely long life and abundance in provision, until that occupied them away from the word of tawhid. He intended by this an extended rebuke of them, because when He gives them enjoyment with increased blessings, it is incumbent upon them to make that a cause for increased gratitude and steadfastness upon tawhid and faith, not that they should associate partners with Him and set up rivals to Him. Its example is: a man complains of the harm done by one who has done him good, then he turns to himself and says: "You are the cause of that by your kindness and benevolence." His purpose with this speech is to reproach the wrongdoer, not to disparage his action. If you say: He made the coming of the truth and the Messenger the endpoint of the enjoyment, then followed it with His saying: ﴿ولَمّا جاءَهُمُ الحَقُّ قالُوا هَذا سِحْرٌ﴾, what is the method and purport of this arrangement? I say: What is meant by enjoyment is that which is its cause, namely their preoccupation with enjoyment away from tawhid and its requirements. So He, Mighty and Exalted, said: rather they were occupied away from tawhid ﴿حَتّى جاءَهُمُ الحَقُّ ورَسُولٌ مُبِينٌ﴾, and by this endpoint it is imagined that they awoke from their heedlessness at that point, because it calls for awakening.

Then He began their story at the coming of the truth, saying: ﴿ولَمّا جاءَهُمُ الحَقُّ﴾, they came with something worse than their heedlessness in which they were (p-13), namely that they added to their polytheism the opposition to the truth, the obstinacy against and enmity toward the Messenger, the disdain for the Book of Allah and His laws, the persistence in the deeds of disbelievers, and the challenge to the wisdom of Allah in choosing Muhammad (ﷺ) from among the people of his time, by their saying: ﴿لَوْلا نُزِّلَ هَذا القُرْآنُ عَلى رَجُلٍ مِنَ القَرْيَتَيْنِ عَظِيمٍ﴾, which is the extreme in disfiguring the image of their affair. End of quote; it is good, but in it there is prolixity. The pronoun in "wa qalu" (and they said) is for the Quraysh; they had considered it far-fetched that Allah would send a messenger from among humans, so the matter of Abraham, Moses, Jesus and other messengers (may Allah bless them) was widely known among them. When they had no way to deny that, they contradicted themselves regarding Muhammad (ﷺ) and said: Why was Muhammad chosen, and why was the Qur'an not sent down to a great man of the two towns? They pointed to one whose rank was great by age, lineage, standing and abundance of wealth. It was read "ʿala rajulin" with a sukun on the jim. "Min al-qaryatayn" means: from one of the two towns. It was said: from a man of the two towns, and they are Mecca and al-Ta'if. Ibn ʿAbbas said: the one from Mecca is al-Walid ibn al-Mughira al-Makhzumi, and from al-Ta'if: Habib ibn ʿAmr ibn ʿUmayr al-Thaqafi. Mujahid said: ʿUtba ibn Rabi'a and Kinana ibn ʿAbd Yalil. Qatada said: al-Walid ibn al-Mughira and ʿUrwa ibn Mas'ud al-Thaqafi. Qatada said: We have been told that no clan of the Quraysh remained without claiming him, and al-Walid ibn al-Mughira was called "the basil of Quraysh," and he used to say: If what Muhammad says were true, it would have been sent down to me or to Ibn Mas'ud, meaning ʿUrwa ibn Mas'ud, who was called Abu Mas'ud.

﴿أهم يَقْسِمُونَ رَحْمَةَ رَبِّكَ﴾? This contains rebuke and wonder at their ignorance, as if it were said: Do the virtues, including prophethood and others, get divided according to their choice and will? Then in the attribution in His saying "the mercy of your Lord" there is an honoring of him (ﷺ), and that this mercy which came to you is none other than from your Lord, who reforms your state and nurtures you. Then Exalted He informed that it is He who apportioned the livelihood among them, so nothing came to anyone except what Exalted He apportioned. If He is the One who undertook that and differentiated among them, and that in worldly affairs which pass away, how then would He not undertake the grave matter, which is sending whom He wills? You have no right to choose who is suitable for that; rather you are incapable of arranging your own affairs. The majority read "maʿishatahum" in the singular, while ʿAbd Allah, al-A'mash, Ibn ʿAbbas and Sufyan read "maʿaishahum" in the plural. The majority read "sukhriyyan" with a damma on the sin, while ʿAmr ibn Maymun, Ibn Muhaysin, Ibn Abi Layla, Abu Raja', al-Walid ibn Muslim and Ibn ʿAmir read it with a kasra, and it is from taskhir, in the sense of enslaving and employing, so that some of them benefit from others and reach their benefits. Had each one undertaken all his tasks by himself, he would not have been able and would have been lost and destroyed. It is unlikely that "sukhriyyan" here is from mockery (al-huzu’), though some have said: i.e., the rich mocks the poor. In His saying "Nahnu qasamna" (We have apportioned), there is discouragement from devoting oneself to the pursuit of the world, and an ease for reliance upon Allah. Muqatil said: We made some to excel over others, so some are leaders and some are led. Qatada said: You find one weak in strength, little in resource, rich in tongue, and he is given expansion; and you find one strong in resource, eloquent in tongue, and he is restricted. Al-Shafi'i, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

Among the proof of decree and its existence
is the misery of the poor and the pleasant life of the fool.

﴿ورَحْمَةُ رَبِّكَ﴾: it was said: prophethood; it was said: guidance and faith. Qatada and al-Suddi said: Paradise is better than what these people gather of the worldly debris, and in this expression is a belittling of the world and what is gathered in it of its goods.

(p-9) And they have made the angels, who are the servants of the Most Merciful, females. Did they witness their creation? Their testimony will be recorded, and they will be questioned. And they say: "Had the Most Merciful willed, we would not have worshipped them." They have no knowledge of that; they only guess. Or have We given them a Book before this, so that they hold fast to it? Rather, they say: "We found our fathers upon a community, and we are guided upon their footsteps." And thus We did not send a warner before you to any town, but its affluent ones said: "We found our fathers upon a community, and we follow in their footsteps." He said: "Even if I brought you something better guided than what you found your fathers upon?" They said: "We disbelieve in what you have been sent with." So We took vengeance on them; so see how was the end of the deniers. And when Abraham said to his father and his people: "Indeed, I am free from what you worship, except He who created me, for He will guide me." And he made it a word remaining among his descendants, that they might return. Rather, I gave enjoyment to these and their fathers until there came to them the truth and a clear messenger. And when the truth came to them, they said: "This is magic, and we disbelieve in it." And they said: "Why was this Qur'an not sent down upon a great man from the two towns?" Is it they who distribute the mercy of your Lord? We have distributed among them their livelihood in the worldly life, and raised some of them above others in degrees, that some of them may take others in service. And the mercy of your Lord is better than what they accumulate.

(p-10) It was not enough for them that they ascribed to Allah a son, and made Him females, and made them (the angels) among the angels. This is from their ignorance of Allah and His attributes, and their belittling of the angels, in that they attributed femininity to them. 

Umar ibn al-Khattab, al-Hasan, Abu Raja', Qatada, Abu Ja'far, Shayba, al-A'raj, al-Ibnan, and Nafi' read: ʿinda al-Raḥmān (عِنْدَ الرَّحْمَنِ), as a zarf (adverbial complement of place/state, "with"), and this is more indicative of elevated rank and nearness of station, in accordance with His saying: ﴿Indeed, those who are with your Lord...﴾ [al-A'raf: 206].

ʿAbd Allah, Ibn ʿAbbas, Ibn Jubayr, ʿAlqama, and the rest of the Seven read: ʿibād al-Raḥmān (عِبادُ الرَّحْمَنِ), as the plural of ʿabd, in accordance with His saying: ﴿Rather, they are honored servants﴾ [al-Anbiya: 26]. Al-A'mash read ʿibāda al-Raḥmān (عِبادَ الرَّحْمَنِ), as a plural, in the accusative case. Ibn Khalawayh related it, and said: "It is likewise in the mushaf (codex) of Ibn Mas'ud." The accusative is governed by an implied verb, meaning: "Those who were created as servants of the Most Merciful, and brought into being as servants of the Most Merciful, females."

Ubayy read ʿabd al-Raḥmān (عَبْدُ الرَّحْمَنِ) in the singular, but its meaning is plural, because it is an ism jins (a noun of genus).

The majority read: ashahidū (أشَهِدُوا), with the interrogative hamza placed before shahidū, as a past tense verb in the active voice, meaning: "Did they attend their creation?" That is not of the kind of testimony which carries the meanings that are sought to be rendered. 

It has been said that the Messenger (ﷺ) asked them: "What makes you know that they are females?" They said: "We heard that from our fathers, and we testify that they did not lie." Then Allah, Exalted, said: ﴿Their testimony will be recorded, and they will be questioned﴾ about it, that is, in the Hereafter.

Nafi' read with a hamza placed before ushhidū (أُشْهِدُوا), a quadriliteral verb in the passive voice, without a madd (lengthening) between the two hamzas. Al-Musayyabi, from him, read with a madd between them. ʿAli ibn Abi Talib, Ibn ʿAbbas, Mujahid, and in the transmission of Abu ʿAmr and Nafi', read with the second hamza softened (tashil), without madd. A group read likewise but with a madd between them. From ʿAli and al-Mufaddal, from ʿAsim, both hamzas are pronounced clearly without madd. Al-Zuhri and others read ushhidū without interrogation, in the passive voice, quadriliteral. It was said: the meaning is by way of interrogation, and the hamza was omitted because the meaning indicates it. It was also said: the clause is a description of the females, that is, "females whose creation was witnessed by them," and they did not claim that they witnessed their creation, but when they claimed, out of their audacity, that they were females, they became as though they claimed that and that they had witnessed their creation.

The majority read: ināthan (إناثًا), and Zayd ibn ʿAli read: unuthan (أُنُثًا), the plural of a plural. It has been said: the meaning of wa-jaʿalū is "named," and they said. The better view is that the meaning is: "and they made their belief about the angels to be females." This interrogation contains mockery of them, and the intended meaning is to show the corruption of their minds, and that their claims are devoid of proof. This is similar to the verse that censures the people of astrology and natures: ﴿I did not call them to witness the creation of the heavens and the earth, nor their own creation﴾ [al-Kahf: 51].

The majority read: sa-tuktabu (سَتُكْتَبُ), with a ta' above, in the passive voice. Shahadatuhum (شَهادَتُهم) with a nominative ending, singular. Al-Zubayri likewise, except with a ya'. Al-Hasan likewise, except with a ta' and as a plural: shahadatihim. Ibn ʿAbbas, Zayd ibn ʿAli, Abu Ja'far, Abu Haywa, Ibn Abi Abla, al-Jahdari, and al-A'raj read with a nun, in the active voice, shahadatuhum in the singular. A group read: sa-yaktubu with a ya' in the active voice, meaning Allah, shahadatahum with a fatha on the ta'. The meaning is: their testimony will be recorded against the angels for their femininity. And they will be questioned. This is a threat.

﴿And they say: "Had the Most Merciful willed, we would not have worshipped them."﴾ The pronoun refers to the angels. Qatada and Muqatil said: "and others." Mujahid said: it refers to the idols. They made the absence of worship conditional upon His will, but worship existed when His will was absent. So the meaning is: He willed worship, and what He willed occurred. They took His granting them respite and His kindness toward them, while they worship other than Him, as proof that He is pleased with that as a religion. The discussion of a similar sentence has already occurred at the end of al-An'am. In the speech there is an ellipsis, meaning: we are not held accountable for that, since it is in accordance with the will of Allah. For this reason He says: ﴿They have no knowledge of that﴾, that is, of what follows from their worship of punishment, ﴿they only guess﴾: that is, they lie. It has been said: the reference of "that" is to their claim that the angels are females. Al-Zamakhshari said: "They are two disbeliefs added to the three disbeliefs: their worship of the angels (p-11) apart from Allah, and their claim that their worship is by His will, as their brethren the Jabriyya say." End of quote. He made the Ahl al-Sunna sisters of the disbelievers who worship the angels, then raised an objection and an answer running according to what he chose from the doctrine of the Mu'tazila, which is explained in his book. When he denied them knowledge that their punishment would be abandoned for worshipping other than Allah, that is, no intellect indicates that, he also denied that revelation indicates it, and said: ﴿Or have We given them a Book﴾ before the revelation of the Qur'an, or before the warning of the messengers, indicating permissibility of their worshipping other than Allah, and that no consequence follows from it. Then Allah, Exalted, informed that they, in that, are imitators of their fathers, and they have no proof from intellect or transmission. The meaning of ʿalā ummatin (عَلى أُمَّةٍ) is: upon a way, a religion, and a custom. So we followed their path, and we are guided in following their footsteps. From this is the saying of Qays ibn al-Khatim:

"We were upon the way of our fathers, and the latter follows the first."

The majority read: ummatin (أُمَّةٍ), with a damma on the hamza. Mujahid and Qutrub said: "upon a religion." Al-Jawhari said: "The ummah is the way, and what is said: 'So-and-so has no ummah,' means he has no religion nor creed." The poet said:

"Can one who has a faith (ummah) be equal to an ingrate?"

The discussion of ummah has already occurred in His saying: ﴿and he remembered after a time﴾ [Yusuf: 45]. Umar ibn ʿAbd al-Aziz, Mujahid, Qatada, and al-Jahdari read with a kasra on the hamza, which is the good way in lexical usage, as opposed to ummah with a damma, as stated by al-Jawhari. Ibn ʿAbbas read: immatin (أمَّةٍ), with a fatha on the hamza, meaning "upon an intention and a state," and the disagreement regarding the second word is like that of the first.

Muqatil related that the verse was revealed concerning al-Walid ibn al-Mughira, Abu Sufyan, Abu Jahl, ʿUtba, and Shayba ibn Abi Rabi'a from Quraysh, meaning that those before them also said it, consoling the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) with that. The mutraf (affluent one) is the pampered one, whom blessings have made insolent, so they preferred the desires and disliked the hardships of obligations.

The majority read: "Qul" (قُلْ), in the imperative. Ibn ʿAmir and Hafs read: "Qala" (قالَ) in the indicative. The majority read: ji'tukum (جِئْتُكم), with the first-person singular ta'. Ubayy, Shayba, Ibn Miqsam, al-Za'farani, Abu Shaykh al-Hunai, and Khalid read: ji'nakum (جِئْناكم), with the first-person plural nun. The apparent reading is that the pronoun in qala or in qul refers to the Messenger, that is: "Say, O Muhammad, to your people: 'Will you follow your fathers? Even if I brought you a religion more guided than the religion upon which you found your fathers?'" This is a rebuke to them, since they follow blindly and do not reflect upon the proofs.

﴿They said: "Indeed, we disbelieve in what you, and the messengers before you, have been sent with."﴾ The address overrides the third person.

﴿So We took vengeance on them﴾ through drought, killing, captivity, and exile.

﴿So see how was the end of﴾ the one who denied you. Ibn ʿAtiyya said: in qala there is a pronoun referring to the warner, and the rest of the verse indicates that "qul" in the reading of whoever reads it is not an imperative to Muhammad (ﷺ), but is rather a narration of what the warner was commanded to say. The word law (لَوْ) in this place seems to be conditional, with the meaning of in (إنْ), as if the meaning of the verse were: "Or if I brought you something clearer and more manifest than what your fathers were upon, your obstinacy and imitation would accompany you." So the disbelievers of the nations who denied their prophets answered then, as they denied Muhammad (ﷺ). What he said is not necessarily fixed; rather, the apparent meaning is what we have mentioned before.

﴿And when Abraham said to his father and his people﴾: and remind the Arabs of the condition of their highest ancestor and his prohibition of worshipping other than Allah, and his singling out of Allah in monotheism and worship, mocking them, so that they might return to the religion of their ancestor, since he was the most honorable of their forefathers and the one upon whose love there is consensus. Also, he (ﷺ) did not imitate his father in worshipping idols, so you should emulate him in abandoning the imitation of your nearest fathers, and return to reflection and following the truth.

The majority read: barāʾun (بَراءٌ), a verbal noun which is used the same for the singular, masculine, and their opposites. It is said: "We are free (al-barāʾ) from you," and this is the dialect of al-ʿĀliya. Al-Za'farani and al-Qawrasi, from Abu Ja'far, and Ibn al-Manadhiri, from Nafi', read: barūʾun with a damma on the bā'. Al-A'mash read: barīʾun, which is the dialect of Najd and its two shaykhs, and it may be pluralized and feminized, like ṭawīlun and ṭiwālun, and karīmun and kirāmun.

Al-A'mash read: innī (إنِّي), with a shadda on the nun, without the nun of protection. The majority read: innanī (إنَّنِي), with two nuns, the first with a shadda.

The apparent view is that His saying ﴿except He who created me﴾ is a disjunctive exception (munqati', a exception not of the same kind), since they did not worship Allah alongside their idols. It has been said: they associated their idols with Him, Exalted, in worship, so it is a connected exception (muttasil). In either case, alladhī is in the accusative position. And if it is a connected exception, mā is inclusive of those who know and those who do not know. Al-Zamakhshari permitted that alladhī be in the genitive, as a substitute for the genitive after min, as if he said: "Indeed I am free from what you worship, except from He who..." and that illā be an adjective meaning "other than," on the basis that mā in mā taʿbudūn is an indefinite qualified noun. The estimate is: "Indeed I am free from gods that you worship, other than He who created me," and this is like His saying: ﴿Had there been in them gods other than Allah, they would both have been ruined﴾ [al-Anbiya: 22]. End of quote.

The substitution is not permissible, because substitution occurs only in non-affirmative contexts: negation, prohibition, and interrogation. Do you not see that what follows illā can serve to empty the governing verb for it? But "innanī barīʾun" is an affirmative sentence, so the governing verb cannot be emptied for alladhī, which is the one "free," in order to be followed by illā. From al-Zamakhshari, the word barīʾ contains the meaning of negation, and yet it is affirmative, and it is not permissible for it to be emptied for what follows illā. As for his estimate of mā as an indefinite qualified noun, he did not keep it as a relative pronoun, because he believed that illā can only be a qualifier for an indefinite noun. This question is disputed among the grammarians: some say that both indefinite and definite nouns may be qualified by it. In that case mā remains a relative pronoun, and illā is in the position of a qualifier for a definite noun. His making "fataranī" (فَطَرَنِي) a relative clause after alladhī is a reminder that no one is worshipped and no one deserves worship except the Creator of the servants.

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 43, verse 19–32 (part 2 of 2):

﴿فَإنَّهُ سَيَهْدِينِ﴾: i.e., He will continue My guidance. Elsewhere: ﴿الَّذِي خَلَقَنِي فَهو يَهْدِينِ﴾ [al-Shu'ara’: 78], so He is his guide in the future and in the present. The pronoun in "jaʿalaha" (He made it) with the nominative (marfu') refers to Abraham, and it was said that it refers to God. The pronoun in the accusative refers to the word of tawhid (monotheism) that he uttered, which is his saying: ﴿إنَّنِي بَراءٌ مِمّا تَعْبُدُونَ﴾ ﴿إلّا الَّذِي فَطَرَنِي﴾. Qatada, Mujahid and al-Suddi said: it is "There is no god but Allah" (la ilaha illa Allah), even though it has not been mentioned explicitly, because the expression includes it. Ibn Zayd said: it is the word of Islam, based on His saying: ﴿ومِن ذُرِّيَّتِنا أُمَّةً مُسْلِمَةً لَكَ﴾ [al-Baqara: 128], ﴿إذْ قالَ لَهُ رَبُّهُ أسْلِمْ قالَ أسْلَمْتُ﴾ [al-Baqara: 131], ﴿هُوَ سَمّاكُمُ المُسْلِمِينَ﴾ [al-Hajj: 78]. Humayd ibn Qays read "kilmatan" with a kasra on the kaf and a sukun on the lam. It was also read "fi ʿaqibihi" with a sukun on the qaf, meaning in his offspring (dhurriyyatihi). It was also read "fi ʿaqibihi" meaning among his descendants, i.e., his successors. So there will always remain among them those who affirm the oneness of Allah and call to His monotheism. ﴿لَعَلَّهم﴾: i.e., perhaps those among them who associated partners will return through the supplication of those among them who affirmed the oneness. The majority read ﴿بَلْ مَتَّعْتُ﴾ with the first-person ta' (of the speaker), and the indication of "these" (هَؤُلاءِ) is to the Quraysh and those of the Arabs who were from the descendants of Abraham (peace be upon him). When He said "in his offspring," He said: but I gave enjoyment to these and blessed them in their disbelief, so they are not among those in whom the word of tawhid is continued. Qatada and al-A'mash read "bal matta'ta" with the ta' of address, and Ya'qub related it from Nafi'. The author of al-Lawami (Sahib al-Lawami) said: it is from Abraham's (peace be upon him) intimate conversation with his Lord, Exalted. The apparent reading is that it is from the intimate conversation of Muhammad (ﷺ), i.e., he said: "O my Lord, rather You have given enjoyment." Al-A'mash read "matta'na" with the plural of majesty (nun al-ʿazama), and this supports the majority reading.

﴿حَتّى جاءَهُمُ الحَقُّ﴾, which is the Qur'an, ﴿ورَسُولٌ مُبِينٌ﴾, which is Muhammad (ﷺ). Al-Zamakhshari said: If you ask: what is the reasoning of one who read "bal matta'ta" with a fatha on the ta'? I say: It is as if Allah, Exalted, objected concerning His own essence in His saying: ﴿وجَعَلَها كَلِمَةً باقِيَةً في عَقِبِهِ لَعَلَّهم يَرْجِعُونَ﴾, and so He said: rather I gave them enjoyment with what I gave them enjoyment of, namely long life and abundance in provision, until that occupied them away from the word of tawhid. He intended by this an extended rebuke of them, because when He gives them enjoyment with increased blessings, it is incumbent upon them to make that a cause for increased gratitude and steadfastness upon tawhid and faith, not that they should associate partners with Him and set up rivals to Him. Its example is: a man complains of the harm done by one who has done him good, then he turns to himself and says: "You are the cause of that by your kindness and benevolence." His purpose with this speech is to reproach the wrongdoer, not to disparage his action. If you say: He made the coming of the truth and the Messenger the endpoint of the enjoyment, then followed it with His saying: ﴿ولَمّا جاءَهُمُ الحَقُّ قالُوا هَذا سِحْرٌ﴾, what is the method and purport of this arrangement? I say: What is meant by enjoyment is that which is its cause, namely their preoccupation with enjoyment away from tawhid and its requirements. So He, Mighty and Exalted, said: rather they were occupied away from tawhid ﴿حَتّى جاءَهُمُ الحَقُّ ورَسُولٌ مُبِينٌ﴾, and by this endpoint it is imagined that they awoke from their heedlessness at that point, because it calls for awakening.

Then He began their story at the coming of the truth, saying: ﴿ولَمّا جاءَهُمُ الحَقُّ﴾, they came with something worse than their heedlessness in which they were (p-13), namely that they added to their polytheism the opposition to the truth, the obstinacy against and enmity toward the Messenger, the disdain for the Book of Allah and His laws, the persistence in the deeds of disbelievers, and the challenge to the wisdom of Allah in choosing Muhammad (ﷺ) from among the people of his time, by their saying: ﴿لَوْلا نُزِّلَ هَذا القُرْآنُ عَلى رَجُلٍ مِنَ القَرْيَتَيْنِ عَظِيمٍ﴾, which is the extreme in disfiguring the image of their affair. End of quote; it is good, but in it there is prolixity. The pronoun in "wa qalu" (and they said) is for the Quraysh; they had considered it far-fetched that Allah would send a messenger from among humans, so the matter of Abraham, Moses, Jesus and other messengers (may Allah bless them) was widely known among them. When they had no way to deny that, they contradicted themselves regarding Muhammad (ﷺ) and said: Why was Muhammad chosen, and why was the Qur'an not sent down to a great man of the two towns? They pointed to one whose rank was great by age, lineage, standing and abundance of wealth. It was read "ʿala rajulin" with a sukun on the jim. "Min al-qaryatayn" means: from one of the two towns. It was said: from a man of the two towns, and they are Mecca and al-Ta'if. Ibn ʿAbbas said: the one from Mecca is al-Walid ibn al-Mughira al-Makhzumi, and from al-Ta'if: Habib ibn ʿAmr ibn ʿUmayr al-Thaqafi. Mujahid said: ʿUtba ibn Rabi'a and Kinana ibn ʿAbd Yalil. Qatada said: al-Walid ibn al-Mughira and ʿUrwa ibn Mas'ud al-Thaqafi. Qatada said: We have been told that no clan of the Quraysh remained without claiming him, and al-Walid ibn al-Mughira was called "the basil of Quraysh," and he used to say: If what Muhammad says were true, it would have been sent down to me or to Ibn Mas'ud, meaning ʿUrwa ibn Mas'ud, who was called Abu Mas'ud.

﴿أهم يَقْسِمُونَ رَحْمَةَ رَبِّكَ﴾? This contains rebuke and wonder at their ignorance, as if it were said: Do the virtues, including prophethood and others, get divided according to their choice and will? Then in the attribution in His saying "the mercy of your Lord" there is an honoring of him (ﷺ), and that this mercy which came to you is none other than from your Lord, who reforms your state and nurtures you. Then Exalted He informed that it is He who apportioned the livelihood among them, so nothing came to anyone except what Exalted He apportioned. If He is the One who undertook that and differentiated among them, and that in worldly affairs which pass away, how then would He not undertake the grave matter, which is sending whom He wills? You have no right to choose who is suitable for that; rather you are incapable of arranging your own affairs. The majority read "maʿishatahum" in the singular, while ʿAbd Allah, al-A'mash, Ibn ʿAbbas and Sufyan read "maʿaishahum" in the plural. The majority read "sukhriyyan" with a damma on the sin, while ʿAmr ibn Maymun, Ibn Muhaysin, Ibn Abi Layla, Abu Raja', al-Walid ibn Muslim and Ibn ʿAmir read it with a kasra, and it is from taskhir, in the sense of enslaving and employing, so that some of them benefit from others and reach their benefits. Had each one undertaken all his tasks by himself, he would not have been able and would have been lost and destroyed. It is unlikely that "sukhriyyan" here is from mockery (al-huzu’), though some have said: i.e., the rich mocks the poor. In His saying "Nahnu qasamna" (We have apportioned), there is discouragement from devoting oneself to the pursuit of the world, and an ease for reliance upon Allah. Muqatil said: We made some to excel over others, so some are leaders and some are led. Qatada said: You find one weak in strength, little in resource, rich in tongue, and he is given expansion; and you find one strong in resource, eloquent in tongue, and he is restricted. Al-Shafi'i, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

Among the proof of decree and its existence
is the misery of the poor and the pleasant life of the fool.

﴿ورَحْمَةُ رَبِّكَ﴾: it was said: prophethood; it was said: guidance and faith. Qatada and al-Suddi said: Paradise is better than what these people gather of the worldly debris, and in this expression is a belittling of the world and what is gathered in it of its goods.

(p-9) And they have made the angels, who are the servants of the Most Merciful, females. Did they witness their creation? Their testimony will be recorded, and they will be questioned. And they say: "Had the Most Merciful willed, we would not have worshipped them." They have no knowledge of that; they only guess. Or have We given them a Book before this, so that they hold fast to it? Rather, they say: "We found our fathers upon a community, and we are guided upon their footsteps." And thus We did not send a warner before you to any town, but its affluent ones said: "We found our fathers upon a community, and we follow in their footsteps." He said: "Even if I brought you something better guided than what you found your fathers upon?" They said: "We disbelieve in what you have been sent with." So We took vengeance on them; so see how was the end of the deniers. And when Abraham said to his father and his people: "Indeed, I am free from what you worship, except He who created me, for He will guide me." And he made it a word remaining among his descendants, that they might return. Rather, I gave enjoyment to these and their fathers until there came to them the truth and a clear messenger. And when the truth came to them, they said: "This is magic, and we disbelieve in it." And they said: "Why was this Qur'an not sent down upon a great man from the two towns?" Is it they who distribute the mercy of your Lord? We have distributed among them their livelihood in the worldly life, and raised some of them above others in degrees, that some of them may take others in service. And the mercy of your Lord is better than what they accumulate.

(p-10) It was not enough for them that they ascribed to Allah a son, and made Him females, and made them (the angels) among the angels. This is from their ignorance of Allah and His attributes, and their belittling of the angels, in that they attributed femininity to them. 

Umar ibn al-Khattab, al-Hasan, Abu Raja', Qatada, Abu Ja'far, Shayba, al-A'raj, al-Ibnan, and Nafi' read: ʿinda al-Raḥmān (عِنْدَ الرَّحْمَنِ), as a zarf (adverbial complement of place/state, "with"), and this is more indicative of elevated rank and nearness of station, in accordance with His saying: ﴿Indeed, those who are with your Lord...﴾ [al-A'raf: 206].

ʿAbd Allah, Ibn ʿAbbas, Ibn Jubayr, ʿAlqama, and the rest of the Seven read: ʿibād al-Raḥmān (عِبادُ الرَّحْمَنِ), as the plural of ʿabd, in accordance with His saying: ﴿Rather, they are honored servants﴾ [al-Anbiya: 26]. Al-A'mash read ʿibāda al-Raḥmān (عِبادَ الرَّحْمَنِ), as a plural, in the accusative case. Ibn Khalawayh related it, and said: "It is likewise in the mushaf (codex) of Ibn Mas'ud." The accusative is governed by an implied verb, meaning: "Those who were created as servants of the Most Merciful, and brought into being as servants of the Most Merciful, females."

Ubayy read ʿabd al-Raḥmān (عَبْدُ الرَّحْمَنِ) in the singular, but its meaning is plural, because it is an ism jins (a noun of genus).

The majority read: ashahidū (أشَهِدُوا), with the interrogative hamza placed before shahidū, as a past tense verb in the active voice, meaning: "Did they attend their creation?" That is not of the kind of testimony which carries the meanings that are sought to be rendered. 

It has been said that the Messenger (ﷺ) asked them: "What makes you know that they are females?" They said: "We heard that from our fathers, and we testify that they did not lie." Then Allah, Exalted, said: ﴿Their testimony will be recorded, and they will be questioned﴾ about it, that is, in the Hereafter.

Nafi' read with a hamza placed before ushhidū (أُشْهِدُوا), a quadriliteral verb in the passive voice, without a madd (lengthening) between the two hamzas. Al-Musayyabi, from him, read with a madd between them. ʿAli ibn Abi Talib, Ibn ʿAbbas, Mujahid, and in the transmission of Abu ʿAmr and Nafi', read with the second hamza softened (tashil), without madd. A group read likewise but with a madd between them. From ʿAli and al-Mufaddal, from ʿAsim, both hamzas are pronounced clearly without madd. Al-Zuhri and others read ushhidū without interrogation, in the passive voice, quadriliteral. It was said: the meaning is by way of interrogation, and the hamza was omitted because the meaning indicates it. It was also said: the clause is a description of the females, that is, "females whose creation was witnessed by them," and they did not claim that they witnessed their creation, but when they claimed, out of their audacity, that they were females, they became as though they claimed that and that they had witnessed their creation.

The majority read: ināthan (إناثًا), and Zayd ibn ʿAli read: unuthan (أُنُثًا), the plural of a plural. It has been said: the meaning of wa-jaʿalū is "named," and they said. The better view is that the meaning is: "and they made their belief about the angels to be females." This interrogation contains mockery of them, and the intended meaning is to show the corruption of their minds, and that their claims are devoid of proof. This is similar to the verse that censures the people of astrology and natures: ﴿I did not call them to witness the creation of the heavens and the earth, nor their own creation﴾ [al-Kahf: 51].

The majority read: sa-tuktabu (سَتُكْتَبُ), with a ta' above, in the passive voice. Shahadatuhum (شَهادَتُهم) with a nominative ending, singular. Al-Zubayri likewise, except with a ya'. Al-Hasan likewise, except with a ta' and as a plural: shahadatihim. Ibn ʿAbbas, Zayd ibn ʿAli, Abu Ja'far, Abu Haywa, Ibn Abi Abla, al-Jahdari, and al-A'raj read with a nun, in the active voice, shahadatuhum in the singular. A group read: sa-yaktubu with a ya' in the active voice, meaning Allah, shahadatahum with a fatha on the ta'. The meaning is: their testimony will be recorded against the angels for their femininity. And they will be questioned. This is a threat.

﴿And they say: "Had the Most Merciful willed, we would not have worshipped them."﴾ The pronoun refers to the angels. Qatada and Muqatil said: "and others." Mujahid said: it refers to the idols. They made the absence of worship conditional upon His will, but worship existed when His will was absent. So the meaning is: He willed worship, and what He willed occurred. They took His granting them respite and His kindness toward them, while they worship other than Him, as proof that He is pleased with that as a religion. The discussion of a similar sentence has already occurred at the end of al-An'am. In the speech there is an ellipsis, meaning: we are not held accountable for that, since it is in accordance with the will of Allah. For this reason He says: ﴿They have no knowledge of that﴾, that is, of what follows from their worship of punishment, ﴿they only guess﴾: that is, they lie. It has been said: the reference of "that" is to their claim that the angels are females. Al-Zamakhshari said: "They are two disbeliefs added to the three disbeliefs: their worship of the angels (p-11) apart from Allah, and their claim that their worship is by His will, as their brethren the Jabriyya say." End of quote. He made the Ahl al-Sunna sisters of the disbelievers who worship the angels, then raised an objection and an answer running according to what he chose from the doctrine of the Mu'tazila, which is explained in his book. When he denied them knowledge that their punishment would be abandoned for worshipping other than Allah, that is, no intellect indicates that, he also denied that revelation indicates it, and said: ﴿Or have We given them a Book﴾ before the revelation of the Qur'an, or before the warning of the messengers, indicating permissibility of their worshipping other than Allah, and that no consequence follows from it. Then Allah, Exalted, informed that they, in that, are imitators of their fathers, and they have no proof from intellect or transmission. The meaning of ʿalā ummatin (عَلى أُمَّةٍ) is: upon a way, a religion, and a custom. So we followed their path, and we are guided in following their footsteps. From this is the saying of Qays ibn al-Khatim:

"We were upon the way of our fathers, and the latter follows the first."

The majority read: ummatin (أُمَّةٍ), with a damma on the hamza. Mujahid and Qutrub said: "upon a religion." Al-Jawhari said: "The ummah is the way, and what is said: 'So-and-so has no ummah,' means he has no religion nor creed." The poet said:

"Can one who has a faith (ummah) be equal to an ingrate?"

The discussion of ummah has already occurred in His saying: ﴿and he remembered after a time﴾ [Yusuf: 45]. Umar ibn ʿAbd al-Aziz, Mujahid, Qatada, and al-Jahdari read with a kasra on the hamza, which is the good way in lexical usage, as opposed to ummah with a damma, as stated by al-Jawhari. Ibn ʿAbbas read: immatin (أمَّةٍ), with a fatha on the hamza, meaning "upon an intention and a state," and the disagreement regarding the second word is like that of the first.

Muqatil related that the verse was revealed concerning al-Walid ibn al-Mughira, Abu Sufyan, Abu Jahl, ʿUtba, and Shayba ibn Abi Rabi'a from Quraysh, meaning that those before them also said it, consoling the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) with that. The mutraf (affluent one) is the pampered one, whom blessings have made insolent, so they preferred the desires and disliked the hardships of obligations.

The majority read: "Qul" (قُلْ), in the imperative. Ibn ʿAmir and Hafs read: "Qala" (قالَ) in the indicative. The majority read: ji'tukum (جِئْتُكم), with the first-person singular ta'. Ubayy, Shayba, Ibn Miqsam, al-Za'farani, Abu Shaykh al-Hunai, and Khalid read: ji'nakum (جِئْناكم), with the first-person plural nun. The apparent reading is that the pronoun in qala or in qul refers to the Messenger, that is: "Say, O Muhammad, to your people: 'Will you follow your fathers? Even if I brought you a religion more guided than the religion upon which you found your fathers?'" This is a rebuke to them, since they follow blindly and do not reflect upon the proofs.

﴿They said: "Indeed, we disbelieve in what you, and the messengers before you, have been sent with."﴾ The address overrides the third person.

﴿So We took vengeance on them﴾ through drought, killing, captivity, and exile.

﴿So see how was the end of﴾ the one who denied you. Ibn ʿAtiyya said: in qala there is a pronoun referring to the warner, and the rest of the verse indicates that "qul" in the reading of whoever reads it is not an imperative to Muhammad (ﷺ), but is rather a narration of what the warner was commanded to say. The word law (لَوْ) in this place seems to be conditional, with the meaning of in (إنْ), as if the meaning of the verse were: "Or if I brought you something clearer and more manifest than what your fathers were upon, your obstinacy and imitation would accompany you." So the disbelievers of the nations who denied their prophets answered then, as they denied Muhammad (ﷺ). What he said is not necessarily fixed; rather, the apparent meaning is what we have mentioned before.

﴿And when Abraham said to his father and his people﴾: and remind the Arabs of the condition of their highest ancestor and his prohibition of worshipping other than Allah, and his singling out of Allah in monotheism and worship, mocking them, so that they might return to the religion of their ancestor, since he was the most honorable of their forefathers and the one upon whose love there is consensus. Also, he (ﷺ) did not imitate his father in worshipping idols, so you should emulate him in abandoning the imitation of your nearest fathers, and return to reflection and following the truth.

The majority read: barāʾun (بَراءٌ), a verbal noun which is used the same for the singular, masculine, and their opposites. It is said: "We are free (al-barāʾ) from you," and this is the dialect of al-ʿĀliya. Al-Za'farani and al-Qawrasi, from Abu Ja'far, and Ibn al-Manadhiri, from Nafi', read: barūʾun with a damma on the bā'. Al-A'mash read: barīʾun, which is the dialect of Najd and its two shaykhs, and it may be pluralized and feminized, like ṭawīlun and ṭiwālun, and karīmun and kirāmun.

Al-A'mash read: innī (إنِّي), with a shadda on the nun, without the nun of protection. The majority read: innanī (إنَّنِي), with two nuns, the first with a shadda.

The apparent view is that His saying ﴿except He who created me﴾ is a disjunctive exception (munqati', a exception not of the same kind), since they did not worship Allah alongside their idols. It has been said: they associated their idols with Him, Exalted, in worship, so it is a connected exception (muttasil). In either case, alladhī is in the accusative position. And if it is a connected exception, mā is inclusive of those who know and those who do not know. Al-Zamakhshari permitted that alladhī be in the genitive, as a substitute for the genitive after min, as if he said: "Indeed I am free from what you worship, except from He who..." and that illā be an adjective meaning "other than," on the basis that mā in mā taʿbudūn is an indefinite qualified noun. The estimate is: "Indeed I am free from gods that you worship, other than He who created me," and this is like His saying: ﴿Had there been in them gods other than Allah, they would both have been ruined﴾ [al-Anbiya: 22]. End of quote.

The substitution is not permissible, because substitution occurs only in non-affirmative contexts: negation, prohibition, and interrogation. Do you not see that what follows illā can serve to empty the governing verb for it? But "innanī barīʾun" is an affirmative sentence, so the governing verb cannot be emptied for alladhī, which is the one "free," in order to be followed by illā. From al-Zamakhshari, the word barīʾ contains the meaning of negation, and yet it is affirmative, and it is not permissible for it to be emptied for what follows illā. As for his estimate of mā as an indefinite qualified noun, he did not keep it as a relative pronoun, because he believed that illā can only be a qualifier for an indefinite noun. This question is disputed among the grammarians: some say that both indefinite and definite nouns may be qualified by it. In that case mā remains a relative pronoun, and illā is in the position of a qualifier for a definite noun. His making "fataranī" (فَطَرَنِي) a relative clause after alladhī is a reminder that no one is worshipped and no one deserves worship except the Creator of the servants.

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 43, verse 19–32 (part 2 of 2):

﴿فَإنَّهُ سَيَهْدِينِ﴾: i.e., He will continue My guidance. Elsewhere: ﴿الَّذِي خَلَقَنِي فَهو يَهْدِينِ﴾ [al-Shu'ara’: 78], so He is his guide in the future and in the present. The pronoun in "jaʿalaha" (He made it) with the nominative (marfu') refers to Abraham, and it was said that it refers to God. The pronoun in the accusative refers to the word of tawhid (monotheism) that he uttered, which is his saying: ﴿إنَّنِي بَراءٌ مِمّا تَعْبُدُونَ﴾ ﴿إلّا الَّذِي فَطَرَنِي﴾. Qatada, Mujahid and al-Suddi said: it is "There is no god but Allah" (la ilaha illa Allah), even though it has not been mentioned explicitly, because the expression includes it. Ibn Zayd said: it is the word of Islam, based on His saying: ﴿ومِن ذُرِّيَّتِنا أُمَّةً مُسْلِمَةً لَكَ﴾ [al-Baqara: 128], ﴿إذْ قالَ لَهُ رَبُّهُ أسْلِمْ قالَ أسْلَمْتُ﴾ [al-Baqara: 131], ﴿هُوَ سَمّاكُمُ المُسْلِمِينَ﴾ [al-Hajj: 78]. Humayd ibn Qays read "kilmatan" with a kasra on the kaf and a sukun on the lam. It was also read "fi ʿaqibihi" with a sukun on the qaf, meaning in his offspring (dhurriyyatihi). It was also read "fi ʿaqibihi" meaning among his descendants, i.e., his successors. So there will always remain among them those who affirm the oneness of Allah and call to His monotheism. ﴿لَعَلَّهم﴾: i.e., perhaps those among them who associated partners will return through the supplication of those among them who affirmed the oneness. The majority read ﴿بَلْ مَتَّعْتُ﴾ with the first-person ta' (of the speaker), and the indication of "these" (هَؤُلاءِ) is to the Quraysh and those of the Arabs who were from the descendants of Abraham (peace be upon him). When He said "in his offspring," He said: but I gave enjoyment to these and blessed them in their disbelief, so they are not among those in whom the word of tawhid is continued. Qatada and al-A'mash read "bal matta'ta" with the ta' of address, and Ya'qub related it from Nafi'. The author of al-Lawami (Sahib al-Lawami) said: it is from Abraham's (peace be upon him) intimate conversation with his Lord, Exalted. The apparent reading is that it is from the intimate conversation of Muhammad (ﷺ), i.e., he said: "O my Lord, rather You have given enjoyment." Al-A'mash read "matta'na" with the plural of majesty (nun al-ʿazama), and this supports the majority reading.

﴿حَتّى جاءَهُمُ الحَقُّ﴾, which is the Qur'an, ﴿ورَسُولٌ مُبِينٌ﴾, which is Muhammad (ﷺ). Al-Zamakhshari said: If you ask: what is the reasoning of one who read "bal matta'ta" with a fatha on the ta'? I say: It is as if Allah, Exalted, objected concerning His own essence in His saying: ﴿وجَعَلَها كَلِمَةً باقِيَةً في عَقِبِهِ لَعَلَّهم يَرْجِعُونَ﴾, and so He said: rather I gave them enjoyment with what I gave them enjoyment of, namely long life and abundance in provision, until that occupied them away from the word of tawhid. He intended by this an extended rebuke of them, because when He gives them enjoyment with increased blessings, it is incumbent upon them to make that a cause for increased gratitude and steadfastness upon tawhid and faith, not that they should associate partners with Him and set up rivals to Him. Its example is: a man complains of the harm done by one who has done him good, then he turns to himself and says: "You are the cause of that by your kindness and benevolence." His purpose with this speech is to reproach the wrongdoer, not to disparage his action. If you say: He made the coming of the truth and the Messenger the endpoint of the enjoyment, then followed it with His saying: ﴿ولَمّا جاءَهُمُ الحَقُّ قالُوا هَذا سِحْرٌ﴾, what is the method and purport of this arrangement? I say: What is meant by enjoyment is that which is its cause, namely their preoccupation with enjoyment away from tawhid and its requirements. So He, Mighty and Exalted, said: rather they were occupied away from tawhid ﴿حَتّى جاءَهُمُ الحَقُّ ورَسُولٌ مُبِينٌ﴾, and by this endpoint it is imagined that they awoke from their heedlessness at that point, because it calls for awakening.

Then He began their story at the coming of the truth, saying: ﴿ولَمّا جاءَهُمُ الحَقُّ﴾, they came with something worse than their heedlessness in which they were (p-13), namely that they added to their polytheism the opposition to the truth, the obstinacy against and enmity toward the Messenger, the disdain for the Book of Allah and His laws, the persistence in the deeds of disbelievers, and the challenge to the wisdom of Allah in choosing Muhammad (ﷺ) from among the people of his time, by their saying: ﴿لَوْلا نُزِّلَ هَذا القُرْآنُ عَلى رَجُلٍ مِنَ القَرْيَتَيْنِ عَظِيمٍ﴾, which is the extreme in disfiguring the image of their affair. End of quote; it is good, but in it there is prolixity. The pronoun in "wa qalu" (and they said) is for the Quraysh; they had considered it far-fetched that Allah would send a messenger from among humans, so the matter of Abraham, Moses, Jesus and other messengers (may Allah bless them) was widely known among them. When they had no way to deny that, they contradicted themselves regarding Muhammad (ﷺ) and said: Why was Muhammad chosen, and why was the Qur'an not sent down to a great man of the two towns? They pointed to one whose rank was great by age, lineage, standing and abundance of wealth. It was read "ʿala rajulin" with a sukun on the jim. "Min al-qaryatayn" means: from one of the two towns. It was said: from a man of the two towns, and they are Mecca and al-Ta'if. Ibn ʿAbbas said: the one from Mecca is al-Walid ibn al-Mughira al-Makhzumi, and from al-Ta'if: Habib ibn ʿAmr ibn ʿUmayr al-Thaqafi. Mujahid said: ʿUtba ibn Rabi'a and Kinana ibn ʿAbd Yalil. Qatada said: al-Walid ibn al-Mughira and ʿUrwa ibn Mas'ud al-Thaqafi. Qatada said: We have been told that no clan of the Quraysh remained without claiming him, and al-Walid ibn al-Mughira was called "the basil of Quraysh," and he used to say: If what Muhammad says were true, it would have been sent down to me or to Ibn Mas'ud, meaning ʿUrwa ibn Mas'ud, who was called Abu Mas'ud.

﴿أهم يَقْسِمُونَ رَحْمَةَ رَبِّكَ﴾? This contains rebuke and wonder at their ignorance, as if it were said: Do the virtues, including prophethood and others, get divided according to their choice and will? Then in the attribution in His saying "the mercy of your Lord" there is an honoring of him (ﷺ), and that this mercy which came to you is none other than from your Lord, who reforms your state and nurtures you. Then Exalted He informed that it is He who apportioned the livelihood among them, so nothing came to anyone except what Exalted He apportioned. If He is the One who undertook that and differentiated among them, and that in worldly affairs which pass away, how then would He not undertake the grave matter, which is sending whom He wills? You have no right to choose who is suitable for that; rather you are incapable of arranging your own affairs. The majority read "maʿishatahum" in the singular, while ʿAbd Allah, al-A'mash, Ibn ʿAbbas and Sufyan read "maʿaishahum" in the plural. The majority read "sukhriyyan" with a damma on the sin, while ʿAmr ibn Maymun, Ibn Muhaysin, Ibn Abi Layla, Abu Raja', al-Walid ibn Muslim and Ibn ʿAmir read it with a kasra, and it is from taskhir, in the sense of enslaving and employing, so that some of them benefit from others and reach their benefits. Had each one undertaken all his tasks by himself, he would not have been able and would have been lost and destroyed. It is unlikely that "sukhriyyan" here is from mockery (al-huzu’), though some have said: i.e., the rich mocks the poor. In His saying "Nahnu qasamna" (We have apportioned), there is discouragement from devoting oneself to the pursuit of the world, and an ease for reliance upon Allah. Muqatil said: We made some to excel over others, so some are leaders and some are led. Qatada said: You find one weak in strength, little in resource, rich in tongue, and he is given expansion; and you find one strong in resource, eloquent in tongue, and he is restricted. Al-Shafi'i, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

Among the proof of decree and its existence
is the misery of the poor and the pleasant life of the fool.

﴿ورَحْمَةُ رَبِّكَ﴾: it was said: prophethood; it was said: guidance and faith. Qatada and al-Suddi said: Paradise is better than what these people gather of the worldly debris, and in this expression is a belittling of the world and what is gathered in it of its goods.

(p-9) And they have made the angels, who are the servants of the Most Merciful, females. Did they witness their creation? Their testimony will be recorded, and they will be questioned. And they say: "Had the Most Merciful willed, we would not have worshipped them." They have no knowledge of that; they only guess. Or have We given them a Book before this, so that they hold fast to it? Rather, they say: "We found our fathers upon a community, and we are guided upon their footsteps." And thus We did not send a warner before you to any town, but its affluent ones said: "We found our fathers upon a community, and we follow in their footsteps." He said: "Even if I brought you something better guided than what you found your fathers upon?" They said: "We disbelieve in what you have been sent with." So We took vengeance on them; so see how was the end of the deniers. And when Abraham said to his father and his people: "Indeed, I am free from what you worship, except He who created me, for He will guide me." And he made it a word remaining among his descendants, that they might return. Rather, I gave enjoyment to these and their fathers until there came to them the truth and a clear messenger. And when the truth came to them, they said: "This is magic, and we disbelieve in it." And they said: "Why was this Qur'an not sent down upon a great man from the two towns?" Is it they who distribute the mercy of your Lord? We have distributed among them their livelihood in the worldly life, and raised some of them above others in degrees, that some of them may take others in service. And the mercy of your Lord is better than what they accumulate.

(p-10) It was not enough for them that they ascribed to Allah a son, and made Him females, and made them (the angels) among the angels. This is from their ignorance of Allah and His attributes, and their belittling of the angels, in that they attributed femininity to them. 

Umar ibn al-Khattab, al-Hasan, Abu Raja', Qatada, Abu Ja'far, Shayba, al-A'raj, al-Ibnan, and Nafi' read: ʿinda al-Raḥmān (عِنْدَ الرَّحْمَنِ), as a zarf (adverbial complement of place/state, "with"), and this is more indicative of elevated rank and nearness of station, in accordance with His saying: ﴿Indeed, those who are with your Lord...﴾ [al-A'raf: 206].
