When the Exalted mentioned the state of the disbelievers and what will be said to them, and Quraysh would hear that and only increase in arrogance and objection, and he (ﷺ) was striving to achieve belief for them, the Exalted addressed him, consoling him, with a question of wonder: Indeed, these are deaf, so you cannot make them hear; blind and bewildered, so you cannot guide them; and that is up to Him, the Exalted. Since their senses would not benefit them in the way that would bring about their deliverance from the punishment of God, they were made deaf, blind, and bewildered. He means by them Quraysh, and they combine the three attributes. For this reason the pronoun returned to them in His saying: ﴿So whether We take you away, indeed We will take vengeance upon them﴾, and no mention of them had occurred except in His saying: ﴿Can you make the deaf hear?﴾, the verse. The meaning is: if We take you before your victory over them, indeed We will take vengeance on them in the hereafter, like His saying: ﴿Or We will cause you to die, and to Us they will be returned﴾ [Ghafir: 77]. ﴿Or We will show you what We have promised them﴾ of the punishment descending upon them, like the Day of Badr, ﴿then indeed We are Able over them﴾: that is, they are in Our grasp, they cannot escape Us. This is the view of the majority. Al-Hasan and Qatadah said: the one threatened is the community (al-ummah). God honored His Prophet by not taking vengeance upon them during his lifetime, just as He took vengeance upon the nations of the prophets during their lifetimes. So vengeance fell upon them after his death, peace be upon him, in the civil strife (al-'ayn al-hadithah) that arose at the beginning of Islam, along with the Kharijites and others. It was read: "nurinnaka" with the light nun.

When the Exalted alternated between his life and his death (ﷺ), He commanded him to hold fast to what was revealed to him. The majority read: "uhiya" in the passive voice (mabniyyan lil-maf'ul), some of the Syrian readers read it with the sukun on the ya', and al-Dahhak read it in the active voice (mabniyyan lil-fa'il). And indeed what We have revealed to you ﴿is indeed a reminder for you and for your people﴾: that is, an honor, since it was revealed to them and in their language, and they were made followers of it. "Al-qawm" (people) here means Quraysh and then the Arabs, as said by Ibn 'Abbas, Mujahid, Qatadah, al-Suddi and Ibn Zayd. He (peace be upon him) used to present himself to the tribes, and when they asked him: "Who will hold authority after you?" he would fall silent, until this verse was revealed. So whenever he was asked about that, he would say: "For Quraysh." The Arabs would not accept until the Ansar accepted him. Al-Hasan said: "al-qawm" here means his community, and the meaning is: it is indeed a reminder and an admonition. It was said: this verse indicates that a person desires good and beautiful praise, and if that were not desirable, the Exalted would not have bestowed it upon His Messenger, saying: ﴿And indeed it is a reminder for you and for your people﴾. Ibrahim (peace be upon him) said: ﴿And grant me a tongue of truth among the later generations﴾ [al-Shu'ara': 84]. Good remembrance stands in the place of life, indeed it is better than life, because the effect of life occurs only in the living, whereas the effect of good remembrance occurs in every place and in every time. End of quote. Ibn Duraid said:

"A man is only a story after him, so be a good story for whoever remembers."

Another said:

"Indeed the world's beauties are only the good report that remains."

It is reported that Hulagu, king of the Tatars, asked his companions: "Who is the king?" They said: "You are the one who subdued the lands, ruled the earth, and kings obeyed you." He said: "No, the king is this one," and at that time the muezzin was calling the adhan, "this one who has been dead for more than six hundred years, and yet he is mentioned on the minarets every day five times?" He meant Muhammad, the Messenger of God (ﷺ).

﴿And you will be questioned﴾. Al-Hasan said: about thanking God for this blessing. Muqatil said: the intended meaning is whoever denied it, and he will be questioned as a rebuke.

﴿And ask those whom We sent before you of Our messengers﴾. It was said: it is on its apparent meaning, that Jibril (peace be upon him) said to him on the night of the Night Journey (al-Isra'), when he led the prophets in prayer: ﴿And ask those whom We sent﴾, but he did not ask them, since he was more certain in conviction, and he was not in doubt. This was narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, Ibn Jubayr, al-Zuhri and Ibn Zayd. And in a report, Mikail said to Jibril: "Did Muhammad ask about that?" He said: "He is greater in conviction and firmer in faith than to ask him that." Ibn 'Abbas also said, and al-Hasan, Mujahid, Qatadah, al-Suddi and 'Ata': he meant: ask the followers of those whom We sent and the bearers of their laws, since it is impossible to ask the messengers themselves, as they were not gathered together in this world. Al-Farra' said: they only inform him about the books of the messengers, so when he asks them, it is as if he asked the messengers. The question here is figurative (majaz) for contemplation, since much of its literal sense is not suitable, like the poets' questioning of the abodes and the ruins, and from it: "O lord of the earth, who split your rivers, planted your trees, and gathered your fruits, if it does not answer you in dialogue, it answers you by reflection." So the question here is figurative for examining their religions: Did the worship of idols ever come in any religion of the religions of the prophets? What appears is that it is an address to the listener who wishes to investigate the religions, and it was said to him: "Ask, O observer, the followers of the messengers: Did their messengers come with worship other than God? They will inform you that this did not occur, and it is not possible for them to bring it." The most remote view is that the meaning is: "Ask me, and ask us about whom We sent," and "ask" is suspended, so "man" is raised, being an interrogative noun in the nominative, and "arsalna" is its predicate in the accusative position, after dropping the preposition. His question would be: "Whom did You send, O Lord, before me, of Your messengers? Did You place in their mission gods to be worshipped?" Then he presented the question and related the meaning, so the address was turned to Muhammad in His saying: "from before you" (min qablika).

**Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 43, verses 33–45 (part 1 of 2):**

(p-14) ﴿And were it not that mankind would become one community, We would have given to those who disbelieve in the All-Merciful silver roofs for their houses, and staircases by which they ascend, and doors for their houses, and couches on which they recline, and ornaments of gold. But all of that is nothing but the enjoyment of the life of this world. And the Hereafter with your Lord is for those who are mindful of Him. And whoever turns away from the remembrance of the All-Merciful, We appoint for him a devil, and he is his companion. And indeed they (the devils) bar them from the path, while they think that they are guided. Until, when he comes to Us, he says, "Would that between me and you were the distance of the two easts! Wretched is the companion!" And it will not benefit you today, since you have wronged, that you are sharing in the punishment. Can you make the deaf hear, or guide the blind, or those who are in manifest error? And whether We take you away, indeed We will take vengeance upon them, or We show you that which We have promised them, indeed We have power over them. So hold fast to what has been revealed to you; indeed you are upon a straight path. And indeed it is a reminder for you and for your people, and you will be questioned. And ask those of Our messengers whom We sent before you: Did We appoint gods besides the All-Merciful to be worshipped?﴾

Abu Hayyan said: The Exalted has explained that the benefits of this world and its pleasures are base and contemptible in the sight of Allah. That is, were it not that people would desire disbelief when they see the disbeliever in ease, and that they would all become one community in disbelief. Ibn Abbas, al-Hasan, Qatadah and al-Suddi said: "We would have given them such-and-such of the adornment of the world, but His wisdom, may He be exalted, required that He make the disbeliever and the believer rich and poor alike." Ibn Atiyyah said: The lam in ﴿for those who disbelieve﴾ is the lam of ownership (lam al-milk), and the lam in ﴿for their houses﴾ is the lam of specification (lam al-takhsis), as you say: "This cloak is for Zayd (li-zayd)," and "for his beast (li-dabbatihi)" — that is, it is for his beast as a saddle-cloth (hils), and for Zayd as property (milk). End of quotation. What he said is not correct, because ﴿li-buyutihim﴾ is a badal al-ishtimal (inclusive apposition) with the governing particle repeated, so it is impossible, as a substitute, for the second lam to be anything but the meaning of the first lam. As for the meaning differing, that is not so; the lam in both is for specification. Al-Zamakhshari said: ﴿li-buyutihim﴾ is a badal al-ishtimal of ﴿li-man yakfuru﴾, and the two lams may be in the position of the two lams in your saying: "I gave him a garment for his shirt." End of quotation. I do not know what he meant by his saying "and it is permissible" to the end.

(p-15) The majority (al-Jumhur) read ﴿suqufan﴾ with two damma, while Abu Raja' read it with one damma and a sukun. Both are plurals of saqf (roof), in the dialect of Tamim, like rahn and ruhun. Ibn Kathir and Abu Amr read it with a fatha on the sin and a sukun, as a singular. Al-Farra' said: it is the plural of saqifah. It was also read with two fathas, as though it were a dialectal form of saqf. It was read as suqufan, a plural on the pattern fu'ul, like ka'b and ku'ub. The majority read ﴿wa-ma'arija﴾, the plural of ma'raj. Talhah read ﴿wa-ma'arij﴾, the plural of mi'raj, and these are the ascents to the upper parts. ﴿'alayha yazharun﴾ means they climb up onto the roofs, as He said: ﴿so they were not able to scale it﴾ [al-Kahf 18:97]. The majority read ﴿wa-surura﴾ with a damma on the sin, and it was also read with a fatha, which is a dialect of some of Tamim and some of Kalb. This applies to the plural of the doubled form fa'il when it is a noun (ism) by agreement, and when it is an adjective (sifah), as in thawbun jadid (a new garment) and thiyabun judud (new garments), with disagreement among the grammarians. These nouns are conjoined (ma'atif) to ﴿suqufan min fiddah﴾, so it is not necessary that the conjoined items be described as being of silver. Al-Zamakhshari said: "suqufan, and ma'arij, and abwaban, and surura are all of silver." End of quotation. It seems he holds that the conjoined items share in the description of what they are conjoined to, along with ﴿wa-zukhrufan﴾. Al-Zamakhshari said: "We made for them zukhrufan (ornaments)." It is also possible that the original was: "suqufan min fiddatin wa-zukhrufin," meaning some of them of silver and some of gold, and so it was put in the accusative as a conjunction to the place (mahall) of ﴿min fiddah﴾. End of quotation. Here zukhruf means gold, as Ibn Abbas, al-Hasan, Qatadah and al-Suddi said. In a hadith: "Beware of red, for it is among the adornments most beloved to Satan." Ibn Atiyyah said: "al-Hasan is red, and desires follow it." End of quotation. One of our poets said:

"You dyed your coat of mail with the blood of their brave men, when you saw Hasan wearing red."

Ibn Zayd said: zukhruf is the household furnishings, and what is made for the house of couches and cushions. Al-Hasan said: it is decorations, and it was said: it is ornamentation like engraving.

The majority read ﴿lamma﴾ with a fatha on the lam and a lightened mim. It is a lightened form of the heavy (thaqilah) particle, the lam being the lam that distinguishes an affirmative from a negative, and ma being superfluous, and ﴿matau﴾ being the predicate of ﴿kullu﴾. Al-Hasan, Talhah, al-A'mash, Isa, Asim and Hamzah read ﴿lamma﴾ with a shadda on the mim, with ﴿in﴾ as a negation, and ﴿lamma﴾ meaning "except." Abu Raja' and Abu Hayah read ﴿lima﴾ with a kasra on the lam, and they explained it as the relative ma (mawsulah), with a deleted returning pronoun, its estimated sense being: "for that which is an enjoyment," like His saying: ﴿completion upon that which was good﴾ [al-An'am 6:154]. In this explanation, ﴿in﴾ is the lightened form of the heavy particle, ﴿kullu﴾ is the subject (mubtada'), and its predicate is in the prepositional phrase, that is: "and indeed all that is surely (la-ka'inun aw la-mustaqarrun) that which is an enjoyment." Since it is the lightened form of the heavy particle, the bringing in of the lam is the proper form, so the construction would have been la-kuma matau'. However, this lam may be deleted when the meaning shows that ﴿in﴾ is the lightened form of the heavy particle, so that one does not need to mention the distinguishing lam. Among this is the poet's saying:

"We are the refusers of oppression from the family of Malik, and indeed Malik was of noble origins."

He means: "la-kanat" (indeed it was), but it was deleted, because there is no possibility of ﴿in﴾ being a negation here, since the opening of the verse indicates praise, and so ﴿in﴾ is specified as the lightened form of the heavy particle.

﴿And the Hereafter with your Lord is for those who are mindful of Him﴾: That is, the bliss of the Hereafter, and in this is an exhortation to piety.

He (Ibn Kathir?) read ﴿wa-man ya'shu﴾ with a damma on the shin, meaning he feigns blindness and ignores the remembrance of Him, while he knows the truth. It was said: he minimises his looking into the law of Allah, and closes his eyelids against looking at ﴿the remembrance of the All-Merciful﴾. Here "dhikr" may mean the Qur'an, and it is possible that it is a verbal noun (masdar) added to its object, meaning he turns away from mentioning the All-Merciful. Ibn Atiyyah said: that is, regarding what He reminded His servants of, so the verbal noun is added to its agent. End of quotation. It seems he means by dhikr the reminding (tadhkir). Yahya ibn Sallam al-Basri (p-16) read ﴿wa-man ya'sha﴾ with a fatha on the shin, meaning he goes blind to the remembrance of the All-Merciful, which is the Qur'an, as in His saying: ﴿deaf, dumb, blind﴾ [al-Baqarah 2:18]. Zayd ibn Ali read ﴿ya'shu﴾ with a waw. Al-Zamakhshari said: "on the basis that man is a relative pronoun not implying the sense of a condition, and whoever reads this way should put nuqayyid in the nominative." End of quotation. What he said is not necessarily fixed, since this reading may be explained in two ways. The first: man is conditional, and ya'shu is jussive by deleting the vowel in estimation. Al-Akhfash mentioned that this is a dialect of some Arabs, who delete the letters of weakness for the jussive particle. The well-known view among the grammarians is that this occurs in poetry, not in ordinary speech. The second: man is a relative pronoun, and the jussive is caused by it, as with a relative that takes on the meaning of the conditional particle. If this is attested for the particle ``alladhi'' (who), which was never a conditional particle, then it is more appropriate that it should be used as both a relative and a conditional. The poet said:

"Do not dig a well wanting a brother in it, for you yourself will fall into it instead of him. So too whoever oversteps against people unjustly, the consequences of what he did will befall him despite himself."

Ibn al-A'rabi recited both of these, and this is the view of the Kufans, and it has a basis in analogy: just as the relative is likened to the conditional particle, so that the predicate takes the fa' (the particle of consequence), so too it may be likened to it so that the predicate is jussive. However, the entry of the fa' is analogically valid when the predicate is a consequence of the relative clause, under the conditions mentioned in the science of grammar, and the Basrans do not deny this. The majority read ﴿nuqayyid﴾ with a nun, and Ali, al-Sulami, al-A'mash, Ya'qub, and Abu Amr (in one of the transmissions from him), and Hammad from Asim, and Isma from al-A'mash and from Asim, and al-Alimi from Abu Bakr, read it with a ya', meaning "the All-Merciful appoints." Ibn Abbas read ﴿yuqayyad﴾ in the passive. ﴿lahu shaytanun﴾ with a nominative, meaning a devil is made easy for him and set upon him. This is a punishment for disbelief by sealing and by the absence of success, just as it is said: "Allah punishes disobedience by increasing evil deeds." Al-Zamakhshari said: "He forsakes him and places between him and the devils, as in His saying: ﴿And We appointed for them companions﴾ [Fussilat 41:25] and ﴿Have you not seen that We sent the devils﴾ [Maryam 19:83]." End of quotation. This is in the manner of the Mu'tazilah.

The apparent meaning is that the pronoun of the object in ﴿wa-innahum la-yasuddunahum﴾ refers to ﴿man﴾ according to its meaning, having first referred to its wording in the singular, and then referred to its meaning. The pronoun in ﴿yasuddunahum﴾ refers to ﴿shaytan﴾, even though it is singular, because it is indefinite in its genus, and every one who is blind has a devil companion, so it is permissible for the pronoun to be plural. Ibn Atiyyah said: the pronoun in His saying ﴿wa-innahum﴾ refers to the devil, and in ﴿la-yasuddunahum﴾ it refers to the disbelievers. End of quotation. What we have mentioned is better, for the pronouns are consistent in ﴿wa-innahum﴾, in ﴿la-yasuddunahum﴾, and in ﴿wa-yahsabun﴾ for one single referent. It is as if the sentence meant: "Indeed the blind ones, the devils bar them from the path," that is, the path of guidance and success, and "they think" refers to the disbelievers.

Abu Ja'far, Shaybah, Qatadah, al-Zuhri, al-Jahdari, Abu Bakr, and the two Haramayn (the Meccan and Medinan readers) read ﴿hatta idha ja'anā﴾ in the dual, meaning the blind one and the companion, referring to the wording of ﴿man﴾ and to the devil companion, even though in meaning it is suitable for the plural. Al-A'mash, al-A'raj, Isa, Ibn Muhaysin, and the two brothers (al-Akhawan) read ﴿ja'ana﴾ in the singular, and the pronoun refers to the wording of ﴿man﴾, which was first referred to by its wording, then by its meaning in the plural, then in the singular again by its wording. A parallel to this is His saying: ﴿And whoever believes in Allah and does righteous deeds, He will admit him to gardens beneath which rivers flow, abiding therein forever; Allah has certainly made good provision for him﴾ [al-Talaq 65:11]: He used the singular first, then the plural in ﴿khalidina﴾, then the singular again in ﴿lahu rizqan﴾. It is narrated that the two (the disbeliever and the devil) will be chained together on the Day of Resurrection, and they will not be separated until Allah sends them both into the Fire. He (the disbeliever) says to the devil: ﴿Would that between me and you were the distance of the two easts!﴾ He wished that this had been in this world, so that it would not bar him from the path of Allah. Or he wished it in the Hereafter, which is the apparent meaning, because it is the answer to ﴿idha﴾, which refers to the future, that is: the east of the sun, its rising point at the shortest day of the year and its rising point at the longest day of the year. This was said by Ibn al-Sa'ib. Or ﴿the distance of the two easts﴾ means the distance between east and west, and the east was given precedence and so the two were made dual, just as they say: "the two Umars" for Abu Bakr and Umar, "the two moons" for the sun and the moon, "the two Mawsils" for al-Jazirah and al-Mawsil, "the two Zahdams" for Zahdam and Kardam, "the two Ajjajs" for Ru'bah and al-Ajjaj, and "the two parents" for father and mother. This is the choice of al-Farra' and al-Zajjaj, but al-Zamakhshari did not mention it. He said: "If you ask, what is the distance of the two easts? I say: their remoteness from one another. The original sense is the distance of the east from the west and the west from the east, and when it was dominant, it joined the two differing parts with the dual, and ascribed the distance to both of them." End of quotation. It was also said: the distance of the two easts from the two wests, and he mentioned only the two easts. It seems that in this saying he means the east and west of the sun and the moon.

﴿Wretched is the companion!﴾: an exaggeration by him in condemning his companion, since it was the cause of his being brought to the Fire. The one being condemned is elided, that is: "Wretched is the companion, you!"

﴿And it will not benefit you today﴾: this is a report of a state that will be said to them on the Day of Resurrection. It is a dreadful statement which deprives them of the comfort of consolation, since it makes them understand that consolation will not benefit them because of the greatness of the calamity, the length of the punishment and the continuance of its duration. Consolation is, in most cases, the relief of every afflicted person in this world. Do you not see the saying of al-Khansa:

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 43, verses 33–45 (part 2 of 2):

If not for the multitude of those weeping around me over their brothers, I would have killed myself. And they do not weep for one like my brother. But I console myself about him with consolation (al-ta'assi). This consolation has spared me the burden of killing myself. Thus God negated for them any benefit from consolation (al-ta'assi), and in that is torment for them and despair of every good. This would not occur except under the assumption that the agent (al-fa'il) is "anna" and what it governs, that is: "Your sharing in the punishment will not benefit you, that they will not lighten your share in the punishment." If the agent is not "anna," which is a pronoun referring to what is understood from the speech before it, that is: he wishes for distance from the companion and to disassociate himself from him, and "anna-kum" is causative (ta'lil), meaning: because you share in the punishment just as you shared in its cause, which is disbelief. Muqatil said the meaning is: "Repentance and regret will not benefit you today, because you and your companions share in the punishment, just as you shared in disbelief in the world." On the agent being other than "anna," which is the reading of the majority (qira'at al-jumhur), the speech does not imply negation of consolation (al-ta'assi). It was read: "innakum" with a kasra, which indicates an implied agent, and what supports it is taking "annakum" with a fatha as causative.

"Al-yawm" (today) and "idh" (when) are both adverbs of time (zarfan). "Al-yawm" is an adverb of the present time (zarf hal), and "idh" is an adverb of past time (zarf madi). As for the adverb of present time, the future tense may govern it because of its nearness to it, or by a figurative extension (tajawwuz) in the future, as in His saying: ﴿Whoever now listens will find a watching flame﴾ [al-Jinn: 9], and the poet's saying:

"I shall be wretched now, since I have attained its goal."

As for "idh" being past, the future tense does not govern it. Al-Zamakhshari said: "Idh" is a substitute (badal) for "al-yawm." End of quote. "Idh zalamtum" was interpreted as "idh tabayyana wa-wadaha zulmukum" (when your wrongdoing became clear and evident), and no one, nor you, retains any doubt that you were wrongdoers. A parallel to this is the poet's saying:

"When we trace our lineage, a base woman did not bear me."

That is: it became clear that I am the son of a noble woman. End of quote. Substitution (badal) is not permissible with "idh" kept in its original sense as an adverb of past time. If it is made to refer to time in general (mutlaq al-waqt), then it is permissible. Its analysis as substitution was taken by al-Zamakhshari from Ibn Jinni. In his questioning of Abu 'Ali (al-Farisi), Ibn Jinni said: "I reviewed it with him several times, and the final result I obtained from him was that this world and the hereafter are connected, and they are equal in God's judgment and knowledge, so 'idh' is a substitute for 'al-yawm,' as if it were future, or as if 'al-yawm' were past." It was said: the estimate is "after when you wronged," and the annexed term was omitted because it is known. It was said: "idh" is a particle of causation (ta'lil) with the meaning of "in" (if). Al-Hufi said: "Al-yawm" is an adverb connected to "yanfa'akum" (will benefit you), and "idh" cannot be connected to it, because they are both adverbs of time, meaning they differ in meaning to a degree that they cannot be combined. He said: so it is not valid for it to be a substitute for the latter, meaning because of that difference, since this is an adverb of present circumstance and that is an adverb of past time. He said: but "idh" is connected to what the meaning indicates, as if he said: "Your gathering together will not benefit you." Then he said: the agent of "yanfa'akum" is the sharing (al-ishtirak). It was said: the agent is omitted, its estimate being "your wrongdoing" or "your denial," and it is what governs "idh," not the pronoun of the agent.

When the Exalted mentioned the state of the disbelievers and what will be said to them, and Quraysh would hear that and only increase in arrogance and objection, and he (ﷺ) was striving to achieve belief for them, the Exalted addressed him, consoling him, with a question of wonder: Indeed, these are deaf, so you cannot make them hear; blind and bewildered, so you cannot guide them; and that is up to Him, the Exalted. Since their senses would not benefit them in the way that would bring about their deliverance from the punishment of God, they were made deaf, blind, and bewildered. He means by them Quraysh, and they combine the three attributes. For this reason the pronoun returned to them in His saying: ﴿So whether We take you away, indeed We will take vengeance upon them﴾, and no mention of them had occurred except in His saying: ﴿Can you make the deaf hear?﴾, the verse. The meaning is: if We take you before your victory over them, indeed We will take vengeance on them in the hereafter, like His saying: ﴿Or We will cause you to die, and to Us they will be returned﴾ [Ghafir: 77]. ﴿Or We will show you what We have promised them﴾ of the punishment descending upon them, like the Day of Badr, ﴿then indeed We are Able over them﴾: that is, they are in Our grasp, they cannot escape Us. This is the view of the majority. Al-Hasan and Qatadah said: the one threatened is the community (al-ummah). God honored His Prophet by not taking vengeance upon them during his lifetime, just as He took vengeance upon the nations of the prophets during their lifetimes. So vengeance fell upon them after his death, peace be upon him, in the civil strife (al-'ayn al-hadithah) that arose at the beginning of Islam, along with the Kharijites and others. It was read: "nurinnaka" with the light nun.

When the Exalted alternated between his life and his death (ﷺ), He commanded him to hold fast to what was revealed to him. The majority read: "uhiya" in the passive voice (mabniyyan lil-maf'ul), some of the Syrian readers read it with the sukun on the ya', and al-Dahhak read it in the active voice (mabniyyan lil-fa'il). And indeed what We have revealed to you ﴿is indeed a reminder for you and for your people﴾: that is, an honor, since it was revealed to them and in their language, and they were made followers of it. "Al-qawm" (people) here means Quraysh and then the Arabs, as said by Ibn 'Abbas, Mujahid, Qatadah, al-Suddi and Ibn Zayd. He (peace be upon him) used to present himself to the tribes, and when they asked him: "Who will hold authority after you?" he would fall silent, until this verse was revealed. So whenever he was asked about that, he would say: "For Quraysh." The Arabs would not accept until the Ansar accepted him. Al-Hasan said: "al-qawm" here means his community, and the meaning is: it is indeed a reminder and an admonition. It was said: this verse indicates that a person desires good and beautiful praise, and if that were not desirable, the Exalted would not have bestowed it upon His Messenger, saying: ﴿And indeed it is a reminder for you and for your people﴾. Ibrahim (peace be upon him) said: ﴿And grant me a tongue of truth among the later generations﴾ [al-Shu'ara': 84]. Good remembrance stands in the place of life, indeed it is better than life, because the effect of life occurs only in the living, whereas the effect of good remembrance occurs in every place and in every time. End of quote. Ibn Duraid said:

"A man is only a story after him, so be a good story for whoever remembers."

Another said:

"Indeed the world's beauties are only the good report that remains."

It is reported that Hulagu, king of the Tatars, asked his companions: "Who is the king?" They said: "You are the one who subdued the lands, ruled the earth, and kings obeyed you." He said: "No, the king is this one," and at that time the muezzin was calling the adhan, "this one who has been dead for more than six hundred years, and yet he is mentioned on the minarets every day five times?" He meant Muhammad, the Messenger of God (ﷺ).

﴿And you will be questioned﴾. Al-Hasan said: about thanking God for this blessing. Muqatil said: the intended meaning is whoever denied it, and he will be questioned as a rebuke.

﴿And ask those whom We sent before you of Our messengers﴾. It was said: it is on its apparent meaning, that Jibril (peace be upon him) said to him on the night of the Night Journey (al-Isra'), when he led the prophets in prayer: ﴿And ask those whom We sent﴾, but he did not ask them, since he was more certain in conviction, and he was not in doubt. This was narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, Ibn Jubayr, al-Zuhri and Ibn Zayd. And in a report, Mikail said to Jibril: "Did Muhammad ask about that?" He said: "He is greater in conviction and firmer in faith than to ask him that." Ibn 'Abbas also said, and al-Hasan, Mujahid, Qatadah, al-Suddi and 'Ata': he meant: ask the followers of those whom We sent and the bearers of their laws, since it is impossible to ask the messengers themselves, as they were not gathered together in this world. Al-Farra' said: they only inform him about the books of the messengers, so when he asks them, it is as if he asked the messengers. The question here is figurative (majaz) for contemplation, since much of its literal sense is not suitable, like the poets' questioning of the abodes and the ruins, and from it: "O lord of the earth, who split your rivers, planted your trees, and gathered your fruits, if it does not answer you in dialogue, it answers you by reflection." So the question here is figurative for examining their religions: Did the worship of idols ever come in any religion of the religions of the prophets? What appears is that it is an address to the listener who wishes to investigate the religions, and it was said to him: "Ask, O observer, the followers of the messengers: Did their messengers come with worship other than God? They will inform you that this did not occur, and it is not possible for them to bring it." The most remote view is that the meaning is: "Ask me, and ask us about whom We sent," and "ask" is suspended, so "man" is raised, being an interrogative noun in the nominative, and "arsalna" is its predicate in the accusative position, after dropping the preposition. His question would be: "Whom did You send, O Lord, before me, of Your messengers? Did You place in their mission gods to be worshipped?" Then he presented the question and related the meaning, so the address was turned to Muhammad in His saying: "from before you" (min qablika).

(p-20) The relevance of this verse to what precedes it has two aspects. The first: when the Quraysh's criticism of the Messenger was mentioned, along with their insistence that the Qur'an be sent down to a great man of the two cities (i.e., great in standing and wealth), and Allah mentioned that Pharaoh had preceded them in the same thing when he said, ﴿Is not the dominion of Egypt mine?﴾ up to the end of the verse, He followed this with dominion and wealth. Pharaoh was thus their model in this, yet despite it he became subdued before Moses and was avenged upon, and so too the Quraysh. The second aspect: when He said, ﴿And ask those whom We sent before you﴾ [al-Zukhruf: 45], He mentioned Moses and Jesus, who had the greatest followings among those prophets who came before, and each of them came calling to Allah and to worshipping Him alone. In what any of them brought there was never a permission to take gods besides Allah, as the Quraysh had done. Therefore the mention of their story fits the verse before it. The "signs" of Moses are the miracles he brought. He singled out the angels for mention because they are the nobles, since other people follow them.

﴿So when he brought them Our signs﴾: before this there is an omitted statement, whose sense is: they demanded from him what would indicate the truth of his claim to be a messenger from Allah.

﴿So when he brought them Our signs﴾: these were the turning of the staff into a serpent and its return to being a staff, and the bringing out of the hand, white and radiant, and its return to its original colour. ﴿Behold, they laughed at them﴾: that is, laughter seized them suddenly, such that they did not reflect or consider, but at the very sight of it they laughed in mockery and derision, just as the Quraysh used to laugh. Al-Zamakhshari said: If you ask, how could *lamma* ("when") be answered by *idha al-fujaʾiyya* (the sudden *idha*)? I say: because the verb of suddenness is implied with it, and it is the governing verb of the accusative in its position, as if it were said: "So when he brought them Our signs, they were suddenly at the time of their laughter." End of quote. We know of no grammarian who held what this man held, that *idha al-fujaʾiyya* is in the accusative governed by an implied verb whose sense is *fajaʾa* ("he suddenly came upon"). Rather, there are three positions on it. One position is that it is a particle (*harf*), and so needs no governing word. A second is that it is an adverb of place: if after the noun a predicate is explicitly stated, that predicate governs it, as in *kharajtu fa-idha Zaydun qāʾimun* ("I went out and behold, Zayd was standing"); *qāʾimun* governs *idha*, as if the sense were: "I went out, and in the place where I went out Zayd was standing." A third is that it is an adverb of time, with the governing element again being the predicate: as if he said, "in the time when I went out, Zayd was standing." If no predicate is mentioned after the noun, or a noun in the accusative of state (*ḥāl*) is mentioned, then *idha* is the predicate of the subject. If the subject is a body (*judda*) and we say *idha* is an adverb of place, the matter is clear; if we say it is an adverb of time, the sentence involves an ellipsis, i.e., "so in the time there is the presence of Zayd." What al-Zamakhshari claimed, that the verb of suddenness is implied, has not been uttered by anyone, not even in a single instance. Moreover, the meaning does not show that the suddenness comes from the preceding speech; rather, the meaning shows that the suddenness comes from the speech in which *idha* occurs. You say, "I went out and behold, a lion," and the meaning is "the lion suddenly confronted me," not "I suddenly confronted the lion."

﴿And We do not show them any sign but it is greater than its sister﴾: Al-Zamakhshari said: If you ask, when there came to them one sign from among the nine, what is "its sister" which it is preferred over in greatness, from among the remaining signs? I say: "its sister" is the one which is a sign like it, and this is the attribute of each of the two, so the meaning is that it is greater than the remaining signs. I say: "its sister" which is a sign like it, is meant in the sense of preference and induction, one after another, just as you say, "He is the best man I have seen," meaning to prefer him over the whole race of men whom you have seen, if you count them as one man. If you ask, this is contradictory speech, for its meaning is: there is no sign among the nine but that it is greater than each one of them, so each one of them is both superior and inferior in one state. I say: the purpose of this speech is that they are all described as great, and they do not differ much in it. This is the custom with things which are alike in excellence and whose ranks are close, with slight difference: when people's opinions differ in preferring them, some prefer this one and some prefer that one. On this basis people have built their speech, saying, "I saw men some of whom are better than others." Sometimes the opinion of one man differs about them: at one time he prefers this, at another time he prefers that. From this is the line in the *Hamasa* (anthology):

*Whomever you meet of them, you will say: I have met their chief,*
*like the stars by which the traveller journeys.*

And al-Anmariyya [a woman of the Banu Anmar] preferred among the perfect ones of her sons, then said: "When I looked at their ranks, close together and little different, I am bereaved of them if I know which of them is the best. They are like a hollow ring, one does not know where its ends are." End of quote. It is a long speech, and its summary is that the description with greatness is metaphorical, and that this is relative to those who look at them. Ibn ʿAṭiyya said: It is an expression of the intensity of their effect upon the souls of the people, by the sharpness of the matter and its occurrence, because a sign which Moses presented, the staff and the hand, was the greatest of his signs, and then every sign after that came and its arrival was great and became large in their eyes, because they had forgotten the one before it. This is as the poet said:

*Indeed, wounds are healed, and the great matter that passes is entrusted only to the nearest.*

Al-Tabari went to the view that the signs here are the proofs and evidences. End of quote. It was also said: they were among the great signs, and each one was greater than the one before it. On this view there is an omitted attribute, meaning "greater than its preceding sister," and no contradiction remains in the speech, and this judgement does not apply to the first sign, since nothing preceded it for it to be greater than. It was also said: the first sign requires knowledge, and the second requires knowledge added to the knowledge of the first, so the certainty increases. He used *ukht* ("sister") to mean "counterpart": you say, "This atom is the sister of this one," meaning its counterpart.

﴿And We seized them with the punishment﴾: [such as] ﴿the years and a loss of fruits﴾ [al-Aʿraf: 130], and ﴿the flood, the locusts, the lice, the frogs and the blood﴾ [al-Aʿraf: 133]. That was a punishment for them, and a sign for Moses, ﴿that they might return﴾ from their disbelief. Al-Zamakhshari said: "that they might return": He intended that they would return from disbelief to faith. If you ask: had He intended their return, it would have happened. I say: His intending the act of another is nothing but that He commands it and asks him to bring it into being. If that is by way of compulsion, it occurs; otherwise it lies between its occurring and its not occurring, according to the choice of the responsible person. Return did not happen because the intention was not compulsion, and they did not choose it. End of quote. This is in the way of the Mu'tazila (the rationalist school). Ibn ʿAṭiyya said: "perhaps they might" expresses hope according to the belief and assumption of humans.

﴿And they said: O you sorcerer, pray to your Lord for us﴾: that is, for the removing of the punishment. The majority said: this is address of honour, because magic was the knowledge of their time; or because they retained for him what they used to claim earlier. Their words ﴿by what He has covenanted with you; surely we will be guided﴾ are a statement in conformity with the intended meaning. It was also said: rather, it is address of mockery and belittlement, and their words ﴿by what He has covenanted with you﴾ mean "according to your claim," and their words ﴿surely we will be guided﴾ are a statement conforming to the condition of his prayer and the removal of the punishment, and a firm covenant upon breaking it. Do you not see: ﴿But when We removed the punishment from them, behold, they broke their word﴾? On the first view, the words ﴿But when We removed the punishment from them, behold, they broke their word﴾ run according to the most common habit of people: when harm touches them, they become humble and pray, and when it is lifted they return to their former habit, as in His saying, ﴿But when He brought them safe to land, behold, they ascribe partners﴾ [al-ʿAnkabut: 65]. ﴿When We removed his harm, he passed on as if he had never called Us to a harm that touched him.﴾ His saying ﴿by what He has covenanted with you﴾ may mean that your prayer is answered. In the speech there is an omission, meaning: Moses prayed, and it was removed: ﴿So when We removed﴾. Abu Haywa recited *yankithūna* with a kasra on the *kaf*.

﴿And Pharaoh proclaimed among his people﴾: he made the people the place of the proclamation. The apparent meaning is that he called the Copts' great men in the place where he and they gathered, raising his voice among them so that his words would spread among all the Copts. It is also possible that he ordered the proclamation and it was attributed to him. The cause of his proclamation was that, when he saw Allah answering Moses' prayer and lifting the punishment, he feared the people's inclination toward him, so he proclaimed: ﴿He said: O my people, is not the dominion of Egypt mine?﴾ He intended to show his superiority over Moses by the dominion of Egypt, which extends from Alexandria to Aswan.

﴿And these rivers﴾: that is, the channels which flow from the Nile, the greatest of which are: the Nahr al-Malik, the Nahr Tulun, the Nahr Damietta, and the Nahr Tinnis. The *waw* in ﴿and these rivers﴾ is the *waw* of circumstance (*ḥāl*), and *tajrī* ("flow") is the predicate. *Hādhihi* and *al-anhār* are an attribute, or an explicative apposition (*ʿatf bayān*). It is permitted that the *waw* be conjunctive with "dominion of Egypt," and *tajrī* a circumstantial clause. ﴿Flowing beneath me﴾: that is, beneath my subjugation and my dominion. Qatada said: its gardens and rivers used to flow beneath his palace. It was said: he had a great throne, and he cut a portion from the Nile of Egypt, which he divided into rivers flowing beneath that throne. Al-Dahhak went far in his interpretation, explaining "the rivers" as the commanders and tyrannical leaders who march beneath his banner. Whoever explained them as wealth took it to mean those under his control. Whoever explained them as horses said: just as the horse is called "sea," it is called "river." These three views come close to the interpretations of the Batiniyya (esoteric sects).

﴿Do you not see﴾: My greatness, My power, and Moses' weakness? Mahdi ibn al-Saffir read *yubṣirūna* with the *yāʾ* of the third person. It is mentioned in *al-Kamil* of al-Hudhali, and by al-Sabʿi, from Yaʿqub; Ibn Khalawayh mentioned it. Al-Zamakhshari said: I wonder how the ambition of one who grew proud of the dominion of Egypt rose to the claim of lordship! The people marvelled at the extent of his greatness; he gave orders and it was proclaimed in the markets and alleys of Egypt, so that this magnificence and majesty would not be hidden from small or great, until the measure of his might and dominion settled in the hearts of the common people. Ibn ʿIsa read the *nūn* in ﴿Do you not see me?﴾ with a kasra. It is reported from al-Rashid that when he read it he said: "I will appoint over it the best of my slaves," and he appointed al-Khasib, who was in his ablution. It is reported from ʿAbd Allah ibn Tahir that he was appointed over it and went out to it; when he approached it and came upon it, he said: "Is this the town which Pharaoh boasted of, until he said, ﴿Is not the dominion of Egypt mine?﴾? By Allah, it is less in my eyes than that I should enter it," and he turned his reins back.

﴿Am I not better than this one who is contemptible and can hardly speak clearly?﴾: The apparent sense is that *am* here is the disconnected *am*, implied with *bal* ("rather") and the interrogative hamza, meaning: "Rather, I am better." And when he asks, "Is he better than one who is weak, who can hardly make his meaning clear when he speaks, and who is the king ruling over them?" They said to him: "Without doubt you are better." Al-Suddi and Abu ʿUbayda said: *am* has the meaning of *bal*, so that he moves from that speech to informing them that he is better than the one mentioned, as in the words of the poet:

*She appeared like the horn of the sun in the splendour of forenoon,*
*and her form, or are you more graceful in the eye?*

Sibawayh said: "Am" here is the equalizing particle (al-mu'adilah), meaning: "Do they not see the matter that is truly to be seen, namely that I am better than Moses?" This view was first put forward by al-Zamakhshari, who said: "Am" here is connected (muttasilah), because the meaning is: "Will you not see? Or will you see?" Except that he placed his words "I am better" in the position of "you see," because when they say "You are better," they are thereby seers in his estimation; this is the placing of the cause in the position of the effect (min inzal al-sabab manzilat al-musabbab). End of quotation. This view is very forced (mutakallif jiddan), since the equalizing element (al-mu'adil) is only in correspondence with what precedes it. If what precedes is a verbal clause (jumlah fi'liyyah), the equalizing element is a verbal clause or a nominal clause from which a verbal clause can be implied, as in His words ﴿Did you call them, or are you silent?﴾ [al-A'raf: 193], because its meaning is: "Or have you remained silent?" Here, a verbal clause cannot be implied from it, because His words ﴿Or am I better?﴾ do not correspond to His words "Will you not see?" If what precedes is a noun, the equalizing element is a noun or a verbal clause from which a noun can be implied, such as the saying of the poet:
"Is he deformed in both hands, or has he become complete?" So "ataммat" (has become complete) corresponds to the noun; the implied sense is: "Or is he complete?"

It was also said: the equalizing element after "am" was omitted because the meaning indicates it, the implied wording being "you see," so "you see" was omitted. This is not permissible except when "am" is followed by "la" (not), as in: "Does Zayd stand, or not?" its implied form being: "Or does he not stand?" And: "Is Zayd with you, or not?" meaning: "Or is he not with you?" As for omitting it without "la," this is not part of their speech. The omission of "am" together with the equalizing element has occurred, though rarely. The poet said:
"The heart called me to her, and I am attentive to her command, but I do not know whether her pursuit is right guidance (rushd) or error (ghayy)."
He means: "or error." Al-Farra' related that he read: "Am ana khayrun" (Am I not better?), with the hamzah of interrogation entering upon the negating "ma," and this conveyed the sense of the estimate.

﴿And he can hardly express himself clearly﴾. The majority hold that there remained in his tongue some trace of the ember (al-jamrah). Whoever holds that God had answered his supplication, ﴿And loosen the knot from my tongue﴾ [Ta-Ha: 27], so that no trace remained, takes the negation of clarity to mean that he cannot make his proof, which shows his truthfulness in what he claims, manifest, since he has no ability to clarify the meaning by means of his speech. It was also said: he disparaged him by what Moses had been in terms of lowliness during the days he was with Pharaoh, so he was attributed to what Pharaoh had known of him, as an exaggeration in reproach. Pharaoh's saying ﴿and he can hardly express himself clearly﴾ is pure falsehood. Do you not see his debating with him, his responding to him, and his silencing him with proof? The prophets, peace be upon them, are all eloquent. Al-Baqir read: "yabyan" (with a fathah on the ya'), from "bana," meaning "to become manifest."

﴿Why then are not bracelets of gold cast upon him?﴾ Mujahid said: when they made a man a chief, they would put two bracelets on him and collar him with a gold torque as a sign of his lordship. Pharaoh said: "Why has not the Lord of Moses cast upon him bracelets of gold, if he is truthful?" This was an indication of casting the keys of kingship to him, since he had described himself with might and kingship and compared himself with Moses, peace be upon him, describing him with weakness and scarcity of helpers. So he objected, saying: "If he is truthful, why did his Lord not make him a king, bestow bracelets upon him, and make the angels his helpers?"

Al-Dahhak read: "fa-lawla alqa" (in the active voice), meaning God, "asawiratan" in the accusative; the majority read "asawiratun" in the nominative. Ubayy and Abdullah read "asawir," and the singular is "iswar," meaning "siwar," and the ha' is a substitute for the ya', as it is in zanadiqah, where the ha' is a substitute for the ya' of zanadiq, which corresponds to the ya' of zindiq; and this corresponds to the alif of asawir. Al-Hasan, Qatadah, Abu Raja', al-A'raj, Mujahid, Abu Haywah, and Hafs read "asworah," the plural of siwar, like khimar and akhmirah. Al-A'mash read "asawir." It is narrated from Ubayy and from Abu 'Amr: ﴿or the angels came with him, attending in succession﴾, that is, they protect him and establish his proof. Ibn 'Abbas said: they help him against whoever opposes him. Al-Suddi said: some of them accompany others. Mujahid said: they walk with him. Qatadah said: successive.

﴿So he made light of his people﴾: that is, he made them foolish due to the lightness of their intellects; this was said by Ibn al-A'rabi. Others said: he led them to become light-minded toward what he wanted from them, so they obeyed him because of their wickedness.

﴿So when they angered Us﴾: it is transmitted with the hamzah from "asifa," meaning he became angry; the meaning is: when they did the wicked deeds that made it necessary that We not forbear toward them. It is transmitted from Ibn 'Abbas: they grieved Our friends, the believers, such as the sorcerers and the Children of Israel. And from him also: they angered Us. From 'Ali: they provoked Us. It was said: they opposed. Al-Qushayri and others said: anger from God, as regards the will to punish, is among the attributes of the Essence, or the punishment itself, and then it is among the attributes of the Act.

The majority read ﴿salafan﴾. Ibn 'Abbas, Zayd ibn Aslam, and Qatadah said: that is, those who precede to the Fire; it is a verbal noun of "salafa, yaslifu, salafan." The "silf" of a man are his preceding forefathers; the plural is asla and sulaf. It was also said it is the plural of sali, like haris and haras; its reality is that it is a collective noun (ism jam'), because fi'l is not among the patterns of broken plurals. Tufayl said, lamenting his people:
"They passed on before, in the direction of the path, upon them the vicissitudes of death, and men turn about."
Al-Farra' and al-Zajjaj said: a precedent, so that the disbelievers contemporary with the Messenger may take warning from them. Abu 'Abdullah and his companions, Sa'id ibn 'Iyad, al-A'mash, Talhah, al-A'raj, Hamzah, and al-Kisa'i read "wa-sulufan," with a damma on the sin and the lam, the plural of "salif," meaning a group. Al-Qasim ibn Ma'n heard the Arabs say: "A group (salif) of people has passed away." Ali, Mujahid, and al-A'raj also read: "wa-sulufan," with a damma on the sin and the lam, the plural of "sulfah," meaning a female slave or a herd. "Silf" in other than this sense means the offspring of ugliness (walad al-qubh), and its plural is silfan.

﴿And an example for the later ones﴾: that is, a wondrous report, going about as a proverb, related by the later disbelievers; it is said to them: "Your case is the case of the people of Pharaoh."

(p-20) The relevance of this verse to what precedes it has two aspects. The first: when the Quraysh's criticism of the Messenger was mentioned, along with their insistence that the Qur'an be sent down to a great man of the two cities (i.e., great in standing and wealth), and Allah mentioned that Pharaoh had preceded them in the same thing when he said, ﴿Is not the dominion of Egypt mine?﴾ up to the end of the verse, He followed this with dominion and wealth. Pharaoh was thus their model in this, yet despite it he became subdued before Moses and was avenged upon, and so too the Quraysh. The second aspect: when He said, ﴿And ask those whom We sent before you﴾ [al-Zukhruf: 45], He mentioned Moses and Jesus, who had the greatest followings among those prophets who came before, and each of them came calling to Allah and to worshipping Him alone. In what any of them brought there was never a permission to take gods besides Allah, as the Quraysh had done. Therefore the mention of their story fits the verse before it. The "signs" of Moses are the miracles he brought. He singled out the angels for mention because they are the nobles, since other people follow them.

﴿So when he brought them Our signs﴾: before this there is an omitted statement, whose sense is: they demanded from him what would indicate the truth of his claim to be a messenger from Allah.

﴿So when he brought them Our signs﴾: these were the turning of the staff into a serpent and its return to being a staff, and the bringing out of the hand, white and radiant, and its return to its original colour. ﴿Behold, they laughed at them﴾: that is, laughter seized them suddenly, such that they did not reflect or consider, but at the very sight of it they laughed in mockery and derision, just as the Quraysh used to laugh. Al-Zamakhshari said: If you ask, how could *lamma* ("when") be answered by *idha al-fujaʾiyya* (the sudden *idha*)? I say: because the verb of suddenness is implied with it, and it is the governing verb of the accusative in its position, as if it were said: "So when he brought them Our signs, they were suddenly at the time of their laughter." End of quote. We know of no grammarian who held what this man held, that *idha al-fujaʾiyya* is in the accusative governed by an implied verb whose sense is *fajaʾa* ("he suddenly came upon"). Rather, there are three positions on it. One position is that it is a particle (*harf*), and so needs no governing word. A second is that it is an adverb of place: if after the noun a predicate is explicitly stated, that predicate governs it, as in *kharajtu fa-idha Zaydun qāʾimun* ("I went out and behold, Zayd was standing"); *qāʾimun* governs *idha*, as if the sense were: "I went out, and in the place where I went out Zayd was standing." A third is that it is an adverb of time, with the governing element again being the predicate: as if he said, "in the time when I went out, Zayd was standing." If no predicate is mentioned after the noun, or a noun in the accusative of state (*ḥāl*) is mentioned, then *idha* is the predicate of the subject. If the subject is a body (*judda*) and we say *idha* is an adverb of place, the matter is clear; if we say it is an adverb of time, the sentence involves an ellipsis, i.e., "so in the time there is the presence of Zayd." What al-Zamakhshari claimed, that the verb of suddenness is implied, has not been uttered by anyone, not even in a single instance. Moreover, the meaning does not show that the suddenness comes from the preceding speech; rather, the meaning shows that the suddenness comes from the speech in which *idha* occurs. You say, "I went out and behold, a lion," and the meaning is "the lion suddenly confronted me," not "I suddenly confronted the lion."

﴿And We do not show them any sign but it is greater than its sister﴾: Al-Zamakhshari said: If you ask, when there came to them one sign from among the nine, what is "its sister" which it is preferred over in greatness, from among the remaining signs? I say: "its sister" is the one which is a sign like it, and this is the attribute of each of the two, so the meaning is that it is greater than the remaining signs. I say: "its sister" which is a sign like it, is meant in the sense of preference and induction, one after another, just as you say, "He is the best man I have seen," meaning to prefer him over the whole race of men whom you have seen, if you count them as one man. If you ask, this is contradictory speech, for its meaning is: there is no sign among the nine but that it is greater than each one of them, so each one of them is both superior and inferior in one state. I say: the purpose of this speech is that they are all described as great, and they do not differ much in it. This is the custom with things which are alike in excellence and whose ranks are close, with slight difference: when people's opinions differ in preferring them, some prefer this one and some prefer that one. On this basis people have built their speech, saying, "I saw men some of whom are better than others." Sometimes the opinion of one man differs about them: at one time he prefers this, at another time he prefers that. From this is the line in the *Hamasa* (anthology):

*Whomever you meet of them, you will say: I have met their chief,*
*like the stars by which the traveller journeys.*

And al-Anmariyya [a woman of the Banu Anmar] preferred among the perfect ones of her sons, then said: "When I looked at their ranks, close together and little different, I am bereaved of them if I know which of them is the best. They are like a hollow ring, one does not know where its ends are." End of quote. It is a long speech, and its summary is that the description with greatness is metaphorical, and that this is relative to those who look at them. Ibn ʿAṭiyya said: It is an expression of the intensity of their effect upon the souls of the people, by the sharpness of the matter and its occurrence, because a sign which Moses presented, the staff and the hand, was the greatest of his signs, and then every sign after that came and its arrival was great and became large in their eyes, because they had forgotten the one before it. This is as the poet said:

*Indeed, wounds are healed, and the great matter that passes is entrusted only to the nearest.*

Al-Tabari went to the view that the signs here are the proofs and evidences. End of quote. It was also said: they were among the great signs, and each one was greater than the one before it. On this view there is an omitted attribute, meaning "greater than its preceding sister," and no contradiction remains in the speech, and this judgement does not apply to the first sign, since nothing preceded it for it to be greater than. It was also said: the first sign requires knowledge, and the second requires knowledge added to the knowledge of the first, so the certainty increases. He used *ukht* ("sister") to mean "counterpart": you say, "This atom is the sister of this one," meaning its counterpart.

﴿And We seized them with the punishment﴾: [such as] ﴿the years and a loss of fruits﴾ [al-Aʿraf: 130], and ﴿the flood, the locusts, the lice, the frogs and the blood﴾ [al-Aʿraf: 133]. That was a punishment for them, and a sign for Moses, ﴿that they might return﴾ from their disbelief. Al-Zamakhshari said: "that they might return": He intended that they would return from disbelief to faith. If you ask: had He intended their return, it would have happened. I say: His intending the act of another is nothing but that He commands it and asks him to bring it into being. If that is by way of compulsion, it occurs; otherwise it lies between its occurring and its not occurring, according to the choice of the responsible person. Return did not happen because the intention was not compulsion, and they did not choose it. End of quote. This is in the way of the Mu'tazila (the rationalist school). Ibn ʿAṭiyya said: "perhaps they might" expresses hope according to the belief and assumption of humans.

﴿And they said: O you sorcerer, pray to your Lord for us﴾: that is, for the removing of the punishment. The majority said: this is address of honour, because magic was the knowledge of their time; or because they retained for him what they used to claim earlier. Their words ﴿by what He has covenanted with you; surely we will be guided﴾ are a statement in conformity with the intended meaning. It was also said: rather, it is address of mockery and belittlement, and their words ﴿by what He has covenanted with you﴾ mean "according to your claim," and their words ﴿surely we will be guided﴾ are a statement conforming to the condition of his prayer and the removal of the punishment, and a firm covenant upon breaking it. Do you not see: ﴿But when We removed the punishment from them, behold, they broke their word﴾? On the first view, the words ﴿But when We removed the punishment from them, behold, they broke their word﴾ run according to the most common habit of people: when harm touches them, they become humble and pray, and when it is lifted they return to their former habit, as in His saying, ﴿But when He brought them safe to land, behold, they ascribe partners﴾ [al-ʿAnkabut: 65]. ﴿When We removed his harm, he passed on as if he had never called Us to a harm that touched him.﴾ His saying ﴿by what He has covenanted with you﴾ may mean that your prayer is answered. In the speech there is an omission, meaning: Moses prayed, and it was removed: ﴿So when We removed﴾. Abu Haywa recited *yankithūna* with a kasra on the *kaf*.

﴿And Pharaoh proclaimed among his people﴾: he made the people the place of the proclamation. The apparent meaning is that he called the Copts' great men in the place where he and they gathered, raising his voice among them so that his words would spread among all the Copts. It is also possible that he ordered the proclamation and it was attributed to him. The cause of his proclamation was that, when he saw Allah answering Moses' prayer and lifting the punishment, he feared the people's inclination toward him, so he proclaimed: ﴿He said: O my people, is not the dominion of Egypt mine?﴾ He intended to show his superiority over Moses by the dominion of Egypt, which extends from Alexandria to Aswan.

﴿And these rivers﴾: that is, the channels which flow from the Nile, the greatest of which are: the Nahr al-Malik, the Nahr Tulun, the Nahr Damietta, and the Nahr Tinnis. The *waw* in ﴿and these rivers﴾ is the *waw* of circumstance (*ḥāl*), and *tajrī* ("flow") is the predicate. *Hādhihi* and *al-anhār* are an attribute, or an explicative apposition (*ʿatf bayān*). It is permitted that the *waw* be conjunctive with "dominion of Egypt," and *tajrī* a circumstantial clause. ﴿Flowing beneath me﴾: that is, beneath my subjugation and my dominion. Qatada said: its gardens and rivers used to flow beneath his palace. It was said: he had a great throne, and he cut a portion from the Nile of Egypt, which he divided into rivers flowing beneath that throne. Al-Dahhak went far in his interpretation, explaining "the rivers" as the commanders and tyrannical leaders who march beneath his banner. Whoever explained them as wealth took it to mean those under his control. Whoever explained them as horses said: just as the horse is called "sea," it is called "river." These three views come close to the interpretations of the Batiniyya (esoteric sects).

﴿Do you not see﴾: My greatness, My power, and Moses' weakness? Mahdi ibn al-Saffir read *yubṣirūna* with the *yāʾ* of the third person. It is mentioned in *al-Kamil* of al-Hudhali, and by al-Sabʿi, from Yaʿqub; Ibn Khalawayh mentioned it. Al-Zamakhshari said: I wonder how the ambition of one who grew proud of the dominion of Egypt rose to the claim of lordship! The people marvelled at the extent of his greatness; he gave orders and it was proclaimed in the markets and alleys of Egypt, so that this magnificence and majesty would not be hidden from small or great, until the measure of his might and dominion settled in the hearts of the common people. Ibn ʿIsa read the *nūn* in ﴿Do you not see me?﴾ with a kasra. It is reported from al-Rashid that when he read it he said: "I will appoint over it the best of my slaves," and he appointed al-Khasib, who was in his ablution. It is reported from ʿAbd Allah ibn Tahir that he was appointed over it and went out to it; when he approached it and came upon it, he said: "Is this the town which Pharaoh boasted of, until he said, ﴿Is not the dominion of Egypt mine?﴾? By Allah, it is less in my eyes than that I should enter it," and he turned his reins back.

﴿Am I not better than this one who is contemptible and can hardly speak clearly?﴾: The apparent sense is that *am* here is the disconnected *am*, implied with *bal* ("rather") and the interrogative hamza, meaning: "Rather, I am better." And when he asks, "Is he better than one who is weak, who can hardly make his meaning clear when he speaks, and who is the king ruling over them?" They said to him: "Without doubt you are better." Al-Suddi and Abu ʿUbayda said: *am* has the meaning of *bal*, so that he moves from that speech to informing them that he is better than the one mentioned, as in the words of the poet:

*She appeared like the horn of the sun in the splendour of forenoon,*
*and her form, or are you more graceful in the eye?*

Sibawayh said: "Am" here is the equalizing particle (al-mu'adilah), meaning: "Do they not see the matter that is truly to be seen, namely that I am better than Moses?" This view was first put forward by al-Zamakhshari, who said: "Am" here is connected (muttasilah), because the meaning is: "Will you not see? Or will you see?" Except that he placed his words "I am better" in the position of "you see," because when they say "You are better," they are thereby seers in his estimation; this is the placing of the cause in the position of the effect (min inzal al-sabab manzilat al-musabbab). End of quotation. This view is very forced (mutakallif jiddan), since the equalizing element (al-mu'adil) is only in correspondence with what precedes it. If what precedes is a verbal clause (jumlah fi'liyyah), the equalizing element is a verbal clause or a nominal clause from which a verbal clause can be implied, as in His words ﴿Did you call them, or are you silent?﴾ [al-A'raf: 193], because its meaning is: "Or have you remained silent?" Here, a verbal clause cannot be implied from it, because His words ﴿Or am I better?﴾ do not correspond to His words "Will you not see?" If what precedes is a noun, the equalizing element is a noun or a verbal clause from which a noun can be implied, such as the saying of the poet:
"Is he deformed in both hands, or has he become complete?" So "ataммat" (has become complete) corresponds to the noun; the implied sense is: "Or is he complete?"

It was also said: the equalizing element after "am" was omitted because the meaning indicates it, the implied wording being "you see," so "you see" was omitted. This is not permissible except when "am" is followed by "la" (not), as in: "Does Zayd stand, or not?" its implied form being: "Or does he not stand?" And: "Is Zayd with you, or not?" meaning: "Or is he not with you?" As for omitting it without "la," this is not part of their speech. The omission of "am" together with the equalizing element has occurred, though rarely. The poet said:
"The heart called me to her, and I am attentive to her command, but I do not know whether her pursuit is right guidance (rushd) or error (ghayy)."
He means: "or error." Al-Farra' related that he read: "Am ana khayrun" (Am I not better?), with the hamzah of interrogation entering upon the negating "ma," and this conveyed the sense of the estimate.

﴿And he can hardly express himself clearly﴾. The majority hold that there remained in his tongue some trace of the ember (al-jamrah). Whoever holds that God had answered his supplication, ﴿And loosen the knot from my tongue﴾ [Ta-Ha: 27], so that no trace remained, takes the negation of clarity to mean that he cannot make his proof, which shows his truthfulness in what he claims, manifest, since he has no ability to clarify the meaning by means of his speech. It was also said: he disparaged him by what Moses had been in terms of lowliness during the days he was with Pharaoh, so he was attributed to what Pharaoh had known of him, as an exaggeration in reproach. Pharaoh's saying ﴿and he can hardly express himself clearly﴾ is pure falsehood. Do you not see his debating with him, his responding to him, and his silencing him with proof? The prophets, peace be upon them, are all eloquent. Al-Baqir read: "yabyan" (with a fathah on the ya'), from "bana," meaning "to become manifest."

﴿Why then are not bracelets of gold cast upon him?﴾ Mujahid said: when they made a man a chief, they would put two bracelets on him and collar him with a gold torque as a sign of his lordship. Pharaoh said: "Why has not the Lord of Moses cast upon him bracelets of gold, if he is truthful?" This was an indication of casting the keys of kingship to him, since he had described himself with might and kingship and compared himself with Moses, peace be upon him, describing him with weakness and scarcity of helpers. So he objected, saying: "If he is truthful, why did his Lord not make him a king, bestow bracelets upon him, and make the angels his helpers?"

Al-Dahhak read: "fa-lawla alqa" (in the active voice), meaning God, "asawiratan" in the accusative; the majority read "asawiratun" in the nominative. Ubayy and Abdullah read "asawir," and the singular is "iswar," meaning "siwar," and the ha' is a substitute for the ya', as it is in zanadiqah, where the ha' is a substitute for the ya' of zanadiq, which corresponds to the ya' of zindiq; and this corresponds to the alif of asawir. Al-Hasan, Qatadah, Abu Raja', al-A'raj, Mujahid, Abu Haywah, and Hafs read "asworah," the plural of siwar, like khimar and akhmirah. Al-A'mash read "asawir." It is narrated from Ubayy and from Abu 'Amr: ﴿or the angels came with him, attending in succession﴾, that is, they protect him and establish his proof. Ibn 'Abbas said: they help him against whoever opposes him. Al-Suddi said: some of them accompany others. Mujahid said: they walk with him. Qatadah said: successive.

﴿So he made light of his people﴾: that is, he made them foolish due to the lightness of their intellects; this was said by Ibn al-A'rabi. Others said: he led them to become light-minded toward what he wanted from them, so they obeyed him because of their wickedness.

﴿So when they angered Us﴾: it is transmitted with the hamzah from "asifa," meaning he became angry; the meaning is: when they did the wicked deeds that made it necessary that We not forbear toward them. It is transmitted from Ibn 'Abbas: they grieved Our friends, the believers, such as the sorcerers and the Children of Israel. And from him also: they angered Us. From 'Ali: they provoked Us. It was said: they opposed. Al-Qushayri and others said: anger from God, as regards the will to punish, is among the attributes of the Essence, or the punishment itself, and then it is among the attributes of the Act.

The majority read ﴿salafan﴾. Ibn 'Abbas, Zayd ibn Aslam, and Qatadah said: that is, those who precede to the Fire; it is a verbal noun of "salafa, yaslifu, salafan." The "silf" of a man are his preceding forefathers; the plural is asla and sulaf. It was also said it is the plural of sali, like haris and haras; its reality is that it is a collective noun (ism jam'), because fi'l is not among the patterns of broken plurals. Tufayl said, lamenting his people:
"They passed on before, in the direction of the path, upon them the vicissitudes of death, and men turn about."
Al-Farra' and al-Zajjaj said: a precedent, so that the disbelievers contemporary with the Messenger may take warning from them. Abu 'Abdullah and his companions, Sa'id ibn 'Iyad, al-A'mash, Talhah, al-A'raj, Hamzah, and al-Kisa'i read "wa-sulufan," with a damma on the sin and the lam, the plural of "salif," meaning a group. Al-Qasim ibn Ma'n heard the Arabs say: "A group (salif) of people has passed away." Ali, Mujahid, and al-A'raj also read: "wa-sulufan," with a damma on the sin and the lam, the plural of "sulfah," meaning a female slave or a herd. "Silf" in other than this sense means the offspring of ugliness (walad al-qubh), and its plural is silfan.

﴿And an example for the later ones﴾: that is, a wondrous report, going about as a proverb, related by the later disbelievers; it is said to them: "Your case is the case of the people of Pharaoh."

(p-20) The relevance of this verse to what precedes it has two aspects. The first: when the Quraysh's criticism of the Messenger was mentioned, along with their insistence that the Qur'an be sent down to a great man of the two cities (i.e., great in standing and wealth), and Allah mentioned that Pharaoh had preceded them in the same thing when he said, ﴿Is not the dominion of Egypt mine?﴾ up to the end of the verse, He followed this with dominion and wealth. Pharaoh was thus their model in this, yet despite it he became subdued before Moses and was avenged upon, and so too the Quraysh. The second aspect: when He said, ﴿And ask those whom We sent before you﴾ [al-Zukhruf: 45], He mentioned Moses and Jesus, who had the greatest followings among those prophets who came before, and each of them came calling to Allah and to worshipping Him alone. In what any of them brought there was never a permission to take gods besides Allah, as the Quraysh had done. Therefore the mention of their story fits the verse before it. The "signs" of Moses are the miracles he brought. He singled out the angels for mention because they are the nobles, since other people follow them.

﴿So when he brought them Our signs﴾: before this there is an omitted statement, whose sense is: they demanded from him what would indicate the truth of his claim to be a messenger from Allah.

﴿So when he brought them Our signs﴾: these were the turning of the staff into a serpent and its return to being a staff, and the bringing out of the hand, white and radiant, and its return to its original colour. ﴿Behold, they laughed at them﴾: that is, laughter seized them suddenly, such that they did not reflect or consider, but at the very sight of it they laughed in mockery and derision, just as the Quraysh used to laugh. Al-Zamakhshari said: If you ask, how could *lamma* ("when") be answered by *idha al-fujaʾiyya* (the sudden *idha*)? I say: because the verb of suddenness is implied with it, and it is the governing verb of the accusative in its position, as if it were said: "So when he brought them Our signs, they were suddenly at the time of their laughter." End of quote. We know of no grammarian who held what this man held, that *idha al-fujaʾiyya* is in the accusative governed by an implied verb whose sense is *fajaʾa* ("he suddenly came upon"). Rather, there are three positions on it. One position is that it is a particle (*harf*), and so needs no governing word. A second is that it is an adverb of place: if after the noun a predicate is explicitly stated, that predicate governs it, as in *kharajtu fa-idha Zaydun qāʾimun* ("I went out and behold, Zayd was standing"); *qāʾimun* governs *idha*, as if the sense were: "I went out, and in the place where I went out Zayd was standing." A third is that it is an adverb of time, with the governing element again being the predicate: as if he said, "in the time when I went out, Zayd was standing." If no predicate is mentioned after the noun, or a noun in the accusative of state (*ḥāl*) is mentioned, then *idha* is the predicate of the subject. If the subject is a body (*judda*) and we say *idha* is an adverb of place, the matter is clear; if we say it is an adverb of time, the sentence involves an ellipsis, i.e., "so in the time there is the presence of Zayd." What al-Zamakhshari claimed, that the verb of suddenness is implied, has not been uttered by anyone, not even in a single instance. Moreover, the meaning does not show that the suddenness comes from the preceding speech; rather, the meaning shows that the suddenness comes from the speech in which *idha* occurs. You say, "I went out and behold, a lion," and the meaning is "the lion suddenly confronted me," not "I suddenly confronted the lion."

I say: "its sister" is the one which is a sign like it, and this is the attribute of each of the two, so the meaning is that it is greater than the remaining signs. I say: "its sister" which is a sign like it, is meant in the sense of preference and induction, one after another, just as you say, "He is the best man I have seen," meaning to prefer him over the whole race of men whom you have seen, if you count them as one man. If you ask, this is contradictory speech, for its meaning is: there is no sign among the nine but that it is greater than each one of them, so each one of them is both superior and inferior in one state. *Whomever you meet of them, you will say: I have met their chief,*
