The majority read ﴿يَعْلَمُونَ﴾ with the ya' of the third person, as in ﴿فَاصْفَحْ عَنْهُمْ﴾. Abu Ja'far, al-Hasan, al-A'raj, Nafi', and Hisham read it with the ta' of address.

al-Suddi said: "*Wa-qul salam*" means "good," in exchange for their evil. Muqatil said: "Offer them kindness." al-Mawardi reported: "Say that by which you are safe from their evil."

**Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 43, verses 74–89 (part 1 of 2)**

﴿Indeed, the criminals will abide forever in the punishment of Hell.﴾ ﴿It will not be lightened for them, and they will be in despair therein.﴾ ﴿We did not wrong them, but they were the wrongdoers.﴾ ﴿And they will call, "O Malik, let your Lord put an end to us." He will say, "Indeed, you will remain."﴾ ﴿We have certainly brought you the truth, but most of you are averse to the truth.﴾ ﴿Or have they decided on a matter? Then, indeed, We are the decreers.﴾ ﴿Or do they think that We do not hear their secrets and their private talk? Yes, and Our messengers are with them, recording.﴾ ﴿Say, "If the Most Merciful had a son, then I would be the first of the worshippers."﴾ ﴿Glory be to the Lord of the heavens and the earth, the Lord of the Throne, above what they describe.﴾ ﴿So leave them to plunge in vain talk and play until they encounter their Day which they are promised.﴾ ﴿And He is the One who is God in the heaven and God on the earth, and He is the All-Wise, the All-Knowing.﴾ ﴿Blessed is He to whom belongs the dominion of the heavens and the earth and what is between them, and with Him is the knowledge of the Hour, and to Him you will be returned.﴾ ﴿Those whom they invoke besides Him do not possess intercession, except one who testifies to the truth while they know.﴾ ﴿And if you asked them who created them, they would surely say, "Allah." So how are they deluded?﴾ ﴿And [the Prophet's] saying, "O my Lord, indeed these are a people who do not believe."﴾ ﴿So turn away from them and say, "Peace." But they will soon know.﴾

When He, exalted is He, mentioned the state of the people of Paradise and the joyful tidings that are said to them, He followed that with mention of the state of the disbelievers and what they reply with when they are questioned. ʿAbdullah [ibn Masʿud] read *wa-hum fīhā* (in it), meaning in Hell, while the majority read *wa-hum fīhi* (in it), meaning in the punishment. It is reported from al-Ḍaḥḥāk: the criminal will be placed in a coffin of fire, then it will be sealed over him, and he will remain in it forever, seeing nothing and seen by no one.

﴿It will not be lightened for them﴾: that is, it will not be eased or reduced, from the expression *fatarat ʿanhu al-ḥummā* ("the fever subsided from him"), when it calmed a little and its heat decreased. *Al-mubliss* is the one who is silent and despairing of good.

﴿(And We did not wrong them)﴾: that is, We did not place the punishment upon one who does not deserve it.

﴿But they were the wrongdoers﴾: that is, those who placed disbelief in the place of faith, and by that they wronged themselves. The majority read *al-ẓālimīna* (the wrongdoers) in the accusative, treating *hum* as a *faṣl* (a separating pronoun, i.e., a particle of separation between subject and predicate, "they" here being not a subject but an intervening element). ʿAbdullah and the two grammarians Abu Zayd read *al-ẓālimūna* in the nominative, treating *hum* as the subject (*mubtada'*, the topic) and the following as its predicate (*khabar*). Abu ʿAmr al-Jarmi mentioned that the dialect of Tamim is to make what is a *faṣl* for others a subject (*mubtada'*), and to put the following in the nominative as the predicate. Abu Zayd said: "I heard them reading: *tajidūhu ʿinda Allāhi huwa khayrun wa-aʿẓamu ajran*," meaning with the nominative on *khayrun wa-aʿẓamu*. Qays ibn Dhurayj said:

*We yearn for Layla while you have left her, and you were over her in gatherings, you are more capable.*

Sibawayh said: Ruʾba used to say: "I think Zayd is he is better than you," meaning with the nominative.

﴿And they will call, "O Malik"﴾: it has already been stated that they are *mubliṣūn*, that is, silent. These are their states at different, extended times, so there is no contradiction between their silence and their calling out. The majority read *yā mālik*. ʿAbdullah, ʿAli, Ibn Wathhab, and al-Aʿmash read *yā māl*, by apocope (*tarkhīm*, the clipping of the end of a vocative), according to the dialect of the one who awaits the (remaining) letter. Abu al-Sirar al-Ghanawi read *yā mālu*, with a *ḍamma* as a built form, making it a name in its own right. The *lām* in *li-yaqḍi* is the *lām* of request and desire. The meaning: "Let Him cause us to die once, so that our punishment does not repeat," like His saying: ﴿So Moses struck him and ended his life﴾ [al-Qasas 28:15], that is, caused him to die.

﴿(He said)﴾: that is, Malik. ﴿Indeed, you will remain﴾: that is, you will stay in the Fire and will not depart from it. Ibn ʿAbbas said: he answers them after a thousand years had passed; Nawf said: after a hundred; it was said: eighty; and ʿAbdullah ibn ʿAmr said: forty.

﴿We have certainly brought you the truth﴾: it appears that this is the speech of Allah, exalted is He. It was also said: it is the speech of some of the angels, as one of a leader's servants says: "We informed you and we did such-and-such to you." It was said: it is possible that ﴿We have certainly brought you﴾ is the speech of Allah to the Quraysh, following the narration of the disbelievers' exchange with Malik, and in this there is a warning and intimidation, meaning: "Look at how your condition will be."

﴿Or have they decided a matter?﴾: the pronoun refers to the Quraysh, that is, "rather, they have firmly determined a matter of their scheming against the Messenger and their plotting," ﴿then, indeed, We are the decreers﴾, that is, of Our scheme, just as they decided their scheme, like His saying: ﴿Or do they intend a scheme? But those who disbelieve, they are the ones who will be ensnared﴾ [al-Tur 52:42]. They used to confer secretly and hasten among themselves regarding the matter of the Messenger, so He, exalted is He, said: ﴿Or do they think that We do not hear their secrets﴾, which is what a man speaks to himself or to another in an empty place. ﴿And their private talk﴾: which is what they speak among themselves. ﴿Yes﴾: that is, We hear it. ﴿Our messengers﴾: and they are the recording angels.

﴿Say, "If the Most Merciful had a son"﴾, as you say, ﴿then I would be the first﴾ to worship Him on that basis, but there is no such thing for Him. Al-Zamakhshari took up this statement and admired it for its eloquence, saying: "If the Most Merciful had a son, and that were established and proven by a sound proof they put forward and a clear argument they offered, then I would be the first to glorify that son and the quickest of you to obey Him and submit to Him, just as a man honors the son of a king because of his father's greatness." This is a statement given in the manner of supposition and illustration for a purpose, which is the emphasis in negating a son and dwelling at length upon it, so that the speaker leaves no doubt except one that is dissolved, together with expressing firmness of foot in the domain of monotheism. For he linked worship to the existence of a son, which is impossible in itself, so what was linked to it was likewise impossible. Thus it is in the form of affirming existence and worship, and in meaning it negates them in the most eloquent and forceful ways. Then al-Zamakhshari said: "Its parallel is that a Qadarite (*ʿadlī*) says to a Jabrite (*mujbir*)" — then he mentioned a statement that deserves disciplining, even the sword; I have exempted my book from mentioning it. Then he said: "People have strained themselves with what they brought out from this noble style, full of subtleties and benefits that stand independently for monotheism in its most eloquent aspects." It was said: "If the Most Merciful had a son, according to your claim, then I would be the first of the monotheists, the ones who worship Allah and deny their statement of ascribing a son to Him." It was also said: "If the Most Merciful had a son, then I would be the first of the *āniftīn* (those who are disdainful), from having a son for Him from a servant who is worshipped, for when his disdain is intense, he is a servant and a worshipper." Some read *ʿabidīn* (with a different vowel pattern). It was also said: the *in* here is negating, meaning: "Allah did not have a son, so I am the first to say this, to worship and to affirm His oneness."

It is related that al-Naḍr ibn ʿAbd al-Dar ibn Qusayy said: "The angels are the daughters of Allah." So this verse was revealed, and al-Naḍr said: "Do you not see that He has confirmed me?" Al-Walid ibn al-Mughira said to him: "He did not confirm you; rather He said: *If the Most Merciful had a son*, then I would be the first of the monotheists of Mecca to affirm that He has no son." End of quotation.

As for the view that *in* means "if, according to your claim," it is the statement of Mujahid. As for the statement "then I would be the first of the *āniftīn*," it is the statement of a group, which Abu Hatim related from them without naming any of them. This is supported by the reading of al-Sulami and al-Yamani: *al-ʿabidīn*. And a reading mentioned by al-Khalil ibn Ahmad in his book *al-ʿAyn* is *al-ʿabdīn*, with the *bāʾ* sunnah (the vowel is sukūn), a lightened form of *al-ʿabidīn* with *kasra*. The author of *al-Lawāmiḥ* mentioned that it was transmitted from Ibn ʿAbbas regarding the meaning of *ʿābidīn* that it means *āniftīn*. Ibn ʿArafa said: it is said *ʿabada yaʿbudu, fa-huwa ʿabd*, and rarely is it said *ʿābid*. The Qur'an does not come with the rare or the anomalous in language. Then he said: "like the statement of Mujahid." Al-Farazdaq said:

*Those are my fathers, so bring me the like of them, and I disdain (aʿbud) to satirize Kulayb in my own tribe.*

That is: I am disdainful (*ānif*) and I refuse. Another said:

*Whenever the one who has affection wills, he cuts off his friend, and he disdains (yaʿbud) over him, undoubtedly, in injustice.*

As for the view that *in* is negating, it is related from Ibn ʿAbbas, al-Hasan, al-Suddi, Qatada, Ibn Zayd, and Zuhayr ibn Muhammad. Makki said: it is not permissible for *in* to mean *mā* (negating), because that implies that you negated a son from Allah only in the past and not in the future, and this is impossible. End of quotation. But nothing impossible follows from it, because *kāna* may be used for what endures and does not cease, as in your saying: *(wa-kāna Allāhu ghafūran raḥīman)* ("and Allah was Forgiving, Merciful"), meaning: He has not ceased to be so. So the meaning is: "what was and what will be." Abu Hatim said: *al-ʿabid*, with the *kasra* on the *bāʾ*, means one who is very angry. Abu ʿUbayda said: its meaning is "the first of the deniers," and the Arabs say *ʿabadanī ḥaqqī*, meaning "my right denied me." Some read *waladun* with two *fatḥas*; ʿAbdullah, Ibn Wathhab, Talha, and al-Aʿmash read it with a *ḍamma* on the *wāw* and sukūn on the *lām*.

Then He said: ﴿Glory be to the Lord of the heavens and the earth, the Lord of the Throne, above what they describe﴾, that is, above attributing a son to Him. The meaning: removal of knowledge must be necessary existence, and whatever is so is a single absolute being that does not accept division. A son (*walad*) is an expression for a part of a thing separating from it so that a person like it is produced from it, and this occurs only in what is by its nature capable of division, and this is impossible with respect to Him, exalted is He, so the affirmation of a son is precluded. When this decisive proof was mentioned, He said: ﴿So leave them to plunge﴾, that is, into their falsehood, ﴿and play﴾, that is, in their worldly life. The apparent sense of these two commands is a truce and abandonment, and this is among what was abrogated (*nusikha*, i.e., superseded by a later ruling) by the verse of the sword. The majority read ﴿until they encounter﴾ (*yulāqū*), while Abu Jaʿfar, Ibn Muhaysin, ʿUbayd ibn ʿAqil, and from Abu ʿAmr read *yalqawā*, the imperfect of *laqiya*.

﴿Their Day which they are promised﴾: the Day of Resurrection. ʿIkrima and others said: the Day of Badr. He attributed the day to them, because it is the one in which their destruction and punishment occur. The majority read ﴿God (*ilāh*) in both﴾. ʿUmar, ʿAbdullah, Ubayy, ʿAli, al-Ḥakam ibn Abi al-ʿAliya, Bilal ibn Abi Burda, Ibn Yaʿmar, Jabir, Ibn Zayd, ʿUmar ibn ʿAbd al-ʿAziz, Abu al-Shaykh al-Hunaʾi, Humayd, Ibn Miqsam, and Ibn al-Sumayfaʿ read *Allāh* in both. The meaning of *ilāh*: one who is worshipped by it (the prepositional phrase is attached), and the meaning: He is worshipped in the heaven and worshipped on the earth. The returning pronoun to the relative is omitted, its estimated form being: "He is a god," as is omitted in their saying: *mā anā bi-alladhī qā'ilun laka shay'an* ("I am not the one who says anything to you"). Its length was made acceptable by the conjunction following it, as the length of *qā'il* was made acceptable in *qā'il laka shay'an* by the operative element (*muʿawwal*). As for the one who reads *Allāh*, he likewise includes in it the meaning of "the one worshipped," as a proper noun is given the sense of an attribute in phrases such as "he is Ḥātim in Ṭayyiʾ," meaning "he is generous in Ṭayyiʾ." It is also permissible that the relative clause be the prepositional phrase, and the meaning: He is in both by divinity and lordship, since it is impossible to take it as "settled" (in the literal sense). In His saying "and in the earth," there is a negation of their deities which were worshipped on the earth.

﴿And with Him is the knowledge of the Hour﴾: that is, knowledge of the exact time of its establishment, which He, exalted is He, has kept exclusively to Himself. The majority read ﴿you will be returned﴾ (*yurjaʿūn*) with the third-person *yāʾ*, while Nafiʿ, ʿAsim, and the two Madanis (Abu Jaʿfar and Shayba) read it with the second-person *tāʾ* (*turjaʿūn*). In both readings it is passive. It was also read with a *fatḥa* on the second-person *tāʾ*, active. The majority read it with the third-person *yāʾ* and a shadda on the *dāl*, and from ʿAbdullah (or another, as recorded) with the second-person *tāʾ* and a shadda on the *dāl*. The meaning: "Those whom they invoke besides Him, their gods, do not possess intercession with Allah." Qatada said: He excepted from those worshipped besides Allah ʿIsa, ʿUzayr, and the angels, for they possess intercession, since Allah grants them that ability, as they are among those who testify to the truth and they know it through their conditions. So the exception on this reading is continuous (*muttaṣil*). Mujahid and others said: "From those for whom intercession is made?" As if He said: "These angels, ʿUzayr, and ʿIsa do not intercede except for one who testifies to the truth, and he knows it," i.e., the monotheism. They said: The exception on this reading is disjunctive (*munfaṣil*), as if He said: "But whoever testifies to the truth, these will intercede for him." This understanding they proposed may allow the exception to be continuous, since the thing excepted from would be omitted, as if He said: "Those who are invoked besides Him do not possess intercession for anyone, except for one who testifies to the truth," so it is an exception from the omitted object, as the poet said:

*Salim escaped, and the soul from him was by his jaw, and he did not escape except with the sheath of a sword and a loincloth.*

That is, "he was not saved except as the sheath of a sword," so it is an exception from the ones granted intercession (al-mashfu' fihim), in which the omission is permissible, and it is a *muttasil* (connected) exception (istithna' muttasil, "connected exception," where the excluded item belongs to the same category as what precedes it). If you take it as an exception from "those they call upon" (alladhina yad'una), it becomes a *munfasil* (disjunct) exception, and the meaning is: "their gods will not possess intercession," meaning the idols and images, as they claimed that they were their intercessors with God. "But whoever testified to the truth," which is the affirmation of God's oneness, "and they know what they testified to," is the one who possesses intercession. If the angels are included among "those they call upon," then it is a connected exception.

The majority read ﴿فَأَنَّى يُؤْفَكُونَ﴾ with the ya' of the third person (ya' al-ghayba), in agreement with His saying ﴿وَلَئِنْ سَأَلْتَهُمْ﴾, meaning: how are they turned away from worshipping the One whom they acknowledge as the creator of the world? 'Abd al-Warith, from Abu 'Amr, read it with the ta' of address (ta' al-khitab).

The majority read ﴿وَقِيلَهُ﴾ in the accusative (manṣūb). Al-Akhfash said it is coordinated with *sirrahum wa-najwahum* ("their secret and their private conference"). He also said it is coordinated with the verb of *qala* ("and he said"). Al-Zajjaj said it is coordinated with the position (mahall) of *al-sa'a* in His saying ﴿وَعِنْدَهُ عِلْمُ السَّاعَةِ﴾. It is also said that it is coordinated with the omitted object of *yaktubūn* (they record), meaning they record their words and their deeds. And it is said that it is coordinated with the object of *ya'lamūn* (they know), meaning they know the truth. ﴿وَقِيلَهُ يَا رَبِّ﴾ is a statement that is hardly intelligible. It is also said that it is in the accusative by an implied verb, meaning "and He knows his saying."

Al-Sulami, Ibn Wathhab, 'Asim, al-A'mash, and Hamzah read ﴿وَقِيلِهِ﴾ in the genitive (khafḍ). This is explained as coordination with *al-sa'a* (the Hour), or as the *waw* of oath (waw al-qasam), with the answer omitted, meaning: "they will surely be helped," or "I will surely do to them what I wish."

Al-A'raj, Abu Qilabah, Mujahid, al-Hasan, Qatadah, and Muslim ibn Jundab read ﴿وَقِيلُهُ﴾ in the nominative (raf'). This is explained as coordination with "knowledge of the Hour" (*'ilm al-sa'a*), with an omitted genitive-modifying noun (hadhf mudaf), meaning "and the knowledge of his saying," where the modified noun is omitted and the modifier (al-mudaf ilayhi) is put in its place. This was reported from al-Kisa'i. It is also explained as an inceptive (mubtada'), whose predicate is *ya rabbi innahum la yu'minun*, or as a predicate that is omitted, with the estimate being "heard" or "accepted." In that case the clause of the call and what follows it is in the accusative position by ﴿وَقِيلُهُ﴾.

Abu Qilabah read *ya rabba* with a fatha on the ba', intending *ya rabban*, as you say *ya ghulamu*. It may be explained according to al-Akhfash's permission: *ya qawma*, with a fatha and the deletion of the alif, with the fatha standing in for it.

Al-Zamakhshari said: "What they said, meaning the coordination, is not strong in meaning, together with the occurrence of a separation between the coordinated and the coordinated-to by something that does not fit well as a parenthetical insertion (i'tiraḍ), and with the disharmony of the composition. Stronger than that is that the genitive and the accusative should be by implying the particle of oath and omitting it, and the nominative should be like their saying: *aymunu Allah* ("by God's right"), *amanatu Allah* ("by God's trust"), *yamin Allah* ("God's oath"), *la'amruka* ("by your life"). And His saying ﴿إِنَّ هَؤُلَاءِ قَوْمٌ لَا يُؤْمِنُونَ﴾ would be the answer to the oath, as if He said: 'And He swore by his saying, or by his saying, "O Lord, my oath..."'"

﴿إِنَّ هَؤُلَاءِ قَوْمٌ لَا يُؤْمِنُونَ﴾ ("Indeed these are a people who will not believe"), and God's swearing by His saying, is an elevation of him and an honouring of his supplication and his appeal to Him. End of quotation. This is contrary to the apparent meaning of the speech, since it appears that His saying "O Lord, indeed these are a people who will not believe" is connected to *qilihi* ("his saying"). And from the speech of the one upon whom be peace: if *inna ha'ula'* is the answer to the oath, then it is from God's report about them and His speech. The pronoun in ﴿وَقِيلِهِ﴾ refers to the Messenger, who is addressed by His saying ﴿فَاصْفَحْ عَنْهُمْ﴾, meaning: turn away from them and leave them. ﴿وَقُلْ سَلَامٌ﴾, meaning: the matter is peace. ﴿فَسَوْفَ يَعْلَمُونَ﴾ is a threat and warning to them and an admonition, and it is abrogated (mansukh) by the verse of the sword (ayat al-sayf).

The majority read ﴿يَعْلَمُونَ﴾ with the ya' of the third person, as in ﴿فَاصْفَحْ عَنْهُمْ﴾. Abu Ja'far, al-Hasan, al-A'raj, Nafi', and Hisham read it with the ta' of address.

al-Suddi said: "*Wa-qul salam*" means "good," in exchange for their evil. Muqatil said: "Offer them kindness." al-Mawardi reported: "Say that by which you are safe from their evil."

**Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 43, verses 74–89 (part 1 of 2)**

﴿Indeed, the criminals will abide forever in the punishment of Hell.﴾ ﴿It will not be lightened for them, and they will be in despair therein.﴾ ﴿We did not wrong them, but they were the wrongdoers.﴾ ﴿And they will call, "O Malik, let your Lord put an end to us." He will say, "Indeed, you will remain."﴾ ﴿We have certainly brought you the truth, but most of you are averse to the truth.﴾ ﴿Or have they decided on a matter? Then, indeed, We are the decreers.﴾ ﴿Or do they think that We do not hear their secrets and their private talk? Yes, and Our messengers are with them, recording.﴾ ﴿Say, "If the Most Merciful had a son, then I would be the first of the worshippers."﴾ ﴿Glory be to the Lord of the heavens and the earth, the Lord of the Throne, above what they describe.﴾ ﴿So leave them to plunge in vain talk and play until they encounter their Day which they are promised.﴾ ﴿And He is the One who is God in the heaven and God on the earth, and He is the All-Wise, the All-Knowing.﴾ ﴿Blessed is He to whom belongs the dominion of the heavens and the earth and what is between them, and with Him is the knowledge of the Hour, and to Him you will be returned.﴾ ﴿Those whom they invoke besides Him do not possess intercession, except one who testifies to the truth while they know.﴾ ﴿And if you asked them who created them, they would surely say, "Allah." So how are they deluded?﴾ ﴿And [the Prophet's] saying, "O my Lord, indeed these are a people who do not believe."﴾ ﴿So turn away from them and say, "Peace." But they will soon know.﴾

When He, exalted is He, mentioned the state of the people of Paradise and the joyful tidings that are said to them, He followed that with mention of the state of the disbelievers and what they reply with when they are questioned. ʿAbdullah [ibn Masʿud] read *wa-hum fīhā* (in it), meaning in Hell, while the majority read *wa-hum fīhi* (in it), meaning in the punishment. It is reported from al-Ḍaḥḥāk: the criminal will be placed in a coffin of fire, then it will be sealed over him, and he will remain in it forever, seeing nothing and seen by no one.

﴿It will not be lightened for them﴾: that is, it will not be eased or reduced, from the expression *fatarat ʿanhu al-ḥummā* ("the fever subsided from him"), when it calmed a little and its heat decreased. *Al-mubliss* is the one who is silent and despairing of good.

﴿(And We did not wrong them)﴾: that is, We did not place the punishment upon one who does not deserve it.

﴿But they were the wrongdoers﴾: that is, those who placed disbelief in the place of faith, and by that they wronged themselves. The majority read *al-ẓālimīna* (the wrongdoers) in the accusative, treating *hum* as a *faṣl* (a separating pronoun, i.e., a particle of separation between subject and predicate, "they" here being not a subject but an intervening element). ʿAbdullah and the two grammarians Abu Zayd read *al-ẓālimūna* in the nominative, treating *hum* as the subject (*mubtada'*, the topic) and the following as its predicate (*khabar*). Abu ʿAmr al-Jarmi mentioned that the dialect of Tamim is to make what is a *faṣl* for others a subject (*mubtada'*), and to put the following in the nominative as the predicate. Abu Zayd said: "I heard them reading: *tajidūhu ʿinda Allāhi huwa khayrun wa-aʿẓamu ajran*," meaning with the nominative on *khayrun wa-aʿẓamu*. Qays ibn Dhurayj said:

*We yearn for Layla while you have left her, and you were over her in gatherings, you are more capable.*

Sibawayh said: Ruʾba used to say: "I think Zayd is he is better than you," meaning with the nominative.

﴿And they will call, "O Malik"﴾: it has already been stated that they are *mubliṣūn*, that is, silent. These are their states at different, extended times, so there is no contradiction between their silence and their calling out. The majority read *yā mālik*. ʿAbdullah, ʿAli, Ibn Wathhab, and al-Aʿmash read *yā māl*, by apocope (*tarkhīm*, the clipping of the end of a vocative), according to the dialect of the one who awaits the (remaining) letter. Abu al-Sirar al-Ghanawi read *yā mālu*, with a *ḍamma* as a built form, making it a name in its own right. The *lām* in *li-yaqḍi* is the *lām* of request and desire. The meaning: "Let Him cause us to die once, so that our punishment does not repeat," like His saying: ﴿So Moses struck him and ended his life﴾ [al-Qasas 28:15], that is, caused him to die.

﴿(He said)﴾: that is, Malik. ﴿Indeed, you will remain﴾: that is, you will stay in the Fire and will not depart from it. Ibn ʿAbbas said: he answers them after a thousand years had passed; Nawf said: after a hundred; it was said: eighty; and ʿAbdullah ibn ʿAmr said: forty.

﴿We have certainly brought you the truth﴾: it appears that this is the speech of Allah, exalted is He. It was also said: it is the speech of some of the angels, as one of a leader's servants says: "We informed you and we did such-and-such to you." It was said: it is possible that ﴿We have certainly brought you﴾ is the speech of Allah to the Quraysh, following the narration of the disbelievers' exchange with Malik, and in this there is a warning and intimidation, meaning: "Look at how your condition will be."

﴿Or have they decided a matter?﴾: the pronoun refers to the Quraysh, that is, "rather, they have firmly determined a matter of their scheming against the Messenger and their plotting," ﴿then, indeed, We are the decreers﴾, that is, of Our scheme, just as they decided their scheme, like His saying: ﴿Or do they intend a scheme? But those who disbelieve, they are the ones who will be ensnared﴾ [al-Tur 52:42]. They used to confer secretly and hasten among themselves regarding the matter of the Messenger, so He, exalted is He, said: ﴿Or do they think that We do not hear their secrets﴾, which is what a man speaks to himself or to another in an empty place. ﴿And their private talk﴾: which is what they speak among themselves. ﴿Yes﴾: that is, We hear it. ﴿Our messengers﴾: and they are the recording angels.

﴿Say, "If the Most Merciful had a son"﴾, as you say, ﴿then I would be the first﴾ to worship Him on that basis, but there is no such thing for Him. Al-Zamakhshari took up this statement and admired it for its eloquence, saying: "If the Most Merciful had a son, and that were established and proven by a sound proof they put forward and a clear argument they offered, then I would be the first to glorify that son and the quickest of you to obey Him and submit to Him, just as a man honors the son of a king because of his father's greatness." This is a statement given in the manner of supposition and illustration for a purpose, which is the emphasis in negating a son and dwelling at length upon it, so that the speaker leaves no doubt except one that is dissolved, together with expressing firmness of foot in the domain of monotheism. For he linked worship to the existence of a son, which is impossible in itself, so what was linked to it was likewise impossible. Thus it is in the form of affirming existence and worship, and in meaning it negates them in the most eloquent and forceful ways. Then al-Zamakhshari said: "Its parallel is that a Qadarite (*ʿadlī*) says to a Jabrite (*mujbir*)" — then he mentioned a statement that deserves disciplining, even the sword; I have exempted my book from mentioning it. Then he said: "People have strained themselves with what they brought out from this noble style, full of subtleties and benefits that stand independently for monotheism in its most eloquent aspects." It was said: "If the Most Merciful had a son, according to your claim, then I would be the first of the monotheists, the ones who worship Allah and deny their statement of ascribing a son to Him." It was also said: "If the Most Merciful had a son, then I would be the first of the *āniftīn* (those who are disdainful), from having a son for Him from a servant who is worshipped, for when his disdain is intense, he is a servant and a worshipper." Some read *ʿabidīn* (with a different vowel pattern). It was also said: the *in* here is negating, meaning: "Allah did not have a son, so I am the first to say this, to worship and to affirm His oneness."

It is related that al-Naḍr ibn ʿAbd al-Dar ibn Qusayy said: "The angels are the daughters of Allah." So this verse was revealed, and al-Naḍr said: "Do you not see that He has confirmed me?" Al-Walid ibn al-Mughira said to him: "He did not confirm you; rather He said: *If the Most Merciful had a son*, then I would be the first of the monotheists of Mecca to affirm that He has no son." End of quotation.

As for the view that *in* means "if, according to your claim," it is the statement of Mujahid. As for the statement "then I would be the first of the *āniftīn*," it is the statement of a group, which Abu Hatim related from them without naming any of them. This is supported by the reading of al-Sulami and al-Yamani: *al-ʿabidīn*. And a reading mentioned by al-Khalil ibn Ahmad in his book *al-ʿAyn* is *al-ʿabdīn*, with the *bāʾ* sunnah (the vowel is sukūn), a lightened form of *al-ʿabidīn* with *kasra*. The author of *al-Lawāmiḥ* mentioned that it was transmitted from Ibn ʿAbbas regarding the meaning of *ʿābidīn* that it means *āniftīn*. Ibn ʿArafa said: it is said *ʿabada yaʿbudu, fa-huwa ʿabd*, and rarely is it said *ʿābid*. The Qur'an does not come with the rare or the anomalous in language. Then he said: "like the statement of Mujahid." Al-Farazdaq said:

*Those are my fathers, so bring me the like of them, and I disdain (aʿbud) to satirize Kulayb in my own tribe.*

That is: I am disdainful (*ānif*) and I refuse. Another said:

*Whenever the one who has affection wills, he cuts off his friend, and he disdains (yaʿbud) over him, undoubtedly, in injustice.*

As for the view that *in* is negating, it is related from Ibn ʿAbbas, al-Hasan, al-Suddi, Qatada, Ibn Zayd, and Zuhayr ibn Muhammad. Makki said: it is not permissible for *in* to mean *mā* (negating), because that implies that you negated a son from Allah only in the past and not in the future, and this is impossible. End of quotation. But nothing impossible follows from it, because *kāna* may be used for what endures and does not cease, as in your saying: *(wa-kāna Allāhu ghafūran raḥīman)* ("and Allah was Forgiving, Merciful"), meaning: He has not ceased to be so. So the meaning is: "what was and what will be." Abu Hatim said: *al-ʿabid*, with the *kasra* on the *bāʾ*, means one who is very angry. Abu ʿUbayda said: its meaning is "the first of the deniers," and the Arabs say *ʿabadanī ḥaqqī*, meaning "my right denied me." Some read *waladun* with two *fatḥas*; ʿAbdullah, Ibn Wathhab, Talha, and al-Aʿmash read it with a *ḍamma* on the *wāw* and sukūn on the *lām*.

Then He said: ﴿Glory be to the Lord of the heavens and the earth, the Lord of the Throne, above what they describe﴾, that is, above attributing a son to Him. The meaning: removal of knowledge must be necessary existence, and whatever is so is a single absolute being that does not accept division. A son (*walad*) is an expression for a part of a thing separating from it so that a person like it is produced from it, and this occurs only in what is by its nature capable of division, and this is impossible with respect to Him, exalted is He, so the affirmation of a son is precluded. When this decisive proof was mentioned, He said: ﴿So leave them to plunge﴾, that is, into their falsehood, ﴿and play﴾, that is, in their worldly life. The apparent sense of these two commands is a truce and abandonment, and this is among what was abrogated (*nusikha*, i.e., superseded by a later ruling) by the verse of the sword. The majority read ﴿until they encounter﴾ (*yulāqū*), while Abu Jaʿfar, Ibn Muhaysin, ʿUbayd ibn ʿAqil, and from Abu ʿAmr read *yalqawā*, the imperfect of *laqiya*.

﴿Their Day which they are promised﴾: the Day of Resurrection. ʿIkrima and others said: the Day of Badr. He attributed the day to them, because it is the one in which their destruction and punishment occur. The majority read ﴿God (*ilāh*) in both﴾. ʿUmar, ʿAbdullah, Ubayy, ʿAli, al-Ḥakam ibn Abi al-ʿAliya, Bilal ibn Abi Burda, Ibn Yaʿmar, Jabir, Ibn Zayd, ʿUmar ibn ʿAbd al-ʿAziz, Abu al-Shaykh al-Hunaʾi, Humayd, Ibn Miqsam, and Ibn al-Sumayfaʿ read *Allāh* in both. The meaning of *ilāh*: one who is worshipped by it (the prepositional phrase is attached), and the meaning: He is worshipped in the heaven and worshipped on the earth. The returning pronoun to the relative is omitted, its estimated form being: "He is a god," as is omitted in their saying: *mā anā bi-alladhī qā'ilun laka shay'an* ("I am not the one who says anything to you"). Its length was made acceptable by the conjunction following it, as the length of *qā'il* was made acceptable in *qā'il laka shay'an* by the operative element (*muʿawwal*). As for the one who reads *Allāh*, he likewise includes in it the meaning of "the one worshipped," as a proper noun is given the sense of an attribute in phrases such as "he is Ḥātim in Ṭayyiʾ," meaning "he is generous in Ṭayyiʾ." It is also permissible that the relative clause be the prepositional phrase, and the meaning: He is in both by divinity and lordship, since it is impossible to take it as "settled" (in the literal sense). In His saying "and in the earth," there is a negation of their deities which were worshipped on the earth.

﴿And with Him is the knowledge of the Hour﴾: that is, knowledge of the exact time of its establishment, which He, exalted is He, has kept exclusively to Himself. The majority read ﴿you will be returned﴾ (*yurjaʿūn*) with the third-person *yāʾ*, while Nafiʿ, ʿAsim, and the two Madanis (Abu Jaʿfar and Shayba) read it with the second-person *tāʾ* (*turjaʿūn*). In both readings it is passive. It was also read with a *fatḥa* on the second-person *tāʾ*, active. The majority read it with the third-person *yāʾ* and a shadda on the *dāl*, and from ʿAbdullah (or another, as recorded) with the second-person *tāʾ* and a shadda on the *dāl*. The meaning: "Those whom they invoke besides Him, their gods, do not possess intercession with Allah." Qatada said: He excepted from those worshipped besides Allah ʿIsa, ʿUzayr, and the angels, for they possess intercession, since Allah grants them that ability, as they are among those who testify to the truth and they know it through their conditions. So the exception on this reading is continuous (*muttaṣil*). Mujahid and others said: "From those for whom intercession is made?" As if He said: "These angels, ʿUzayr, and ʿIsa do not intercede except for one who testifies to the truth, and he knows it," i.e., the monotheism. They said: The exception on this reading is disjunctive (*munfaṣil*), as if He said: "But whoever testifies to the truth, these will intercede for him." This understanding they proposed may allow the exception to be continuous, since the thing excepted from would be omitted, as if He said: "Those who are invoked besides Him do not possess intercession for anyone, except for one who testifies to the truth," so it is an exception from the omitted object, as the poet said:

*Salim escaped, and the soul from him was by his jaw, and he did not escape except with the sheath of a sword and a loincloth.*

That is, "he was not saved except as the sheath of a sword," so it is an exception from the ones granted intercession (al-mashfu' fihim), in which the omission is permissible, and it is a *muttasil* (connected) exception (istithna' muttasil, "connected exception," where the excluded item belongs to the same category as what precedes it). If you take it as an exception from "those they call upon" (alladhina yad'una), it becomes a *munfasil* (disjunct) exception, and the meaning is: "their gods will not possess intercession," meaning the idols and images, as they claimed that they were their intercessors with God. "But whoever testified to the truth," which is the affirmation of God's oneness, "and they know what they testified to," is the one who possesses intercession. If the angels are included among "those they call upon," then it is a connected exception.

The majority read ﴿فَأَنَّى يُؤْفَكُونَ﴾ with the ya' of the third person (ya' al-ghayba), in agreement with His saying ﴿وَلَئِنْ سَأَلْتَهُمْ﴾, meaning: how are they turned away from worshipping the One whom they acknowledge as the creator of the world? 'Abd al-Warith, from Abu 'Amr, read it with the ta' of address (ta' al-khitab).

The majority read ﴿وَقِيلَهُ﴾ in the accusative (manṣūb). Al-Akhfash said it is coordinated with *sirrahum wa-najwahum* ("their secret and their private conference"). He also said it is coordinated with the verb of *qala* ("and he said"). Al-Zajjaj said it is coordinated with the position (mahall) of *al-sa'a* in His saying ﴿وَعِنْدَهُ عِلْمُ السَّاعَةِ﴾. It is also said that it is coordinated with the omitted object of *yaktubūn* (they record), meaning they record their words and their deeds. And it is said that it is coordinated with the object of *ya'lamūn* (they know), meaning they know the truth. ﴿وَقِيلَهُ يَا رَبِّ﴾ is a statement that is hardly intelligible. It is also said that it is in the accusative by an implied verb, meaning "and He knows his saying."

Al-Sulami, Ibn Wathhab, 'Asim, al-A'mash, and Hamzah read ﴿وَقِيلِهِ﴾ in the genitive (khafḍ). This is explained as coordination with *al-sa'a* (the Hour), or as the *waw* of oath (waw al-qasam), with the answer omitted, meaning: "they will surely be helped," or "I will surely do to them what I wish."

Al-A'raj, Abu Qilabah, Mujahid, al-Hasan, Qatadah, and Muslim ibn Jundab read ﴿وَقِيلُهُ﴾ in the nominative (raf'). This is explained as coordination with "knowledge of the Hour" (*'ilm al-sa'a*), with an omitted genitive-modifying noun (hadhf mudaf), meaning "and the knowledge of his saying," where the modified noun is omitted and the modifier (al-mudaf ilayhi) is put in its place. This was reported from al-Kisa'i. It is also explained as an inceptive (mubtada'), whose predicate is *ya rabbi innahum la yu'minun*, or as a predicate that is omitted, with the estimate being "heard" or "accepted." In that case the clause of the call and what follows it is in the accusative position by ﴿وَقِيلُهُ﴾.

Abu Qilabah read *ya rabba* with a fatha on the ba', intending *ya rabban*, as you say *ya ghulamu*. It may be explained according to al-Akhfash's permission: *ya qawma*, with a fatha and the deletion of the alif, with the fatha standing in for it.

Al-Zamakhshari said: "What they said, meaning the coordination, is not strong in meaning, together with the occurrence of a separation between the coordinated and the coordinated-to by something that does not fit well as a parenthetical insertion (i'tiraḍ), and with the disharmony of the composition. Stronger than that is that the genitive and the accusative should be by implying the particle of oath and omitting it, and the nominative should be like their saying: *aymunu Allah* ("by God's right"), *amanatu Allah* ("by God's trust"), *yamin Allah* ("God's oath"), *la'amruka* ("by your life"). And His saying ﴿إِنَّ هَؤُلَاءِ قَوْمٌ لَا يُؤْمِنُونَ﴾ would be the answer to the oath, as if He said: 'And He swore by his saying, or by his saying, "O Lord, my oath..."'"

﴿إِنَّ هَؤُلَاءِ قَوْمٌ لَا يُؤْمِنُونَ﴾ ("Indeed these are a people who will not believe"), and God's swearing by His saying, is an elevation of him and an honouring of his supplication and his appeal to Him. End of quotation. This is contrary to the apparent meaning of the speech, since it appears that His saying "O Lord, indeed these are a people who will not believe" is connected to *qilihi* ("his saying"). And from the speech of the one upon whom be peace: if *inna ha'ula'* is the answer to the oath, then it is from God's report about them and His speech. The pronoun in ﴿وَقِيلِهِ﴾ refers to the Messenger, who is addressed by His saying ﴿فَاصْفَحْ عَنْهُمْ﴾, meaning: turn away from them and leave them. ﴿وَقُلْ سَلَامٌ﴾, meaning: the matter is peace. ﴿فَسَوْفَ يَعْلَمُونَ﴾ is a threat and warning to them and an admonition, and it is abrogated (mansukh) by the verse of the sword (ayat al-sayf).

The majority read ﴿يَعْلَمُونَ﴾ with the ya' of the third person, as in ﴿فَاصْفَحْ عَنْهُمْ﴾. Abu Ja'far, al-Hasan, al-A'raj, Nafi', and Hisham read it with the ta' of address.

al-Suddi said: "*Wa-qul salam*" means "good," in exchange for their evil. Muqatil said: "Offer them kindness." al-Mawardi reported: "Say that by which you are safe from their evil."

**Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 43, verses 74–89 (part 1 of 2)**

﴿Indeed, the criminals will abide forever in the punishment of Hell.﴾ ﴿It will not be lightened for them, and they will be in despair therein.﴾ ﴿We did not wrong them, but they were the wrongdoers.﴾ ﴿And they will call, "O Malik, let your Lord put an end to us." He will say, "Indeed, you will remain."﴾ ﴿We have certainly brought you the truth, but most of you are averse to the truth.﴾ ﴿Or have they decided on a matter? Then, indeed, We are the decreers.﴾ ﴿Or do they think that We do not hear their secrets and their private talk? Yes, and Our messengers are with them, recording.﴾ ﴿Say, "If the Most Merciful had a son, then I would be the first of the worshippers."﴾ ﴿Glory be to the Lord of the heavens and the earth, the Lord of the Throne, above what they describe.﴾ ﴿So leave them to plunge in vain talk and play until they encounter their Day which they are promised.﴾ ﴿And He is the One who is God in the heaven and God on the earth, and He is the All-Wise, the All-Knowing.﴾ ﴿Blessed is He to whom belongs the dominion of the heavens and the earth and what is between them, and with Him is the knowledge of the Hour, and to Him you will be returned.﴾ ﴿Those whom they invoke besides Him do not possess intercession, except one who testifies to the truth while they know.﴾ ﴿And if you asked them who created them, they would surely say, "Allah." So how are they deluded?﴾ ﴿And [the Prophet's] saying, "O my Lord, indeed these are a people who do not believe."﴾ ﴿So turn away from them and say, "Peace." But they will soon know.﴾

When He, exalted is He, mentioned the state of the people of Paradise and the joyful tidings that are said to them, He followed that with mention of the state of the disbelievers and what they reply with when they are questioned. ʿAbdullah [ibn Masʿud] read *wa-hum fīhā* (in it), meaning in Hell, while the majority read *wa-hum fīhi* (in it), meaning in the punishment. It is reported from al-Ḍaḥḥāk: the criminal will be placed in a coffin of fire, then it will be sealed over him, and he will remain in it forever, seeing nothing and seen by no one.

﴿It will not be lightened for them﴾: that is, it will not be eased or reduced, from the expression *fatarat ʿanhu al-ḥummā* ("the fever subsided from him"), when it calmed a little and its heat decreased. *Al-mubliss* is the one who is silent and despairing of good.

﴿(And We did not wrong them)﴾: that is, We did not place the punishment upon one who does not deserve it.

﴿But they were the wrongdoers﴾: that is, those who placed disbelief in the place of faith, and by that they wronged themselves. The majority read *al-ẓālimīna* (the wrongdoers) in the accusative, treating *hum* as a *faṣl* (a separating pronoun, i.e., a particle of separation between subject and predicate, "they" here being not a subject but an intervening element). ʿAbdullah and the two grammarians Abu Zayd read *al-ẓālimūna* in the nominative, treating *hum* as the subject (*mubtada'*, the topic) and the following as its predicate (*khabar*). Abu ʿAmr al-Jarmi mentioned that the dialect of Tamim is to make what is a *faṣl* for others a subject (*mubtada'*), and to put the following in the nominative as the predicate. Abu Zayd said: "I heard them reading: *tajidūhu ʿinda Allāhi huwa khayrun wa-aʿẓamu ajran*," meaning with the nominative on *khayrun wa-aʿẓamu*. Qays ibn Dhurayj said:

*We yearn for Layla while you have left her, and you were over her in gatherings, you are more capable.*

Sibawayh said: Ruʾba used to say: "I think Zayd is he is better than you," meaning with the nominative.

﴿And they will call, "O Malik"﴾: it has already been stated that they are *mubliṣūn*, that is, silent. These are their states at different, extended times, so there is no contradiction between their silence and their calling out. The majority read *yā mālik*. ʿAbdullah, ʿAli, Ibn Wathhab, and al-Aʿmash read *yā māl*, by apocope (*tarkhīm*, the clipping of the end of a vocative), according to the dialect of the one who awaits the (remaining) letter. Abu al-Sirar al-Ghanawi read *yā mālu*, with a *ḍamma* as a built form, making it a name in its own right. The *lām* in *li-yaqḍi* is the *lām* of request and desire. The meaning: "Let Him cause us to die once, so that our punishment does not repeat," like His saying: ﴿So Moses struck him and ended his life﴾ [al-Qasas 28:15], that is, caused him to die.

﴿(He said)﴾: that is, Malik. ﴿Indeed, you will remain﴾: that is, you will stay in the Fire and will not depart from it. Ibn ʿAbbas said: he answers them after a thousand years had passed; Nawf said: after a hundred; it was said: eighty; and ʿAbdullah ibn ʿAmr said: forty.

﴿We have certainly brought you the truth﴾: it appears that this is the speech of Allah, exalted is He. It was also said: it is the speech of some of the angels, as one of a leader's servants says: "We informed you and we did such-and-such to you." It was said: it is possible that ﴿We have certainly brought you﴾ is the speech of Allah to the Quraysh, following the narration of the disbelievers' exchange with Malik, and in this there is a warning and intimidation, meaning: "Look at how your condition will be."

﴿Or have they decided a matter?﴾: the pronoun refers to the Quraysh, that is, "rather, they have firmly determined a matter of their scheming against the Messenger and their plotting," ﴿then, indeed, We are the decreers﴾, that is, of Our scheme, just as they decided their scheme, like His saying: ﴿Or do they intend a scheme? But those who disbelieve, they are the ones who will be ensnared﴾ [al-Tur 52:42]. They used to confer secretly and hasten among themselves regarding the matter of the Messenger, so He, exalted is He, said: ﴿Or do they think that We do not hear their secrets﴾, which is what a man speaks to himself or to another in an empty place. ﴿And their private talk﴾: which is what they speak among themselves. ﴿Yes﴾: that is, We hear it. ﴿Our messengers﴾: and they are the recording angels.

﴿Say, "If the Most Merciful had a son"﴾, as you say, ﴿then I would be the first﴾ to worship Him on that basis, but there is no such thing for Him. Al-Zamakhshari took up this statement and admired it for its eloquence, saying: "If the Most Merciful had a son, and that were established and proven by a sound proof they put forward and a clear argument they offered, then I would be the first to glorify that son and the quickest of you to obey Him and submit to Him, just as a man honors the son of a king because of his father's greatness." This is a statement given in the manner of supposition and illustration for a purpose, which is the emphasis in negating a son and dwelling at length upon it, so that the speaker leaves no doubt except one that is dissolved, together with expressing firmness of foot in the domain of monotheism. For he linked worship to the existence of a son, which is impossible in itself, so what was linked to it was likewise impossible. Thus it is in the form of affirming existence and worship, and in meaning it negates them in the most eloquent and forceful ways. Then al-Zamakhshari said: "Its parallel is that a Qadarite (*ʿadlī*) says to a Jabrite (*mujbir*)" — then he mentioned a statement that deserves disciplining, even the sword; I have exempted my book from mentioning it. Then he said: "People have strained themselves with what they brought out from this noble style, full of subtleties and benefits that stand independently for monotheism in its most eloquent aspects." It was said: "If the Most Merciful had a son, according to your claim, then I would be the first of the monotheists, the ones who worship Allah and deny their statement of ascribing a son to Him." It was also said: "If the Most Merciful had a son, then I would be the first of the *āniftīn* (those who are disdainful), from having a son for Him from a servant who is worshipped, for when his disdain is intense, he is a servant and a worshipper." Some read *ʿabidīn* (with a different vowel pattern). It was also said: the *in* here is negating, meaning: "Allah did not have a son, so I am the first to say this, to worship and to affirm His oneness."

It is related that al-Naḍr ibn ʿAbd al-Dar ibn Qusayy said: "The angels are the daughters of Allah." So this verse was revealed, and al-Naḍr said: "Do you not see that He has confirmed me?" Al-Walid ibn al-Mughira said to him: "He did not confirm you; rather He said: *If the Most Merciful had a son*, then I would be the first of the monotheists of Mecca to affirm that He has no son." End of quotation.

As for the view that *in* means "if, according to your claim," it is the statement of Mujahid. As for the statement "then I would be the first of the *āniftīn*," it is the statement of a group, which Abu Hatim related from them without naming any of them. This is supported by the reading of al-Sulami and al-Yamani: *al-ʿabidīn*. And a reading mentioned by al-Khalil ibn Ahmad in his book *al-ʿAyn* is *al-ʿabdīn*, with the *bāʾ* sunnah (the vowel is sukūn), a lightened form of *al-ʿabidīn* with *kasra*. The author of *al-Lawāmiḥ* mentioned that it was transmitted from Ibn ʿAbbas regarding the meaning of *ʿābidīn* that it means *āniftīn*. Ibn ʿArafa said: it is said *ʿabada yaʿbudu, fa-huwa ʿabd*, and rarely is it said *ʿābid*. The Qur'an does not come with the rare or the anomalous in language. Then he said: "like the statement of Mujahid." Al-Farazdaq said:

*Those are my fathers, so bring me the like of them, and I disdain (aʿbud) to satirize Kulayb in my own tribe.*

That is: I am disdainful (*ānif*) and I refuse. Another said:

*Whenever the one who has affection wills, he cuts off his friend, and he disdains (yaʿbud) over him, undoubtedly, in injustice.*

As for the view that *in* is negating, it is related from Ibn ʿAbbas, al-Hasan, al-Suddi, Qatada, Ibn Zayd, and Zuhayr ibn Muhammad. Makki said: it is not permissible for *in* to mean *mā* (negating), because that implies that you negated a son from Allah only in the past and not in the future, and this is impossible. End of quotation. But nothing impossible follows from it, because *kāna* may be used for what endures and does not cease, as in your saying: *(wa-kāna Allāhu ghafūran raḥīman)* ("and Allah was Forgiving, Merciful"), meaning: He has not ceased to be so. So the meaning is: "what was and what will be." Abu Hatim said: *al-ʿabid*, with the *kasra* on the *bāʾ*, means one who is very angry. Abu ʿUbayda said: its meaning is "the first of the deniers," and the Arabs say *ʿabadanī ḥaqqī*, meaning "my right denied me." Some read *waladun* with two *fatḥas*; ʿAbdullah, Ibn Wathhab, Talha, and al-Aʿmash read it with a *ḍamma* on the *wāw* and sukūn on the *lām*.

Then He said: ﴿Glory be to the Lord of the heavens and the earth, the Lord of the Throne, above what they describe﴾, that is, above attributing a son to Him. The meaning: removal of knowledge must be necessary existence, and whatever is so is a single absolute being that does not accept division. A son (*walad*) is an expression for a part of a thing separating from it so that a person like it is produced from it, and this occurs only in what is by its nature capable of division, and this is impossible with respect to Him, exalted is He, so the affirmation of a son is precluded. When this decisive proof was mentioned, He said: ﴿So leave them to plunge﴾, that is, into their falsehood, ﴿and play﴾, that is, in their worldly life. The apparent sense of these two commands is a truce and abandonment, and this is among what was abrogated (*nusikha*, i.e., superseded by a later ruling) by the verse of the sword. The majority read ﴿until they encounter﴾ (*yulāqū*), while Abu Jaʿfar, Ibn Muhaysin, ʿUbayd ibn ʿAqil, and from Abu ʿAmr read *yalqawā*, the imperfect of *laqiya*.

﴿Their Day which they are promised﴾: the Day of Resurrection. ʿIkrima and others said: the Day of Badr. He attributed the day to them, because it is the one in which their destruction and punishment occur. The majority read ﴿God (*ilāh*) in both﴾. ʿUmar, ʿAbdullah, Ubayy, ʿAli, al-Ḥakam ibn Abi al-ʿAliya, Bilal ibn Abi Burda, Ibn Yaʿmar, Jabir, Ibn Zayd, ʿUmar ibn ʿAbd al-ʿAziz, Abu al-Shaykh al-Hunaʾi, Humayd, Ibn Miqsam, and Ibn al-Sumayfaʿ read *Allāh* in both. The meaning of *ilāh*: one who is worshipped by it (the prepositional phrase is attached), and the meaning: He is worshipped in the heaven and worshipped on the earth. The returning pronoun to the relative is omitted, its estimated form being: "He is a god," as is omitted in their saying: *mā anā bi-alladhī qā'ilun laka shay'an* ("I am not the one who says anything to you"). Its length was made acceptable by the conjunction following it, as the length of *qā'il* was made acceptable in *qā'il laka shay'an* by the operative element (*muʿawwal*). As for the one who reads *Allāh*, he likewise includes in it the meaning of "the one worshipped," as a proper noun is given the sense of an attribute in phrases such as "he is Ḥātim in Ṭayyiʾ," meaning "he is generous in Ṭayyiʾ." It is also permissible that the relative clause be the prepositional phrase, and the meaning: He is in both by divinity and lordship, since it is impossible to take it as "settled" (in the literal sense). In His saying "and in the earth," there is a negation of their deities which were worshipped on the earth.

﴿And with Him is the knowledge of the Hour﴾: that is, knowledge of the exact time of its establishment, which He, exalted is He, has kept exclusively to Himself. The majority read ﴿you will be returned﴾ (*yurjaʿūn*) with the third-person *yāʾ*, while Nafiʿ, ʿAsim, and the two Madanis (Abu Jaʿfar and Shayba) read it with the second-person *tāʾ* (*turjaʿūn*). In both readings it is passive. It was also read with a *fatḥa* on the second-person *tāʾ*, active. The majority read it with the third-person *yāʾ* and a shadda on the *dāl*, and from ʿAbdullah (or another, as recorded) with the second-person *tāʾ* and a shadda on the *dāl*. The meaning: "Those whom they invoke besides Him, their gods, do not possess intercession with Allah." Qatada said: He excepted from those worshipped besides Allah ʿIsa, ʿUzayr, and the angels, for they possess intercession, since Allah grants them that ability, as they are among those who testify to the truth and they know it through their conditions. So the exception on this reading is continuous (*muttaṣil*). Mujahid and others said: "From those for whom intercession is made?" As if He said: "These angels, ʿUzayr, and ʿIsa do not intercede except for one who testifies to the truth, and he knows it," i.e., the monotheism. They said: The exception on this reading is disjunctive (*munfaṣil*), as if He said: "But whoever testifies to the truth, these will intercede for him." This understanding they proposed may allow the exception to be continuous, since the thing excepted from would be omitted, as if He said: "Those who are invoked besides Him do not possess intercession for anyone, except for one who testifies to the truth," so it is an exception from the omitted object, as the poet said:

*Salim escaped, and the soul from him was by his jaw, and he did not escape except with the sheath of a sword and a loincloth.*

That is, "he was not saved except as the sheath of a sword," so it is an exception from the ones granted intercession (al-mashfu' fihim), in which the omission is permissible, and it is a *muttasil* (connected) exception (istithna' muttasil, "connected exception," where the excluded item belongs to the same category as what precedes it). If you take it as an exception from "those they call upon" (alladhina yad'una), it becomes a *munfasil* (disjunct) exception, and the meaning is: "their gods will not possess intercession," meaning the idols and images, as they claimed that they were their intercessors with God. "But whoever testified to the truth," which is the affirmation of God's oneness, "and they know what they testified to," is the one who possesses intercession. If the angels are included among "those they call upon," then it is a connected exception.

The majority read ﴿فَأَنَّى يُؤْفَكُونَ﴾ with the ya' of the third person (ya' al-ghayba), in agreement with His saying ﴿وَلَئِنْ سَأَلْتَهُمْ﴾, meaning: how are they turned away from worshipping the One whom they acknowledge as the creator of the world? 'Abd al-Warith, from Abu 'Amr, read it with the ta' of address (ta' al-khitab).

The majority read ﴿وَقِيلَهُ﴾ in the accusative (manṣūb). Al-Akhfash said it is coordinated with *sirrahum wa-najwahum* ("their secret and their private conference"). He also said it is coordinated with the verb of *qala* ("and he said"). Al-Zajjaj said it is coordinated with the position (mahall) of *al-sa'a* in His saying ﴿وَعِنْدَهُ عِلْمُ السَّاعَةِ﴾. It is also said that it is coordinated with the omitted object of *yaktubūn* (they record), meaning they record their words and their deeds. And it is said that it is coordinated with the object of *ya'lamūn* (they know), meaning they know the truth. ﴿وَقِيلَهُ يَا رَبِّ﴾ is a statement that is hardly intelligible. It is also said that it is in the accusative by an implied verb, meaning "and He knows his saying."

Al-Sulami, Ibn Wathhab, 'Asim, al-A'mash, and Hamzah read ﴿وَقِيلِهِ﴾ in the genitive (khafḍ). This is explained as coordination with *al-sa'a* (the Hour), or as the *waw* of oath (waw al-qasam), with the answer omitted, meaning: "they will surely be helped," or "I will surely do to them what I wish."

Al-A'raj, Abu Qilabah, Mujahid, al-Hasan, Qatadah, and Muslim ibn Jundab read ﴿وَقِيلُهُ﴾ in the nominative (raf'). This is explained as coordination with "knowledge of the Hour" (*'ilm al-sa'a*), with an omitted genitive-modifying noun (hadhf mudaf), meaning "and the knowledge of his saying," where the modified noun is omitted and the modifier (al-mudaf ilayhi) is put in its place. This was reported from al-Kisa'i. It is also explained as an inceptive (mubtada'), whose predicate is *ya rabbi innahum la yu'minun*, or as a predicate that is omitted, with the estimate being "heard" or "accepted." In that case the clause of the call and what follows it is in the accusative position by ﴿وَقِيلُهُ﴾.

Abu Qilabah read *ya rabba* with a fatha on the ba', intending *ya rabban*, as you say *ya ghulamu*. It may be explained according to al-Akhfash's permission: *ya qawma*, with a fatha and the deletion of the alif, with the fatha standing in for it.

Al-Zamakhshari said: "What they said, meaning the coordination, is not strong in meaning, together with the occurrence of a separation between the coordinated and the coordinated-to by something that does not fit well as a parenthetical insertion (i'tiraḍ), and with the disharmony of the composition. Stronger than that is that the genitive and the accusative should be by implying the particle of oath and omitting it, and the nominative should be like their saying: *aymunu Allah* ("by God's right"), *amanatu Allah* ("by God's trust"), *yamin Allah* ("God's oath"), *la'amruka* ("by your life"). And His saying ﴿إِنَّ هَؤُلَاءِ قَوْمٌ لَا يُؤْمِنُونَ﴾ would be the answer to the oath, as if He said: 'And He swore by his saying, or by his saying, "O Lord, my oath..."'"

﴿إِنَّ هَؤُلَاءِ قَوْمٌ لَا يُؤْمِنُونَ﴾ ("Indeed these are a people who will not believe"), and God's swearing by His saying, is an elevation of him and an honouring of his supplication and his appeal to Him. End of quotation. This is contrary to the apparent meaning of the speech, since it appears that His saying "O Lord, indeed these are a people who will not believe" is connected to *qilihi* ("his saying"). And from the speech of the one upon whom be peace: if *inna ha'ula'* is the answer to the oath, then it is from God's report about them and His speech. The pronoun in ﴿وَقِيلِهِ﴾ refers to the Messenger, who is addressed by His saying ﴿فَاصْفَحْ عَنْهُمْ﴾, meaning: turn away from them and leave them. ﴿وَقُلْ سَلَامٌ﴾, meaning: the matter is peace. ﴿فَسَوْفَ يَعْلَمُونَ﴾ is a threat and warning to them and an admonition, and it is abrogated (mansukh) by the verse of the sword (ayat al-sayf).

The majority read ﴿يَعْلَمُونَ﴾ with the ya' of the third person, as in ﴿فَاصْفَحْ عَنْهُمْ﴾. Abu Ja'far, al-Hasan, al-A'raj, Nafi', and Hisham read it with the ta' of address.

al-Suddi said: "*Wa-qul salam*" means "good," in exchange for their evil. Muqatil said: "Offer them kindness." al-Mawardi reported: "Say that by which you are safe from their evil."

**Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 43, verses 74–89 (part 1 of 2)**

﴿Indeed, the criminals will abide forever in the punishment of Hell.﴾ ﴿It will not be lightened for them, and they will be in despair therein.﴾ ﴿We did not wrong them, but they were the wrongdoers.﴾ ﴿And they will call, "O Malik, let your Lord put an end to us." He will say, "Indeed, you will remain."﴾ ﴿We have certainly brought you the truth, but most of you are averse to the truth.﴾ ﴿Or have they decided on a matter? Then, indeed, We are the decreers.﴾ ﴿Or do they think that We do not hear their secrets and their private talk? Yes, and Our messengers are with them, recording.﴾ ﴿Say, "If the Most Merciful had a son, then I would be the first of the worshippers."﴾ ﴿Glory be to the Lord of the heavens and the earth, the Lord of the Throne, above what they describe.﴾ ﴿So leave them to plunge in vain talk and play until they encounter their Day which they are promised.﴾ ﴿And He is the One who is God in the heaven and God on the earth, and He is the All-Wise, the All-Knowing.﴾ ﴿Blessed is He to whom belongs the dominion of the heavens and the earth and what is between them, and with Him is the knowledge of the Hour, and to Him you will be returned.﴾ ﴿Those whom they invoke besides Him do not possess intercession, except one who testifies to the truth while they know.﴾ ﴿And if you asked them who created them, they would surely say, "Allah." So how are they deluded?﴾ ﴿And [the Prophet's] saying, "O my Lord, indeed these are a people who do not believe."﴾ ﴿So turn away from them and say, "Peace." But they will soon know.﴾

When He, exalted is He, mentioned the state of the people of Paradise and the joyful tidings that are said to them, He followed that with mention of the state of the disbelievers and what they reply with when they are questioned. ʿAbdullah [ibn Masʿud] read *wa-hum fīhā* (in it), meaning in Hell, while the majority read *wa-hum fīhi* (in it), meaning in the punishment. It is reported from al-Ḍaḥḥāk: the criminal will be placed in a coffin of fire, then it will be sealed over him, and he will remain in it forever, seeing nothing and seen by no one.

﴿It will not be lightened for them﴾: that is, it will not be eased or reduced, from the expression *fatarat ʿanhu al-ḥummā* ("the fever subsided from him"), when it calmed a little and its heat decreased. *Al-mubliss* is the one who is silent and despairing of good.

﴿(And We did not wrong them)﴾: that is, We did not place the punishment upon one who does not deserve it.

﴿But they were the wrongdoers﴾: that is, those who placed disbelief in the place of faith, and by that they wronged themselves. The majority read *al-ẓālimīna* (the wrongdoers) in the accusative, treating *hum* as a *faṣl* (a separating pronoun, i.e., a particle of separation between subject and predicate, "they" here being not a subject but an intervening element). ʿAbdullah and the two grammarians Abu Zayd read *al-ẓālimūna* in the nominative, treating *hum* as the subject (*mubtada'*, the topic) and the following as its predicate (*khabar*). Abu ʿAmr al-Jarmi mentioned that the dialect of Tamim is to make what is a *faṣl* for others a subject (*mubtada'*), and to put the following in the nominative as the predicate. Abu Zayd said: "I heard them reading: *tajidūhu ʿinda Allāhi huwa khayrun wa-aʿẓamu ajran*," meaning with the nominative on *khayrun wa-aʿẓamu*. Qays ibn Dhurayj said:

*We yearn for Layla while you have left her, and you were over her in gatherings, you are more capable.*

Sibawayh said: Ruʾba used to say: "I think Zayd is he is better than you," meaning with the nominative.

﴿And they will call, "O Malik"﴾: it has already been stated that they are *mubliṣūn*, that is, silent. These are their states at different, extended times, so there is no contradiction between their silence and their calling out. The majority read *yā mālik*. ʿAbdullah, ʿAli, Ibn Wathhab, and al-Aʿmash read *yā māl*, by apocope (*tarkhīm*, the clipping of the end of a vocative), according to the dialect of the one who awaits the (remaining) letter. Abu al-Sirar al-Ghanawi read *yā mālu*, with a *ḍamma* as a built form, making it a name in its own right. The *lām* in *li-yaqḍi* is the *lām* of request and desire. The meaning: "Let Him cause us to die once, so that our punishment does not repeat," like His saying: ﴿So Moses struck him and ended his life﴾ [al-Qasas 28:15], that is, caused him to die.

﴿(He said)﴾: that is, Malik. ﴿Indeed, you will remain﴾: that is, you will stay in the Fire and will not depart from it. Ibn ʿAbbas said: he answers them after a thousand years had passed; Nawf said: after a hundred; it was said: eighty; and ʿAbdullah ibn ʿAmr said: forty.

﴿We have certainly brought you the truth﴾: it appears that this is the speech of Allah, exalted is He. It was also said: it is the speech of some of the angels, as one of a leader's servants says: "We informed you and we did such-and-such to you." It was said: it is possible that ﴿We have certainly brought you﴾ is the speech of Allah to the Quraysh, following the narration of the disbelievers' exchange with Malik, and in this there is a warning and intimidation, meaning: "Look at how your condition will be."

﴿Or have they decided a matter?﴾: the pronoun refers to the Quraysh, that is, "rather, they have firmly determined a matter of their scheming against the Messenger and their plotting," ﴿then, indeed, We are the decreers﴾, that is, of Our scheme, just as they decided their scheme, like His saying: ﴿Or do they intend a scheme? But those who disbelieve, they are the ones who will be ensnared﴾ [al-Tur 52:42]. They used to confer secretly and hasten among themselves regarding the matter of the Messenger, so He, exalted is He, said: ﴿Or do they think that We do not hear their secrets﴾, which is what a man speaks to himself or to another in an empty place. ﴿And their private talk﴾: which is what they speak among themselves. ﴿Yes﴾: that is, We hear it. ﴿Our messengers﴾: and they are the recording angels.

﴿Say, "If the Most Merciful had a son"﴾, as you say, ﴿then I would be the first﴾ to worship Him on that basis, but there is no such thing for Him. Al-Zamakhshari took up this statement and admired it for its eloquence, saying: "If the Most Merciful had a son, and that were established and proven by a sound proof they put forward and a clear argument they offered, then I would be the first to glorify that son and the quickest of you to obey Him and submit to Him, just as a man honors the son of a king because of his father's greatness." This is a statement given in the manner of supposition and illustration for a purpose, which is the emphasis in negating a son and dwelling at length upon it, so that the speaker leaves no doubt except one that is dissolved, together with expressing firmness of foot in the domain of monotheism. For he linked worship to the existence of a son, which is impossible in itself, so what was linked to it was likewise impossible. Thus it is in the form of affirming existence and worship, and in meaning it negates them in the most eloquent and forceful ways. Then al-Zamakhshari said: "Its parallel is that a Qadarite (*ʿadlī*) says to a Jabrite (*mujbir*)" — then he mentioned a statement that deserves disciplining, even the sword; I have exempted my book from mentioning it. Then he said: "People have strained themselves with what they brought out from this noble style, full of subtleties and benefits that stand independently for monotheism in its most eloquent aspects." It was said: "If the Most Merciful had a son, according to your claim, then I would be the first of the monotheists, the ones who worship Allah and deny their statement of ascribing a son to Him." It was also said: "If the Most Merciful had a son, then I would be the first of the *āniftīn* (those who are disdainful), from having a son for Him from a servant who is worshipped, for when his disdain is intense, he is a servant and a worshipper." Some read *ʿabidīn* (with a different vowel pattern). It was also said: the *in* here is negating, meaning: "Allah did not have a son, so I am the first to say this, to worship and to affirm His oneness."

It is related that al-Naḍr ibn ʿAbd al-Dar ibn Qusayy said: "The angels are the daughters of Allah." So this verse was revealed, and al-Naḍr said: "Do you not see that He has confirmed me?" Al-Walid ibn al-Mughira said to him: "He did not confirm you; rather He said: *If the Most Merciful had a son*, then I would be the first of the monotheists of Mecca to affirm that He has no son." End of quotation.

As for the view that *in* means "if, according to your claim," it is the statement of Mujahid. As for the statement "then I would be the first of the *āniftīn*," it is the statement of a group, which Abu Hatim related from them without naming any of them. This is supported by the reading of al-Sulami and al-Yamani: *al-ʿabidīn*. And a reading mentioned by al-Khalil ibn Ahmad in his book *al-ʿAyn* is *al-ʿabdīn*, with the *bāʾ* sunnah (the vowel is sukūn), a lightened form of *al-ʿabidīn* with *kasra*. The author of *al-Lawāmiḥ* mentioned that it was transmitted from Ibn ʿAbbas regarding the meaning of *ʿābidīn* that it means *āniftīn*. Ibn ʿArafa said: it is said *ʿabada yaʿbudu, fa-huwa ʿabd*, and rarely is it said *ʿābid*. The Qur'an does not come with the rare or the anomalous in language. Then he said: "like the statement of Mujahid." Al-Farazdaq said:

*Those are my fathers, so bring me the like of them, and I disdain (aʿbud) to satirize Kulayb in my own tribe.*

That is: I am disdainful (*ānif*) and I refuse. Another said:

*Whenever the one who has affection wills, he cuts off his friend, and he disdains (yaʿbud) over him, undoubtedly, in injustice.*

As for the view that *in* is negating, it is related from Ibn ʿAbbas, al-Hasan, al-Suddi, Qatada, Ibn Zayd, and Zuhayr ibn Muhammad. Makki said: it is not permissible for *in* to mean *mā* (negating), because that implies that you negated a son from Allah only in the past and not in the future, and this is impossible. End of quotation. But nothing impossible follows from it, because *kāna* may be used for what endures and does not cease, as in your saying: *(wa-kāna Allāhu ghafūran raḥīman)* ("and Allah was Forgiving, Merciful"), meaning: He has not ceased to be so. So the meaning is: "what was and what will be." Abu Hatim said: *al-ʿabid*, with the *kasra* on the *bāʾ*, means one who is very angry. Abu ʿUbayda said: its meaning is "the first of the deniers," and the Arabs say *ʿabadanī ḥaqqī*, meaning "my right denied me." Some read *waladun* with two *fatḥas*; ʿAbdullah, Ibn Wathhab, Talha, and al-Aʿmash read it with a *ḍamma* on the *wāw* and sukūn on the *lām*.

Then He said: ﴿Glory be to the Lord of the heavens and the earth, the Lord of the Throne, above what they describe﴾, that is, above attributing a son to Him. The meaning: removal of knowledge must be necessary existence, and whatever is so is a single absolute being that does not accept division. A son (*walad*) is an expression for a part of a thing separating from it so that a person like it is produced from it, and this occurs only in what is by its nature capable of division, and this is impossible with respect to Him, exalted is He, so the affirmation of a son is precluded. When this decisive proof was mentioned, He said: ﴿So leave them to plunge﴾, that is, into their falsehood, ﴿and play﴾, that is, in their worldly life. The apparent sense of these two commands is a truce and abandonment, and this is among what was abrogated (*nusikha*, i.e., superseded by a later ruling) by the verse of the sword. The majority read ﴿until they encounter﴾ (*yulāqū*), while Abu Jaʿfar, Ibn Muhaysin, ʿUbayd ibn ʿAqil, and from Abu ʿAmr read *yalqawā*, the imperfect of *laqiya*.

﴿Their Day which they are promised﴾: the Day of Resurrection. ʿIkrima and others said: the Day of Badr. He attributed the day to them, because it is the one in which their destruction and punishment occur. The majority read ﴿God (*ilāh*) in both﴾. ʿUmar, ʿAbdullah, Ubayy, ʿAli, al-Ḥakam ibn Abi al-ʿAliya, Bilal ibn Abi Burda, Ibn Yaʿmar, Jabir, Ibn Zayd, ʿUmar ibn ʿAbd al-ʿAziz, Abu al-Shaykh al-Hunaʾi, Humayd, Ibn Miqsam, and Ibn al-Sumayfaʿ read *Allāh* in both. The meaning of *ilāh*: one who is worshipped by it (the prepositional phrase is attached), and the meaning: He is worshipped in the heaven and worshipped on the earth. The returning pronoun to the relative is omitted, its estimated form being: "He is a god," as is omitted in their saying: *mā anā bi-alladhī qā'ilun laka shay'an* ("I am not the one who says anything to you"). Its length was made acceptable by the conjunction following it, as the length of *qā'il* was made acceptable in *qā'il laka shay'an* by the operative element (*muʿawwal*). As for the one who reads *Allāh*, he likewise includes in it the meaning of "the one worshipped," as a proper noun is given the sense of an attribute in phrases such as "he is Ḥātim in Ṭayyiʾ," meaning "he is generous in Ṭayyiʾ." It is also permissible that the relative clause be the prepositional phrase, and the meaning: He is in both by divinity and lordship, since it is impossible to take it as "settled" (in the literal sense). In His saying "and in the earth," there is a negation of their deities which were worshipped on the earth.

﴿And with Him is the knowledge of the Hour﴾: that is, knowledge of the exact time of its establishment, which He, exalted is He, has kept exclusively to Himself. The majority read ﴿you will be returned﴾ (*yurjaʿūn*) with the third-person *yāʾ*, while Nafiʿ, ʿAsim, and the two Madanis (Abu Jaʿfar and Shayba) read it with the second-person *tāʾ* (*turjaʿūn*). In both readings it is passive. It was also read with a *fatḥa* on the second-person *tāʾ*, active. The majority read it with the third-person *yāʾ* and a shadda on the *dāl*, and from ʿAbdullah (or another, as recorded) with the second-person *tāʾ* and a shadda on the *dāl*. The meaning: "Those whom they invoke besides Him, their gods, do not possess intercession with Allah." Qatada said: He excepted from those worshipped besides Allah ʿIsa, ʿUzayr, and the angels, for they possess intercession, since Allah grants them that ability, as they are among those who testify to the truth and they know it through their conditions. So the exception on this reading is continuous (*muttaṣil*). Mujahid and others said: "From those for whom intercession is made?" As if He said: "These angels, ʿUzayr, and ʿIsa do not intercede except for one who testifies to the truth, and he knows it," i.e., the monotheism. They said: The exception on this reading is disjunctive (*munfaṣil*), as if He said: "But whoever testifies to the truth, these will intercede for him." This understanding they proposed may allow the exception to be continuous, since the thing excepted from would be omitted, as if He said: "Those who are invoked besides Him do not possess intercession for anyone, except for one who testifies to the truth," so it is an exception from the omitted object, as the poet said:

*Salim escaped, and the soul from him was by his jaw, and he did not escape except with the sheath of a sword and a loincloth.*

That is, "he was not saved except as the sheath of a sword," so it is an exception from the ones granted intercession (al-mashfu' fihim), in which the omission is permissible, and it is a *muttasil* (connected) exception (istithna' muttasil, "connected exception," where the excluded item belongs to the same category as what precedes it). If you take it as an exception from "those they call upon" (alladhina yad'una), it becomes a *munfasil* (disjunct) exception, and the meaning is: "their gods will not possess intercession," meaning the idols and images, as they claimed that they were their intercessors with God. "But whoever testified to the truth," which is the affirmation of God's oneness, "and they know what they testified to," is the one who possesses intercession. If the angels are included among "those they call upon," then it is a connected exception.

The majority read ﴿فَأَنَّى يُؤْفَكُونَ﴾ with the ya' of the third person (ya' al-ghayba), in agreement with His saying ﴿وَلَئِنْ سَأَلْتَهُمْ﴾, meaning: how are they turned away from worshipping the One whom they acknowledge as the creator of the world? 'Abd al-Warith, from Abu 'Amr, read it with the ta' of address (ta' al-khitab).

The majority read ﴿وَقِيلَهُ﴾ in the accusative (manṣūb). Al-Akhfash said it is coordinated with *sirrahum wa-najwahum* ("their secret and their private conference"). He also said it is coordinated with the verb of *qala* ("and he said"). Al-Zajjaj said it is coordinated with the position (mahall) of *al-sa'a* in His saying ﴿وَعِنْدَهُ عِلْمُ السَّاعَةِ﴾. It is also said that it is coordinated with the omitted object of *yaktubūn* (they record), meaning they record their words and their deeds. And it is said that it is coordinated with the object of *ya'lamūn* (they know), meaning they know the truth. ﴿وَقِيلَهُ يَا رَبِّ﴾ is a statement that is hardly intelligible. It is also said that it is in the accusative by an implied verb, meaning "and He knows his saying."

Al-Sulami, Ibn Wathhab, 'Asim, al-A'mash, and Hamzah read ﴿وَقِيلِهِ﴾ in the genitive (khafḍ). This is explained as coordination with *al-sa'a* (the Hour), or as the *waw* of oath (waw al-qasam), with the answer omitted, meaning: "they will surely be helped," or "I will surely do to them what I wish."

Al-A'raj, Abu Qilabah, Mujahid, al-Hasan, Qatadah, and Muslim ibn Jundab read ﴿وَقِيلُهُ﴾ in the nominative (raf').
